The provided table is not a conventional multi-column data table; it is an excerpt formatted as a hierarchical **contents index** (table of contents) from the SOFiSTiK documentation: **“SOFiLOAD Loads and Load Functions”**, **Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146** (copyright 2025, SOFiSTiK AG). The “table” therefore functions as a structured **navigation mapping** of program modules/topics to their corresponding **page numbers**. This makes it highly relevant for RAG retrieval because it tells you where specific functionalities are documented.

### Structure and elements
1. **Document header/context**
   - Title: *SOFiLOAD Loads and Load Functions*
   - Metadata: *Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146*
   - Copyright and publisher information: SOFiSTiK AG, Nuremberg, Germany, including contact details.
   - Legal notes about copyright, modification rights, and user responsibility.

2. **Hierarchical contents layout**
   - The contents are organized by **main sections** and **subsections**, using numeric dotted identifiers (e.g., **3.20.1**, **4.2.12**, **5.5.5**).
   - Each entry appears as: **Section/Topic title … Page number** (often with leader dots).

3. **Key topic grouping (Loads and Input Description)**
   - The excerpt includes especially detailed coverage for **Section 3: Input Description** (pages around 3-1 to 3-81).
   - Prominent record types/modules include:
     - **GRP** (groups), **ACT** (action), **LC** (load case)
     - **NODE** (nodal loads), **CABL** (cable loading), **TRUS** (truss element loading)
     - Beam-related entries: **BEAM**, **BEPL**, **BEAM**/distributed beam, point beam
     - Element/loading definitions: **QUAD**, **BRIC**, **COPY**, **Free Loading** modules (**POIN**, **LINE,CURV**, **AREA**, **VOLU**, etc.)
     - Special utilities: **GUID**, **EXPO**, **EVAL**, **CTRL**, **ECHO**
   - Also included are subsection pages on evaluations such as:
     - **Eigen Stress and Equivalent Linear Temperature Load**
     - **Spectral densities of loadings**

4. **Additional major sections referenced**
   - **Dynamic Loads** (Section 4), with subsections like:
     - **Pushover Analysis – Theoretical Background**
     - **RESP – Response Spectrum**
     - Reference codes and building/spectral content (Eurocode EC8, UBC/IBC, EN 1998-1, SIA, ÖNORM, NTC, EAK, SNiP, etc.)
   - **Train Loading** (Section 5), including:
     - **GAX**, **LANE**, and especially **TRAI – Load Train Definition**
     - Subtopics on **Impact Factor**, **Centrifugal Forces**, and multiple standards (Eurocode, SLW/LKW, BS, IS, AASHTO, etc.)
   - The excerpt also shows references to other parts (Wind/Wave/Snow/Load Take Down), but without the full granular list for those sections.

### Semantics for RAG
Each row/entry corresponds to a **retrievable query target**: “What is module X and where is it documented (page Y)?” The table therefore acts as an index linking **SOFiLOAD command/feature names** (e.g., *LC, NODE, BEAM, WAVE, RESP, TRAI*) to their **documentation location** (page numbers).

The provided table content is not a conventional data matrix; it is a *table of contents index* from the **SOFiLOAD** manual (“SOFiLOAD Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146”, © 2025 SOFiSTiK AG). The “table” effectively lists **section numbers, topic headings, and page references**. This structure is useful for RAG because it encodes where specific loading-related functions are documented.

### Overall structure
- **Columns (implied):**
  1. **Section/Subsection identifier** (e.g., “3.20 VOLU”, “7.5 WAVE – Wave”)
  2. **Topic title / command or module name** (e.g., “NODE – Nodal Loads”, “CTRL – Optional Control Values”)
  3. **Page number reference** (e.g., “3-19”, “7-12”, “10-5”)
- **Rows (implied):** each line corresponds to one documented item (command, concept, or subsection), sometimes including nested subsection numbers (e.g., “3.23.1 Eigen Stress…”).

### Content domain
The headings cluster into major manual parts related to **loading definitions and load processing** in SOFiSTiK:
- **Input description section (Part 3):** covers the input language and a large catalog of load definitions and record types such as:
  - “GRP – Selection and Properties of Groups”
  - “ACT – Definition of an Action”
  - “LC – Definition of a Load Case”
  - “NODE – Nodal Loads”, “CABL – Cable Loading”, “TRUS – Truss Element Loading”
  - Beam/element loading variants: “BEAM – Distributed Beam Loading”, “BEPL – Point Beam Loading”, “QUAD – Element Loading”, “BRIC – Element Loading”
  - Higher-level utilities: “COPY – Loads from Other Sources”, “Free Loading” constructs (“Poin”, “LINE,CURV”, “AREA”, “VOLU”), “LAR – Load Distribution Areas”, “GUID – Globally Unique Identifier”
  - Management/output: “EXPO – Export of Load Cases”, “EVAL – Evaluations” with subtopics like “Eigen Stress and Equivalent Linear Temperature Load” and “Spectral densities of loadings”
  - Formatting/control: “CTRL – Optional Control Values”, “ECHO – Printout Options”
- **Dynamic/Wind/Wave/Snow and load take-down (parts 4–9):**
  - “Dynamic Loads” appears as a major topic.
  - “Wind Loading”, “Wave Loading” including “Irregular Waves” and “WAVE – Wave”.
  - “Snow Loads”.
  - “Load Take Down” with “Source – Target Assignment” and assignment modes (“1:1 Assignment”, “N:M Assignment”, automatic target selection, and correction/generation subsections).
- **Output description (Part 10):** summarizes produced/checked outputs:
  - “Check List of Actions”, “Check List of Load Case Selection”
  - “Meshfree Loading”, “Nodal Loads”, “QUAD Element Loads”, “BRIC Element Loads”
  - “Beam Loads”, “Truss and Cable Loads”
  - “Accelerations”, “Wind Loading”, “Load and Time Function”
  - “Export of Load Cases”, and “Load Combinations”

### Notable features for indexing
- **Command-like identifiers** (e.g., NODE, BEAM, WAVE, VOLU, LC, ACT) recur throughout, indicating that the manual documents specific *record types* or *load generators*.
- Some lines contain **nested subsections** (e.g., 3.23.1, 3.23.2), which implies more granular content under the “EVAL – Evaluations” topic.
- The bottom portion shows **subtopics under Load Take Down** (“All Loads – Corrections”, “Load Transfer Functions”, “Modes for Target Geometries”, “LTD – Load Take Down”, “LTDG – ... Geometry Generation”), again with page spans.

### RAG relevance
This “table” is effectively a **routing map**: given a query like “how to define WAVE” or “how to perform Load Take Down (N:M assignment)”, the entry provides the **exact manual section name and approximate page**, enabling retrieval or citation of the correct documentation passages.

 SOFiLOAD generates loading for all SOFiSTiK-Modules.
 Loads are organized in load cases, which are members of a unique action. Load cases are addressed via a number, while the action is designated by up to 4 characters, 48 combinations have been reserved for designated types of actions.
 The combination of the load cases within the actions may be done in a very general way, there are however three predefined combination methods: permanent, optional, exclusive.
 The final combination of the actions is then done within MAXIMA or AQB via combination coefficients (ψ) and safety factors (γ), which may vary in there value from load case to load case, but will be always applied with the same kind of factor.
 The loads can be defined independently of a FEM-mesh. SOFiLOAD will handle the transition from the geometric model to the analysis model by converting general loading patterns to more specific nodal or elemental loads. The user may influence the conversion process if needed.
 The loads are either already in the database or may be defined via SOFiLOAD. If the element mesh is changed, SOFiLOAD has to repeat the elemental assignment. Beside that you may specify nodal or elemental loads directly as known from other finite element systems. Those loads will be deleted however if the element mesh is changed or explicit redefinition of a load case takes place.
 Record names and items have been change compared to former definitions in SOFiSTiK to become more simple and unified. Thus it is not possible in general to copy old CADINP-data, but the export-function may be helpful in many cases. All input load values will be converted according to the units defined in SOFiSTiK. DIM.
 There are also possibilities to generate loads from results in the database. These are especially support forces converted to loads, imperfections, creep deformations or prestressing effects.
 As an special extension we have provided or intended load generators to deal with the rather complex loading of load trains on bridges, earth quake, wind and snow on the structure with very extended features. These options are not part of the basic program version however.

These are especially support forces converted to loads, imperfections, creep deformations or prestressing effects.. These options are not part of the basic program version however..
 This manual starts with the simple nodal and elemental loads, will then cover the geometric load definitions and finally come to the more complex load generators.

The image is a schematic comparison titled **“Figure 2.1: Equivalent nodal loads for mesh refinement.”** It is divided into **two main columns**: a **left column** with a simplified depiction of a distributed load and a **right column** showing how that load is represented as **equivalent nodal loads** after discretization. The overall focus is on how changing **mesh density** alters the nodal-load pattern that an FE model produces.

### Left side (distributed load shown as continuous pressure)
Across the left column, there are **three stacked horizontal bands** representing the same structural region under a **distributed downward load**. In each band, multiple **short downward arrows** depict the load distributed over a span.  
- In the **upper-left group**, there are **fewer arrows**, meaning a **coarser mesh resolution** for the load representation.  
- In the **middle-left group**, the number of arrows increases, suggesting a **finer mesh**.  
- In the **lower-left group**, there are **even more arrows**, indicating further mesh refinement.  
Beneath each group, there are **long horizontal lines** that represent element/mesh lines (or nodal rows) to show where the distributed load would be sampled in the FE discretization. The magnitude is implied by arrow length, but the key visual change is the **number and placement** of load contributions as the “mesh” gets finer.

### Right side (equivalent nodal loads at nodes)
The right column has a matching three-row structure, but instead of many arrows, it shows a **grid-like set of nodes** represented by small **circle symbols** positioned along vertical and horizontal lines.  
- In the **top-right**, several nodes receive **downward concentrated arrows**, indicating **nodal forces** derived from the original distributed loading.  
- In the **middle-right**, the arrows shift/redistribute to additional nodes as mesh refinement increases.  
- In the **bottom-right**, the nodal pattern becomes **more finely resolved**, with forces applied to a greater number of nodes.  
Notably, some nodes show **no load** (empty circles), while others have downward arrows. This emphasizes that the FE system can only apply load through **nodal force equivalence**, not as a true continuous point/moment in the physical sense.

### Meaning conveyed
Overall, the diagram illustrates that as the **mesh is refined**, the FE model generates **different nodal load patterns** for a **distributed load** (since the distributed load is “projected” onto discrete nodes). However, the underlying equivalence remains tied to the discretization: the load representation’s accuracy depends on whether the mesh can resolve the load region. This aligns with the accompanying text explaining that nodal loads from tools like SOFiLOAD are only as accurate as the given FE mesh, and that representing loads correctly may require using distributed loads or refining the mesh near load application.

The Finite Element system is a discrete system and is therefore only enabled to treat with equivalent nodal load contributions, not with real point loads or moments. The difference of the two meanings can be seen in Figure 2.1.
 When the mesh density is increased, you will have different load patterns for a distributed load, but the same for a point load. This indicates also that a given mesh has a distinct resolution for load distributions. The coarser mesh can not distinguish between two point loads, a distributed load or a point load between the nodes.
 On the other side this states that a load may be specified as a single nodal load only if the size of load is less than the element mesh size. If you refine the mesh near that load point you will get higher and higher stresses or forces, as the finite elements will approximate you infinite solution better and better. So you choose either a mesh size not smaller than the minimum load distribution area (thickness for plates for example) or you have to specify the loads as distributed loads.
 From that we conlude further, that the generated nodal loads by SOFiLOAD may be only as accurate as the given Finite Element mesh.
 For beam loading we have the special case, that loading is also defined within the element having an effect on all internal forces. But we have to distinguish between a standard FE- Beam-Element having only cubic displacement functions and a more generalized Beam Ele- ment according to the Transfer-Method. The first will require a finer mesh to model complex loading accurately, the latter may have restrictions on the modelling of the stiffness. (Piece- wise constant in STAR2 e.g).

For springs, cables and trusses you may specify in SOFiMSHA a constant value of prestress, acting in any load case. For cables and trusses you may also define a load case dependant prestress. Any type of prestress will introduce like a thermal expansion strains acting on the element.
 Cables and trusses will be prestresses by some external influence. For fixed ends these strains will introduce the prestress, for flexible supports you will get deformations diminishing your given prestress. If you want to achieve a given value of prestress you have to define external loading or use an element with low stiffness and the given prestress.
 For beams, by contrast, prestress is defined as an equilibrium state of stress (prestressed concrete via tendons). Thus we have an additional component to consider. Since the prestress is imposed on the element itself, the resulting forces on freely deformable beams are the input prestress forces themselves. If the deformation is constraint however, constraining forces arise. In the limiting case, e.g. if a beam is not allowed to deform at all the resultant force is zero, because the forces imposed by the prestress are beared by the support instead of the beam.
 For beams you may specify a statically determinate part of the prestress by the tendon force and its eccentricity and inclination. The distribution along the axis is linear for the stress, but cubically for the eccentricity. The effect of the prestress has to aspects. First we have the additional forces within a section, second we have deformations, introducing new forces if constraints exist.
 Due to the shear forces it is strongly recommended not to combine different tendons in a single one if the eccentricity is not the same.

The input occurs in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ”FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”).
 Input is defined within blocks of CADINP-Input language, separated by the record name END. Within each block, values to CTRL and ECHO will be active for the total block, while all other values cover only the current load case.
 There are the following possibilities:
 • Only definition of LC with a number Will print all loads of that load case.
 • Definition of LC with parameters but without any loading Will change those parameters and redistribute all global loading to a the current mesh.
 Input of LC with loads

 The load case is redefined, deleting all old data.
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The input table is a schema/metadata definition for multiple “Record” types. It has two major columns: **Record** (a compact identifier for the record category) and **Items** (a list of field names/parameters that appear in that record, describing expected attributes and their roles). Many fields are shown multiple times across different record types, indicating they are reused in a structured file format. The overall purpose appears to be documenting the allowable keys and their grouping for geometry/structural modeling data (e.g., nodes, members, coordinate references).

## Table structure
- **Column 1: Record**  
  Contains record names such as **GRP, ACT, LC, NODE, CABLE, TRUS, BEAM, BEPL, QUAD, BRIC, COPY, LAR, POIN, LINECURV** (some are shown with icons in the left margin).
- **Column 2: Items**  
  Lists the “fields” (parameters) associated with each record. Fields are mostly short tokens (e.g., **NO, TYPE, FROM, TO, INC, TITLE/ TITL/ NO/ PROJ/ WIDE/ REF**), sometimes repeated as alternatives.

## Record definitions (field-level description)
### GRP / ACT / LC (top block)
These records define selection or mapping constructs:
- **GRP** includes **NO, VAL, CS, WIND, CW, CFR** plus a **TYPE** family and multiple PS* and PSI* fields (**PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PSI3** etc.), suggesting piecewise thresholds or constraints.
- **ACT** includes items like **TYPE, GAMU, GAMA, PART, SUP, TITLE (TITL), CRI1/CRI2/CRI3**, along with **FACT/FACD**, **DLX/DLY/D LZ**, and repeated sets of parameters (GAMF, PIS0/PSI1/PSI2/PSI3).
- **LC** appears as another selection/location-like record containing repeated **NO/TYPE/FACT/FACD** and coordinate/offset fields (**DLX/DLY/DLZ**), plus **TITL**.

### NODE
Defines node-related entries with:
- **NO**, **TYPE** and point parameters **P, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7**
- Coordinate/reference triplets like **EXX/EYY/EZZ** and related parameters (**FRAD, FRA?**).

### CABLE, TRUS, BEAM
All three share a similar connectivity/endpoint pattern:
- **FROM, TO, INC** (increment or interpolation control)
- **TYPE** for segment or element type
- **PA/PE** and coordinate endpoint modifiers (**A, REF**)
- In some cases it includes **L, EYA/EZA/EYE/EZE**, plus **REF**.

### BEPL
A beam/plate-like record with:
- **FROM, TO, INC, TYPE, P**
- **A** and coordinate bounds **EY/EZ**
- **REF** and **REFT** and **OPT** (optional parameterization)

### QUAD
A quadrilateral or 4-point element definition:
- **FROM, TO, INC, TYPE, P**
- Direction/placement axes: **X, Y, Z**
- **DPX/DPY/DPZ** offsets and **NTYP/VTYP** type selectors.

### BRIC
A “brick”/hexahedral-like record:
- Similar to QUAD but with **FROM/TO/INC/TYPE/P/X/Y** and **Z**
- Also uses **DPX/DPY/DPZ** and **NTYP/VTYP**.

### COPY
A generic copy/transform record:
- **NO, FACT, TYPE, FROM, TO, INC, REF**
- Optional translation/scale items: **DX, DY, DZ, ALPH** (alpha rotation/angle)
- **WIDE** and **YEX** fields (suggesting width and extended coordinate mapping).

### LAR
A local/arrayed/parametric arrangement record:
- **NO**, and parameters **NAR, GRP, GRP1/GRP2/GRP3**
- Includes indices **T, N, M** and coordinate mapping **X1/Y1/Z1, X2/Y2/Z2, X3/Y3/Z3, X4/Z4**
- Appears to define multiple groupings/instances.

### POIN and LINECURV
Two geometry point/curve reference records:
- **POIN**: **REF, NO, TITL, PROJ, WIDE, NREF, TYPE** and position components **P, X, Y, Z**.
- **LINECURV**: **REF, NO, TITL, PROJ, WIDE, NREF, TYPE** with additional curve control points like **P1, X1, Y1, Z1, P2, X2, …** (and continues beyond the visible row with ellipsis).

The table is a configuration/specification record that defines how structural elements are grouped and how different environmental load types (wind and wave) are generated and/or restricted. It lists five main parameter items (“NO”, “VAL”, “CS”, “WIND”, “CW”, “CFR”, “WAVE”) with corresponding descriptions, unit types, and default behaviors.

**NO (Group number)**  
- **Meaning:** Identifier of a group used to select elements for which loading options may apply.  
- **Unit:** “—” (categorical).  
- **Default:** “—” (no specific default shown; likely must be provided).  

**VAL (Value of selection)**  
Controls how the group is applied and whether the program should output information.  
- **OFF:** “do not use group” (group selection disabled).  
- **YES:** “use without printout” (group influences element selection silently).  
- **FULL:** “use and print” (group influences selection with additional reporting).  
- **Unit:** “LIT” (enumerated literal).  
- **Default:** “FULL” (group is applied with printing if not overridden).

**CS (Construction stage for sections)**  
- **Meaning:** Selects or ties the group-related behavior to a construction stage affecting the available/active cross sections. This allows different loads to be computed for elements whose sections/cross-sections vary by construction phase.  
- **Unit:** “—”.  
- **Default:** “—”.

**WIND (Option for wind loading)**  
Defines whether wind loads are computed and how the wind loading parameters are interpreted.  
- **NONE:** no wind loads generated.  
- **MEAN:** uses mean reference values for wind generation mode **WGEN**.  
- **GUST:** uses direct equivalent static loading for gust effects.  
- **INFL:** uses an inflow boundary condition for **DOLFYN**.  
- **SHOW:** visualization of wind loading on the surface (for inspection rather than analysis load application).  
- **Unit:** “LIT”.  
- **Default:** “MEAN”.

**CW (Factor for wind pressure coefficients)**  
- **Meaning:** Global multiplier for wind pressure coefficients. These pressure coefficients are defined for different element types:  
  - **Plane elements:** coefficients via record name **QUAD**  
  - **Beam elements:** coefficients defined with their sections  
  Additionally, reduction factors **ψ** can be part of wind pressure coefficient definitions (e.g., chimneys as a function of total height).  
- **Unit:** “—”.  
- **Default:** “—” (not numerically specified in the table).  
- **Context tie-in:** The provided notes clarify that CW is a global factor scaling the already-defined coefficients.

**CFR (Factor for wind pressure for frictional parts)**  
- **Meaning:** Sets or scales frictional coefficients (relevant to frictional wind actions) following **EC 1 Part 2-4, Table 10.13.1**.  
- **Friction coefficient mapping (from context):**  
  - Surface smooth (e.g., steel, smooth concrete): **cfr = 0.01**  
  - Rough (e.g., rough concrete, tar roofs): **cfr = 0.02**  
  - Very rough (e.g., corrugated/ripped/folded surfaces): **cfr = 0.04**  
- **Unit:** “—”.  
- **Default:** “—”.

**WAVE (Option for wave loading)**  
Controls whether wave loading is included and whether it is applied or visualized.  
- **NONE:** no wave loading.  
- **LOAD:** apply wave loading.  
- **SHOW:** visualization of surface for wave-related load behavior.  
- **Unit:** “LIT”.  
- **Default:** “LOAD”.

Overall, this table acts as a compact “policy” for loading generation: it decides **which elements are affected by group selection (NO/VAL)** and **how environmental loads are computed (WIND/CW/CFR/WAVE)**, with **CS** linking behavior to **construction stages**. The accompanying context also notes that, without explicit selection, all elements are used; and that group selection can be ignored if free defined loadings are applied based on structural element types (SLN, SAR, LAR and AUTO on them), making this group selection primarily relevant when geometric selection alone is insufficient.

sections: 3.3 GRP – Selection and Properties of Groups

content:
GRP
 Without specification all elements will be used. If defining values only the selected groups will be used for the elemental loads of the following load cases. Group selections will be ignored, if a free defined loading is applied based on structural elements (SLN, SAR, LAR as well as AUTO on these) Thus this selection will be needed only for those cases where the geometric selection is not sufficient.
 The selection of groups may be different for different load cases. For very complex load pat- terns you may generate the loading within several load cases and combine them then via the command COPY to a single load case.
 The value CW defines a global factor to the wind pressure coefficients. The pressure coeffi- cients are defined for plane elements via the record name QUAD, for beam elements they are defined with the sections. Reduction factors ψ are f.e. defined for chimneys as a function of the total height.
 The value CFR defines the frictional coefficients cfr according Table 10.13.1. of EC 1 part 2-4:
 Surface smooth (e.g. Steel, smooth concrete) 0.01 rough (e.g. rough concrete, tar roofs) 0.02 very rough (e.g. corrugated, ripped, folded) 0.04
 Frictional value cfr
 With CS you may select between different variants of cross sections defined in AQUA with different wind loading areas and roughness values.

The table defines the schema and defaulting rules for an “action” record used in the structural verification workflow (SOFiLOAD / SOFi-PLUS / MAXIMA). It specifies each input item (columns “Item”, “Description”, “Unit”, “Default”) and clarifies what the item means, which regulatory action type it represents, and how the stored values drive later load-case combinations.

**Core purpose / keys**
- **TYPE (unit: —, default: “!”)**: The designation of the action (e.g., G, Q, L, A, E, and any action category variants). The description text elsewhere explains that action types may accept literals up to 4 characters; certain combinations are reserved and are defined by INI files for a given design code. Some action types support subdivision into categories appended with an underscore (e.g., `Q_A`, `Q_B`), enabling distinct combination coefficients or partial safety factors per category.
- **TITL (unit: —, default: “*”)**: Human-readable action name/label (“Designation of action”). This is mainly for identification.

**Safety and combination coefficients**
The table enumerates several numeric parameters with unit “—” (dimensionless factors) and default marked by `*` (i.e., default comes from design-code INI or program defaults and may be overridden):
- **GAMU**: Unfavourable partial safety factor.
- **GAMF**: Favourable partial safety factor.
- **PSI0**: Combination coefficient “rare”.
- **PSI1**: Combination coefficient “frequent”.
- **PSI2**: Combination coefficient “quasi-permanent”.
- **PSIS**: Combination coefficient “infrequent”.
- **GAMA**: Partial safety factor for accidental action.
These values are later copied into load cases when actions are instantiated; load-case-specific modification is possible but the source text warns it can create ambiguity if used excessively.

**Action grouping / temporal variance classification**
- **PART (unit: —, default: “*”)**: Indicates which superposition equation group the action belongs to, based on temporal variance and equation structure used later in MAXIMA. Allowed values shown:
  - `G`: permanent (e.g., dead load)
  - `P`: prestress
  - `Q`: variable action (default for free-defined user actions per the text)
  - `Q_1` … `Q_99`: variable action load groups (for bridge-like modeling to avoid intermediate superpositions)
  - `A`: accidental action
  - `E`: seismic action
The narrative further states: for preset actions, PART depends on TYPE; for user-defined actions, PART must be provided to avoid defaulting to `Q`.

**Load-case superposition rule within an action**
- **SUP (unit: —, default: “*”)**: Default treatment of multiple load cases belonging to the same action during combination. Listed options:
  - **PERM**: permanent with unique factor (sum across load cases; unfavourable vs favourable applied to the summed effect)
  - **PERC**: permanent with individual factors (load-case-wise unfavourable/favourable handling)
  - **COND**: conditional (only decisive contributions for combination are taken)
  - **EXCL**: mutually exclusive within category
  - **EXEX**: mutually exclusive within action
  - **UNSI**: COND with unfavourable sign
  - **USEX**: EXCL with unfavourable sign
  - **ALEX**: permanent but exclusive within action (per-action handling; only one load case considered; ignores favourable contribution for exclusion logic)
These rules interact with the “categories” mechanism (`X_A`, `X_B`, etc.), where EXCL/EXEX control exclusivity boundaries (category vs action).

**Design-code defaults and initialization**
The text explains the table values are populated from INI-files for the selected design code; otherwise, fallback defaults exist (only actions **G** and **Q** may be predefined in some cases). Changing design code or categories requires redefinition; **ACT INIT** deletes existing actions and superposition rules (and may reset defaults for subsequent load cases).

Overall, this table specifies the parameter set required to define an action: its identifier (**TYPE**, **TITL**), safety/combination factors (**GAMU/GAMF/PSI0/PSI1/PSI2/PSIS/GAMA**), and how it enters global combinations (**PART**, **SUP**).

The table summarizes the mapping between **SOFiLOAD “ACT SUP”** semantics and the corresponding **MAXIMA “LC TYPE”** codes used to control how multiple load cases belonging to an **action** (and possibly its categories) are combined for superposition. It is essentially a cross-reference that defines the default combination behavior for load cases within the same action, including whether they are always included, conditionally included, or mutually exclusive in different senses.

### Columns
- **SOFiLOAD (ACT SUP):** User-facing preset option that selects the superposition rule for an action in the SOFiLOAD input.
- **MAXIMA (LC TYPE):** The internal MAXIMA record “TYPE” value that implements that rule during combination processing.
- **Explanation:** Text describing the mechanical meaning of the rule.

### Rows / Rules
1. **PERM → PERM,G**
   - Interpretation: **Always (permanent)**. The partial safety factor application is **action-wise** (i.e., same factor basis for the set of permanent contributions).
   - MAXIMA label includes “PERM,G”, indicating a permanent action combination type where the same approach is applied consistently.

2. **PERC → PERC**
   - Interpretation: **Always (permanent) with variable factors**, where partial safety factors are applied **load-case-wise** rather than action-wise.
   - This differs from PERM because each load case of the permanent action can carry its own unfavorable/favorable factor logic.

3. **COND → COND,Q**
   - Interpretation: **Conditional (only unfavorable)**.
   - Only unfavorable contributions are considered, matching the idea that the combination should include those parts that increase the unfavorable effect.

4. **EXCL → A no**
   - Interpretation: **Mutually exclusive**; specifically “mutually exclusive categories” within the action.
   - The note “MAXIMA record LC different alternative group numbers per category” indicates that exclusions are realized by using separate alternative-group identifiers per category so that only one relevant alternative from each category set can drive the combination.

5. **EXF → A no**
   - Interpretation: **Mutually exclusive but conditional inclusive categories**, with only **one alternative group number for the whole action**.
   - “Only one alternative group number for the categories of an action” implies that the action-level selection couples categories more strongly than EXCL, while still treating them as alternatives.

6. **UNSI → W**
   - Interpretation: **Changing sign** (e.g., seismic actions).
   - This rule is intended for actions where the sign/influence direction reverses and combination must reflect that behavior.

7. **USEX → X no**
   - Interpretation: **Changing sign and mutually exclusive within an alternative group**.
   - The table notes that mutual exclusivity occurs “with input of an alternative group number” in MAXIMA record LC, meaning the user/processing provides grouping metadata that governs which alternative is eligible.

8. **ALEX → A G no**
   - Interpretation: **Always but exclusive** (within an action or alternative structure).
   - The description: “always but exclusive (only within action) with input of an alternative group number in MAXIMA record LC.” This indicates exclusivity is enforced at the level defined by those alternative groups, not across different actions.

9. **F → (not shown as LC TYPE)**
   - Interpretation: An **additional load case to be combined**.
   - The row indicates “F” corresponds to adding another load component during combination; the MAXIMA LC type is omitted here, implying either a shorthand or the corresponding MAXIMA code is context-dependent.

The input table defines the header/meta-data for a **load case (LC)** in SOFiLOAD. Each row specifies one keyword field, its meaning, unit (if applicable), and a default value. The table is structured to guide how load cases are identified, scaled, combined for safety/design verifications, and parameterized for time- or post-processing-related criteria.

- **NO (Number of load case)**: Integer identifier of the load case. Default is **0**. This number is used to select the load case for later processing.

- **TYPE / Action of load case**: Specifies the **type/action classification** governing how the load case participates in design combinations (e.g., safety factors and combination coefficients). The unit is not applicable (shown as “-”). Default is **LIT4** (as indicated by an asterisk meaning “star/default per system/action definition”). TYPE can also be explicitly set to special literals such as **NONE / '-'** (not assigned to an action), or special combination roles like **(D)** ultimate design, **(A)** ultimate accidental, **(E)** ultimate earthquake, and service-level combinations **(P,F,N,R,H,HZ,PT,LT,MT,ST,VT)**. This ties the load case to combination logic.

- **FACT (Factor of load case)**: Global scaling factor applied to the load case during analysis usage. Default is **1.0**. Importantly, FACT affects **forces and moment loadings** but **not** temperature, strain, or prestressing loadings, and it does **not** affect dead-load factors **FACD, DLX, DLY, DLZ**. (In the referenced context, these behaviors are explicitly described; the table itself shows FACT’s core purpose and default.)

- **FACD (Factor of structural dead weight)**: Scaling for structural dead weight contribution. Default is **0.0**. Setting dead load factors implicitly controls whether dead weight is present; redefining or specifying dead-load definition behavior can delete other loads of the same LC per the provided context.

- **DLX, DLY, DLZ (Dead load components in X/Y/Z directions)**: Components of dead weight in global axes. Their direction must match the requested global axis sign convention; the context notes you must supply the correct sign for DLX–DLZ. Units are “-” and defaults are marked with * (indicating action/system dependent or no fixed default in the table).

- **GAMU (Unfavourable safety factor)** and **GAMF (Favourable safety factor)**: Separate safety factors for unfavourable/favourable verification cases. Default marked as *.

- **PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PSI3 (Combination coefficients)**: Standardized combination factors used to represent different recurrence scenarios:
  - **PSI0**: standard
  - **PSI1**: frequent
  - **PSI2**: quasi-permanent
  - **PSI3**: non-frequent  
  All have unit “-” and defaults marked *.

- **GAMA (Safety factor accidental)**: Accidental safety factor. Default marked *.

- **CRIT (Time criteria)**: A time-related criterion. Unit is **sec** with default **0**. This is used for time-dependent evaluation contexts (e.g., actions/criteria in transient or time-based design checks).

- **CRI1, CRI2, CRI3 (User criteria I–III)**: Generic user-defined criteria fields. Units are “-” with defaults **0**. Per the context, CRI1–CRI3 are also used for flexible post-processing via tools like DBVIEW; they can be set in advance or after analysis based on results.

- **TITL (Title of loadcase)**: Human-readable descriptive title. Unit “-”, and default is **LIT32** shown in the table header context; the row indicates TITL is used to label the load case.

Overall, this table provides the **control parameters** for a load case: identification (NO), action/combination role (TYPE), analysis scaling (FACT), dead-load specification (FACD and DLX/DLY/DLZ), safety/combination factors (GAMU/GAMF/PSI*/GAMA), and criteria used for time- or user-defined logic (CRIT, CRI1–CRI3), plus a title (TITL).

sections: 3.5 LC – Definition of a Load Case

content:
The input table segment describes the **definition of load cases (LC)** in *SOFiLOAD* (and related workflows), focusing on what fields are used to identify a load case and how its **type and parameters control generation, modification, and deletion of loading**. The table context also includes notes about **load components** (e.g., nodal vs. elemental) and a mapping for **influence line computation**.

**Key fields / columns:**  
- **LC / TITL**: “LC” denotes the load case identifier (number). **TITL** is the *Title of loadcase* (text) associated with that LC. A dash (“-”) is shown as the default/placeholder. The load case number **selects the load case for further treatment** (i.e., subsequent operations reference it by its LC number).  
- **Minus sign**: A literal “-” appears as a placeholder in the “TITL” description, implying an optional title entry or empty title behavior.

**Loading classification and how loading is specified:**  
The text enumerates the different ways a load case can include loading data:
- **Nodal loads** via **NODE**  
- **Elemental loading** via element load types such as **BEPL, BEAM TRUS, CABL, QUAD, BRIC**  
- **Copy loading** via **COPY, EVAL** (load cases can be constructed from others)  
- **Meshless loading**: point (**POIN**), line (**LINE**), areal (**AREA**), and volume (**VOLU**)

**Dynamic / specialized loading sources:**  
It also notes support for **Dynamic Loads**, **Load Trains on bridges**, and **Wind loads** as additional load-generating categories.

**Load-case “levels of working” (how modifications behave):**  
A major part of the table description explains that load cases can be modified in several ways, with specific deletion/reconstruction rules:
1. **Change of parameters of an action** (load type coefficients/safety factors derive from the action TYPE).  
2. **Change of load case parameters** (e.g., **TYPE, FACT, CRIT → CRI3 or TITL** can change for existing LCs). It warns that defining factors for dead load or other loading may *delete the total loading* of that LC.  
3. **Load generation via REST**: if a load case contains load generators (REST), all generated loading is **re-established** from generators.  
4. **COPY commands inside LC**: when updated via REST, **all loads are deleted** and recreated by reapplying COPY commands.  
5. **Explicit definition after LC record**: defining dead weight factors afterward deletes previous loading data for that LC to allow clean redefinition.  
6. **Deletion**: using **TYPE DEL** deletes the entire load case immediately.

**Meaning of LC scaling factor (FACT) and dead load factors:**  
- The **factor of the load case (FACT)** affects forces/moments scaling but has **no influence** on temperature, strain, and prestressing loadings.  
- It does **not affect dead-load factors** (**FACD, DLX/DLY/DLZ**) and those must be entered with correct global-axis sign conventions. Dead weight components apply in the gravity-direction convention unless stated otherwise.

**Action / TYPE assignments and special TYPE literals:**  
- TYPE can either reference a predefined/explicit **action** or be **NONE / '-'** if unassigned.  
- Special literals define combination purposes: **(D), (A), (E), (P), (F), (N), (R)** and timber term combinations **(PT, LT, MT, ST, VT)**.  
- Some special design/analysis use-cases: **IMP** (imperfections for 2nd order combination), **EINF** (influence lines), etc.

**Influence line mapping shown in the table context:**  
The bottom portion effectively provides a small table mapping “Influence Line” to the “needed Loading” and an example command:
- **Beam-moment** → unit rotation/disrotation → e.g., **BEPL D?**  
- **Beam-force** → unit displacement → e.g., **BEPL W?**  
- **QUAD-force** → Dirac-delta curvature → e.g., **QUAD E\***  
- **Support force** → nodal displacement → e.g., **NODE W?**  
- **Displacement** → nodal load → e.g., **NODE P?**  
This supports how to construct influence line LCs using appropriate unit load responses.

**Overall structure implication for a RAG table description:**  
The described “input table” is not just a schema—it explains how the LC record ties together: **identity (LC number), metadata (TITL), load content (NODE/element/meshless/COPY), and behavior controls (TYPE/FACT/CRI parameters and modification semantics, especially REST and deletion rules).**

 There are levels of working on load cases for SOFiLOAD:

 • Load generation
 Via load type REST you may change not only parameters but all the generated loading will be reestablished from the load generators - This is especially useful for postprocessing from graphical input definitions.
 For a load case containing COPY commands, i.e. is composed by other load cases, all loads are deleted and repeated all the COPY commands with REST.
 • Explicit definition of loading
 If factors of the structural dead weight or other loading are defined after a LC record, all loading data for that load case will be deleted, to allow the redefinition of loading for a given load case.
 • Explicit deletion of a load case
 If defining the TYPE DEL the total load case including all known data will be deleted imme- diately .
 The factor of the load case has (despite the wind load generator) no specific influence in SOFiLOAD and may be changed later at any time. Loads will be multiplied by this factor only when used in the analysis itself. The factor FACT affects all forces and moment loadings, however, not temperature, strain and prestressing loadings! It does also not affect dead load factors FACD, DLX, DLY or DLZ.

content:
The factor of the load case has (despite the wind load generator) no specific influence in SOFiLOAD and may be changed later at any time. Loads will be multiplied by this factor only when used in the analysis itself. The factor FACT affects all forces and moment loadings, however, not temperature, strain and prestressing loadings! It does also not affect dead load factors FACD, DLX, DLY or DLZ..
 The components of the dead weight will be in the positive direction of the requested global axis. You have to enter the correct sign for DLX to DLZ. If you specify only FACD, SOFiLOAD will apply the dead load in the direction defined as the gravity direction. A definition will delete all loads of this load case automatically.
 As type of the load case on may specify the name of an action. Only predefined or explicitly defined actions may be used with LC (see ACT). If the load case is supposed not to be assigned for an action, the literal NONE or ’-’ has to be input for TYPE. There are also some special literals possible, assigning a (e.g. non linear) load case to be of a spcific type used for special design tasks:
 (D) Ultimate Design combination
 (A) Ultimate accidental combination
 (E) Ultimate Earthquake combination
 (P) Service: Quasi permanent combination
 (F) Service: Frequent combination
 (N) Service: Non-frequent combination
 (R) Service: Rare (characteristic) combination
 (H) Comb. of principal loading
 (HZ) Comb. of principal+supplemental loading
 (PT) permanent load combination e.g. for timber
 (LT) long term load combination e.g. for timber
 (MT) middle term load combination e.g. for timber
 (ST) short term load combination e.g. for timber
 (VT) very short term load combination e.g. for timber
 Values GAMU to PS1S belong to the action TYPE in general. However they may have indi- vidual values for every specific load case. Thus at the time of the creation of a load case, the current values from the action will be taken as default for the individual load case for Version 23. Starting with version 2010 however only the explicitly defined values will be kept, all other values will adopt to those of the action itself if the action is changed.
 Values CRI1 to CRI3 are very general parameters of the load case. They may be used freely for postprocessing via DBVIEW. You may specify them in advance or set them after the analysis by reading some results from the database. (e.g. a system dimension, a strength reduction etc.) TALPA uses CRI1 for the safety factor of the material needed by analysis according to Fellenius.

 Example for the influence line for moment MY at beam 1001 at location 2.0 to be saved as load case number 91:

content:
### Table: **NODE – Definition of Loads at Nodes (SOFiMSHC / structural FEM input)**

This table describes how to specify **loads applied to individual nodes** in a finite element model. A single node can receive loading either as **complete vector components** or via up to **seven load values** whose meaning depends on the selected **load type**. The entry row is keyed by the **NODE item**, indicating the target node (or a secondary group/designation).

---

#### Main identifier and grouping
- **NO** (Number of node or designation of secondary group)  
  - **Unit:** “– / LITT” (no physical unit)  
  - **Default:** required (“!”)  
  - Purpose: identifies where the load is applied. It can be a **specific node number** or a **secondary group name/number** that the program expands.

---

#### Load definition mode
- **TYPE** (Type of Loading)  
  - **Unit:** **LIT** (load type identifier)  
  - **Default:** `PG`  
  - Purpose: determines the interpretation of the subsequent load values **P1–P7** (and potentially other parameters like FRA D). In other words, the load type controls what each component represents (e.g., forces/moments, directional components, etc.).

---

#### Load components
- **P1 … P7** (Load values)  
  - **Units:** `[*]` (units depend on the load type)  
  - **Default:** `-`  
  - Purpose: allows **up to seven components** to be defined depending on the load type. The documentation indicates that loads can be provided either as:
    - a **complete vector** using literal component grouping (P, M, V), or  
    - up to **seven individual components** tied to the chosen load type.

---

#### Radial scaling for special loading cases
- **F R A D** (Radial factor for load values)  
  - **Unit:** **LIT**  
  - **Default:** `-`  
  - Purpose: provides a multiplier that scales load values with the **node’s radius**.  
  - The radius is defined as the **distance of the node to the global axis** selected as the **gravity direction**.  
  - The table specifies two interpretations:
    - multiply with **radius** (centrifugal forces, internal pressures, etc.), or  
    - multiply with the **square of radius** via the **RR** option.

This enables modeling of loads varying with position relative to an axis.

---

#### Eccentricity-based moment generation
- **EXX** / **EYY** / **EZZ** (Eccentricity to node)  
  - **Unit:** **[m]1001**  
  - **Default:** `-`  
  - Purpose: defines an **offset (eccentricity)** of a load application point relative to the node.  
  - The table states that **EYY and similar eccentricities are immediately converted to moments**—i.e., eccentricity is not kept as a separate geometric offset during the load application, but is translated into equivalent **moment components** applied at the node.

---

#### Key behavioral notes (from surrounding context)
- **Local load directions** require nodes that have a **local coordinate system** (SOFiMSHC capability). If no such local system exists for structural points (SPT) with local axes, the system falls back to **global coordinate directions**.
- If a **kinematic constraint** exists for a degree of freedom and a nodal displacement is imposed, the constraint is **deactivated**; there is no inversion of that support condition. This implies that **local displacements are unavailable** and must be modeled using **stiff spring elements** if needed.
- Additional special note: in **axial symmetry**, load values are interpreted as **circumference-related**. Example given: a radial load of `2 kN/m` must be expressed as `PYY ±2.0`, and the program accounts for the actual radial application point automatically.

---

Overall, this table defines a flexible scheme for applying nodal loads with: (1) node targeting, (2) load type–dependent component values, (3) optional radial scaling, and (4) eccentricity-to-moment conversion, with clear rules for local vs global coordinate interpretation.

The table (Table 3.8) defines the “Type of the Nodal Loadings” for a structural analysis program, i.e., how loads applied at a specific **NODE [m]** are interpreted by the solver. It organizes load components by their physical quantity (force, moment, reaction, displacement/rotation) and gives the expected **unit** for each entry.

## Node context
At each nodal location (“NODE [m] 1001” in the extract), the load can be specified either directly as individual components or as complete load vectors using literals:
- **P, M, V** (force, moment, and optionally a third vector type depending on the program’s convention)
- corresponding combined notations **PP, MM, VV**
The text indicates that up to **seven components** may be defined within such a nodal vector description. Direction handling is important: **local load directions require nodes with a local coordinate system** (SOFiMSHC). If no local system is available, **global directions are used**.

## Coordinate system implications
The table entries include both **global** and **local** directions:
- “global X/Y/Z-direction” entries are interpreted relative to the model’s global axes.
- “local X/Y/Z-direction” entries require a node-local coordinate system; if absent, the program falls back to global axes.

Additionally, special cases are mentioned (centrifugal/internal pressures, etc.), where load magnitudes may need scaling by **radius** (distance to a global gravity axis). For **axial symmetry**, circumferential interpretation applies (e.g., a radial load given per circumference).

## Load and unit types shown in the table
The table lists nodal load component “types” and their units:

### Forces (kN)
- **direction (kN)** repeated multiple times in the header area indicates the three translational force components.
- **Global X-direction (kN), Global Y-direction (kN), Global Z-direction (kN)**: standard nodal forces.
- Another group labeled “reaction (kN)” appears three times, indicating reaction-force components in the same translational directions.

There is also a set of shorthand/parameterized quantities:
- **… of force PXX–PZZ (kN)** (partially truncated in the extract)
- and explicit “terms of force” like **… of force PX–PZ (kN)**

Finally, the bottom part includes “net” style entries:
- **MXX, MYZ, MZB (kN)** (also truncated/partial), suggesting additional force-like component groupings depending on the DOF ordering used by the program.

### Moments / rotational effects (kNm, mrad)
- **Global X-direction (kNm), Global Y-direction (kNm), Global Z-direction (kNm)** under a moment/reaction-like header indicates **nodal moments** about global axes.
- **local X-direction (kNm), local Y-direction (kNm), local Z-direction (kNm)**: corresponding nodal moments but in local coordinates.
- A moment component with **kNm²** is shown (“… kNm²”). This likely represents a higher-order or product-type quantity (the extract is truncated), but the key is that it is dimensioned differently than standard moments.

For nodal rotational displacements/rotations, the table provides:
- **displacement/rotation in global X-direction (mm) / global Y-direction (mm) / global Z-direction (mm)** (linear displacements)
- **about global X/Y/Z-direction (mrad)** (rotations), indicating the units for rotational kinematic components.

### Mixed parameter naming
Near the middle, the table references component ranges:
- “... of force PXX–PZZ” / “... of moment MXX–MZZ”
- “... have to be defined via P1 to P3 resp. P1 to P7”
This indicates that some load types are not single scalar entries but **vectors** requiring several parameters (up to **P1–P3** or **P1–P7**) to represent coupled force/moment data.

## Overall meaning for RAG indexing
In summary, this table is a schema-like mapping between **nodal load component names** (global/local force directions, global/local moment directions, reaction components, and special parameterized vector components) and their **expected units**: **kN** for forces, **kNm** (and one **kNm²** case) for moments, **mm** for translations, and **mrad** for rotations. It also emphasizes that correct interpretation of “local” directions depends on whether a node has an associated **local coordinate system** in SOFiMSHC; otherwise the solver uses **global directions**.

See also: LC, TRUS, CABL, beam-loading, QUAD, BRIC, COPY, free- loading
 NODE
 [m]1001
 Loads in nodes will be defined in individual components or as complete vectors with the Literals P, M and V resp. PP. MM and VV. In those cases up to seven components may be defined.
 Local load directions require nodes with a local coordinate system (SOFiMSHC). Only nodes which are input as structural points (SPT points) with a local coordinate system in SOFiMSHC can be used here. If no such system is found, the global coordinate directions will be used instead.
 For special cases you may multiply the load values with the radius (e.g. centrifugal forces, internal pressures etc) or with the square of the radius. The radius is the distance of the node to the global axis which has been selected as gravity direction.
 In the case of axial symmetry load values are interpreted as circumference related, e.g. a radial load of 2 kN/m must be provided as PYY ±2.0. The program then automatically accounts for the radial position of the load application point.
 If a degree of freedom which has a kinematic constraint gets a nodal displacement, the con- straint will be deactivated. There is no way to invert that support condition. That’s why there are no local displacements available. They have to to be modelled with stiff spring elements if desired.

The table describes the **CABL** loading command, which applies a load to a *range of cable elements* that share the same loading conditions. Instead of specifying explicit element numbers, the user may enter the literal **GRP** followed by a group number in the **FROM** field and the corresponding group number in **TO** to automatically select all cable elements in that group.

This command converts cable-element loading into **equivalent nodal loads**, because a cable element has **no basic bearing capacity transverse to the cable** (i.e., it cannot sustain crosswise load directly). Therefore, the load is transferred to nodes, and in a subsequent **nonlinear analysis** the program evaluates the **cable deflection**. The description recommends inserting **nodes at all important points along the cable** to ensure that the nodal load distribution captures the intended geometry and deformation behavior.

### Table fields

- **Item: FROM**  
  - **Description:** Number of the first cable element to load, or a **group selection** token of the form `GRP <group_number>`.  
  - **Unit:** —  
  - **Default:** `!` (required)

- **Item: TO**  
  - **Description:** Number of the last cable element to load, or the group number when using group selection (selects all elements in the group).  
  - **Unit:** —  
  - **Default:** `FROM` (if not provided, defaults to the starting selection)

- **Item: INC**  
  - **Description:** Increment step for element numbers when applying the loading to multiple elements in a sequence.  
  - **Unit:** —  
  - **Default:** `1`

- **Item: TYPE**  
  - **Description:** Specifies the **load type and direction** applied to the cable elements (displayed as `LIT` in the unit column).  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** `PG` (implies a particular default load type/direction setting; exact meaning depends on the software’s load-type catalog)

- **Item: PA**  
  - **Description:** Load value at the **cable start point** (end associated with the FROM position/direction).  
  - **Unit:** `[*]` (value parameter; exact unit depends on TYPE)  
  - **Default:** `!` (required)

- **Item: PE**  
  - **Description:** Load value at the **cable end point** (end associated with the TO position/direction).  
  - **Unit:** `[*]` (value parameter; exact unit depends on TYPE)  
  - **Default:** `PA` (so both ends default to the same value unless a gradient/variation is required)

### Overall behavior
By defining FROM/TO (or GRP selection), choosing a load TYPE and specifying PA/PE, the command generates nodal forces along the selected cable elements. If PA and PE differ, the load varies from start to end; then the nonlinear analysis computes the resulting cable deflection.

The input table (Table 3.10: **Type of the Cable Loading**) specifies how a distributed load applied to cable elements is defined in terms of direction, reference conventions, and resulting units. It is intended for the **CABL** command context, where a “range of cable elements with the same loading” is assigned. In this modeling approach, cable element loads are converted into **nodal loads** because a cable element has no transverse basic bearing capacity; the cable deflection is then computed in a subsequent nonlinear analysis. To capture effects accurately, the guidance recommends inserting **nodes at important cable points**.

## Structure of the table
The table is arranged into **parameter fields** (names/labels) and an associated **Unit** column. The unit column indicates the expected physical dimension of the entered quantity. The table contains several repeated “direction” entries, implying a multi-component definition of the load vector.

## Fields described
1. **Direction (x/y/z components implied)**
   - Appears as multiple “direction” rows (three times).
   - The unit for these direction components is **kN/m**.
   - This indicates that each directional component corresponds to a **distributed line load intensity** (force per unit length) applied along the cable span.

2. **Direction measured in projection**
   - Also appears as multiple “direction … measured in projection” rows (three times).
   - Each has unit **kN/m**.
   - This suggests an alternative way to specify the same load components, but expressed as **projected components** (e.g., onto a global or chosen coordinate system axes), rather than using the cable’s local orientation.

3. **0/00 / kN / mm / K / – (miscellaneous parameter units)**
   - The lower part of the table shows several standalone unit labels:
     - **0/00** (dimensionless-like indicator or angular/ratio-style convention)
     - **kN**
     - **mm**
     - **K**
     - **–**
   - These likely correspond to additional auxiliary inputs (not fully visible in the excerpt) such as offsets, scale factors, temperature-related parameters, reference angles/ratios, or identifiers that do not carry physical units.

## Interpretation in the CABL workflow
When using **CABL**, the user selects a cable element range (either by explicit element numbers using **FROM/TO**, or by using **literal GRP** and a group number at **TO** to select all elements in that group). Then the load “TYPE” determines how the distributed cable loading is translated into nodal loads. The table’s direction entries (standard vs. projection) indicate two coordinate interpretation options for distributing the load along the cable.

In summary, the table defines the **directional components** of cable loading as **kN/m** and distinguishes between direct direction specification and **direction-by-projection** specification, with additional parameter categories indicated by units such as **kN**, **mm**, **K**, and dimensionless forms.

See also: LC, NODE, TRUS, beam-loading, QUAD, BRIC, COPY, free-loading
 CABL
 CABL is loading a range of cable elements with the same loading. Instead of a number FROM you may enter the literal GRP and the group number at TO to select all elements of a group.
 For TYPE you have the choice of:
 Loading on cable elements will be converted to nodal loads, as the element has no basic bearing capacity transverse to the cable. In a following nonlinear analysis the deflection of the cable will be evaluated. Thus it is recommended to insert nodes at all important points of a cable.

The table defines the **TRUS** command for applying loads to a *range of truss elements* that share the same load definition. Instead of specifying only an explicit element number range, the inputs allow selection by **element group**: the user can enter the literal **`GRP`** together with a **group number** to target all elements belonging to that group. This enables consistent loading of multiple truss elements without enumerating each element individually.

A key behavioral note (from the surrounding context) is that **loads applied to truss elements are converted into nodal loads**. The reason given is that a truss element has **no basic bearing capacity transverse to its own axis**. Therefore, to ensure the model correctly represents the intended structural behavior, the guidance recommends **inserting nodes at all important points** along the truss geometry, since the resulting loads act at nodes after conversion.

### Column meaning (table structure)
The table has four columns:
- **Item**: the parameter/field name.
- **Description**: what the field controls.
- **Unit**: the expected unit or value type.
- **Default**: the default setting if not specified.

### Field-by-field description
1. **FROM**  
   - **What it selects**: either the **number of the first truss element** in the range, or (alternatively) the **first target group** via `GRP`.  
   - **Unit**: shown as “–” (no physical unit; it is an identifier).  
   - **Default**: marked with `!`, implying it is **required**.

2. **TO**  
   - **What it selects**: the **number of the last truss element** in the range, or the **group number** if using `GRP`-based selection.  
   - **Unit**: “–” (identifier).  
   - **Default**: set to **FROM**, meaning if TO is omitted, the range collapses to a single element/group starting at FROM.

3. **INC**  
   - **Purpose**: defines the **increment between element numbers** when applying the load across a range. For example, `INC = 2` would apply the definition to every second element in the specified FROM–TO span.  
   - **Unit**: “–”.  
   - **Default**: **1**.

4. **TYPE**  
   - **Purpose**: specifies the **load type and direction** for truss loading. While the table labels it as `LIT` (likely a list/enum), it governs how the provided values are interpreted directionally.  
   - **Unit**: `LIT` (literally a selection list).  
   - **Default**: **PG**.

5. **PA**  
   - **Purpose**: the **load value at the truss start point** (one end of the selected truss element span).  
   - **Unit**: `[*]` indicating a value whose specific unit depends on TYPE.

### BEAM table — description for RAG indexing

The **BEAM** table defines **loads applied to a sequence of beam elements**. It is used to specify how a load varies **along the beam length** and how it is positioned **eccentrically** relative to the beam’s **local coordinate system** and **reference axis**. Conceptually, each record covers a segment of the overall beam (from **FROM** to **TO**) and assigns a load type (**TYPE**) with values at the start (**PA**) and end (**PE**), optionally including geometric offsets (**A, EYA, EZA, EYE, EZE**) and reference-system control (**REF, REFT**).

#### Element selection and coverage
- **FROM**: start element number or identifier (**number of first element**, a **group** via GRP, or a **special SLN** reference). Default is flagged (shown as “!”), meaning it must be provided.
- **TO**: last element number; can also be a **group number** or **SLN identifier**. Defaults to **FROM**.
- **INC**: increment step for iterating element numbers (default **1**).

#### Load type definition
- **TYPE**: encodes **load type and direction**, stored as a literal list item (**LIT**). Documented options include:
  - **UZS** (primary lateral imperfection as factor of total length)
  - **PNX** (external prestressing force in local x, unit **kN**)
  - **PMY** / **PMZ** (external prestressing moments in local y/z, unit **kNm**)
- Additionally, the table supports the literal **CONT**: when **TYPE = CONT**, the record activates **defaults derived from the previous BEAM record**, simplifying the definition of **piecewise/trapezoidal combined loads** (e.g., continued TYP/PA/PE/A behavior).

#### Load magnitude along the beam axis
- **PA**: load value at the load start point (default “!” meaning required in normal cases).
- **PE**: load value at the load end point (default **PA**, enabling constant loads when start and end values are equal).
- **L**: length of the loading region.
- **A**: distance from the **total beam start** to the loading start/end reference (the table allows specifying positions and lengths consistently; in fire/combined-load scenarios A and L coordinate the spatial extent).

This enables varying loads such as ascending/descending distributions (example given: load increasing from **0→100** then **100→120** across specified sub-lengths, then decreasing).

#### Eccentricity and reference axis positioning
The load eccentricities are defined in the **local beam coordinate system** with respect to the **connecting line between nodes** (the **reference axis**):
- **EYA, EZA**: local coordinates of the loading position at start, relative to the beam/reference axis (**mm**).
- **EYE, EZE**: same at end.
These eccentricities affect the resulting **moments**: loads of type **P** create moments when eccentricities are present. For nonlinear analysis, eccentric loading additionally leads to **geometric stiffness and forces**.

The specification also distinguishes whether loads act on the **upper or lower side** of a section, which influences sign conventions and the moment direction.

#### Reference-system control
- **REF**: reference system used for **A and L** (unit **LIT**). Default **S**. Options are described as “see beam-loading” for allowed variants.
- **REFT**: reference system for **EYA … EZ** (unit **LIT**, default “*” meaning depends on model). Allowed/defined meanings in the context include:
  - **S**: center system (NP=0)
  - **NULL**: sectional coordinate system
  - **ID**: point ID within a section/centerline context (see beam-loading)

#### Temperature and advanced processing (related to TYPE usage)
While not shown as explicit TYPE rows in the provided snippet, the accompanying text explains that BEAM load records can also define **temperature profiles** along the **cross-sectional height**, processed by **2D FiberBeam (TALPA)**:
- Temperature ordinates **ZA, ZE** are interpreted depending on **REFT -Z** or **REFT +Z**:
  - If **REFT −Z** is defined: ordinates refer to **uppermost fibre**, requiring **ZA, ZE ≥ 0**
  - If **REFT +Z** is defined: ordinates refer to **lowermost fibre**, requiring **ZA, ZE ≤ 0**
  - Otherwise: ordinates are **relative** measures scaled to section dimensions
Positive **DTY/DTZ** raise temperature in the positive y/z axis direction. Temperature profiles along the local **z-axis** combined with **EVAL TEQV** can be transformed to equivalent linear distributions.

#### Prestressing semantics
For prestressing-specific types (**PNX, PMY, PMZ**):
- The loading corresponds to an imposed strain/curvature.
- If the element is fixed, resulting forces/moments match imposed loading.
- If the element can deform, prestress is **reduced** (deformability limits activation).
A contrasting mechanism exists for tendon prestressing defined via **BEPL** (eigen stress state), which **requires deformability to become active**. Special whole-beam tendon prestress may be representable with **PNXI** in a single BEAM record.

The table describes the keyword record layout for applying loads to a set of finite elements identified by a range or by group numbers (the surrounding text focuses on “QUAD” elements and their load definitions). It specifies how elements are selected, how the global load value is computed and scaled, and how optional additional data and through-thickness (local z) distributions are provided.

**Element selection and stepping**
- **FROM**: Number of the first element (or GRP). Unit: `- / LIT`. Default: **!** (mandatory).
- **TO**: Number of the last element or a group number. Unit: `-`. Default: **FROM** (if omitted).
- **INC**: Increment of element numbers between FROM and TO. Unit: `-`. Default: **1**.  
  Together, these allow selecting all elements within a numeric range, or selecting all elements of a specified group by using a GRP-style specification in place of explicit element numbers. The text notes that the range must include at least one element.

**Load definition fundamentals**
- **TYPE**: Load type and direction. Unit: `LIT`. Default: **PG**.  
  The earlier context states that many load types exist (e.g., PRE for tendon prestress on QUADs, and several wind-related variants such as STD/CYL/CYLR/CYLF/CYLK), and some types use **NTYP** to define extra options (e.g., prestress stage, wind factor patterns, or inclination/orientation constraints).
- **P**: Main load value. Unit: `[*]` (scaled by load unit factor). Default: **!** (mandatory).
- **X, Y, Z**: Reference point coordinates for evaluating the load value. Unit: `[m]1001` (geometry unit scaled). Defaults: **0.0** each.
- **DPX, DPY, DPZ**: Linear increments of the load value in global coordinates:  
  - `p(x,y,z) = P + (x − X)*DPX + (y − Y)*DPY + (z − Z)*DPZ`  
  Units for all are `[*]`. Default for each: **0.0**.  
  The context explains that for “global varying loads” (e.g., earth/water pressure), **P** is the value at `(X,Y,Z)` while **DPX..DPZ** define the increments in global coordinate directions.

**Additional option controls**
- **NTYP**: Additional option selector. Unit: `LIT/-`. Default: **-** (not provided).  
  From the context: **NTYP** can encode stage numbers or special actions (prestress, wind/snow patterns). For certain load types (e.g., PXP/PYP/PZP), NTYP can represent a maximum roof inclination angle and its sign controls allowed surface-normal orientation relative to the load direction.

**Additional option value**
- **VTYP**: A value used together with the additional option (i.e., when NTYP activates a CYL/CYL* wind model, etc.). Unit: `*`. Default: **-**.  
  The context indicates VTYP can relate to an equivalent cylinder diameter and thus how Reynolds-dependent cylinder wind pressure coefficients are evaluated.

**Through-thickness (local z) load distribution for QUAD**
- **Z0, F0, …, Z15, F15**: Up to 16 ordinates defining how the load value is distributed along the **local z-axis** (interpreted as thickness direction for QUAD elements).  
  - **Z0/Z15**: Coordinate along local z (thickness). Unit: `[mm]1010`. Default: **!** for required first ordinate(s) is implied by the mandatory marker in the table for Z0.
  - **F0/F15**: Multipliers (factors) applied to the base load value at each defined thickness coordinate. Default: **1.0** at least for F0 and similarly **1.0** for F15 per the table.  
  The context explains the reference rule: if all ordinates are positive they are referenced to the uppermost QUAD fibre; if all are negative, to the lowermost fibre; otherwise they are referenced to the QUAD mid-surface. If the QUAD element thickness does not match the definition, the distribution is scaled with a warning in the mixed-ordinate (mid-surface-referenced) case.

Overall, this record format allows selecting which QUAD elements receive a specified load type, computing a possibly spatially varying load from a reference point plus linear gradients, optionally refining behavior with NTYP/VTYP, and prescribing how the load varies across thickness using Z/F ordinates.

A positive factor selects for those regions with changing sign the suction, a negative factor will select the pressure value. To define the loading areas the outer dimensions of the building are needed.
