In SOFiLOAD there are different methods to deal with loading for beam structures. The most general method is based on explicit load distribution areas LAR and will then distribute all loads, even point loads, on multiple beams.
 This method is based on load distribution influence areas, constructed from regions either al- ready subdivided in quadrilaterals or to be established automatically in simple cases of four edges. There is a tiny plate-bending FE-program involved creating the support forces for sup- ported edges or edges with a beam section. These values are permanently saved to the database.
 If now an arbitrary loading is defined it will be first converted to nodal loads for the distribution mesh of the distribution region and then within a second step it is converted to support forces and eventually beam loading along the edges of the area.
 The other methods will load only a single distinct beam for any created part of the loading area. For point and line loads there is a hierarchic search method, where beams are selected based on their distance to the load. In this sequence the load will be projected onto the beams, subdividing line loads if necessary. A point load will be always applied entirely on one beam.
 For area loading however a primary and secondary span direction is selected (automatically or explicitly). Loading will be distributed in the secondary span direction.

Coordinate definitions relative to nodes are best performed by putting the coordinates to a variable with COOR beforehand. For simple cases for all coordinates a specification of the literal GPT instead of the X-value and for the number of a geometric point or a node instead of the Y-value will directly use the coordinates of that point. It is also possible to specify all
 coordinates relative to a special nodal point, which is given with its number and the the item NREF for all loadings but VOLU.
 With the literals DXY, DYZ or DZX instead of an X-value it is possibel to specify coordinates relative to the first defined load point. With literals DDXY, DDYZ and DDZX the differences are taken relative to the last load point.
 It is not required to specify a load value in all load points. Missing load values will be interpo- lated before saving the load (e.g. linear variant load value along a complex geometric curve)
 The problem of multiple loading may occur if the user has defined overlapping elements or there are multiple nodes with the same coordinates. For Point and LINE-loads there is a rather easy way to assure, that no part of the loading will be applied more than once. However, for QUAD-elements this is a very difficult task. Therefore the program will load all possible elements. The user has to define a WIDE-value which defines all elements within a distance WIDE before or behind the load plane will be treated as loaded. For special cases a sound group selection may be helpful.
 For all loading the percentage of the active load area based on the defined loading area respec- tive length will be calculated and printed. A value deviating from 100 percent will be marked. With ECHO LOAD the generated loads may be printed and controlled.
 For numerical reasons tiny load components will not bes saved. load areas with a dimension less than the factored part of the total dimensions defined by CTRL STOL will be ignored.

The table defines the **LAR (Load distribution area) record layout** used to create **load distribution areas for beam systems**. LAR converts defined free loads (specifically forces) applied at an action position into equivalent beam loads acting on the corresponding beams. It supports loads represented as **point, line, and area loads**. It does **not** treat other load types such as **moments** or **temperature** (those must be handled differently).

## Columns/fields
The table is structured with five columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

### 1) LAR identification and selection
- **NO**: *Load distribution area for selection via AREA_REF / LAR NO*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `!` (mandatory/unspecified in table; typically user-defined)
- **NAR**: *Number of a geometrical area (GAR)*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `0`  
  - Meaning: selects an existing geometric area instead of defining an explicit structure.
- **GRP**: *Selection of a group of QUAD elements*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `-` (not set)
- **GRP1**: *Group selection for beam groups*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `all`  
  - Meaning: determines which beam groups within the system are eligible to receive loads.
- **GRP2**: *which should be loaded* (the specific subset within the selected beam groups).  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `-` (not constrained)
- **GRP3**: additional group selection control (listed as separate field; the table groups GRP1–GRP3 under “beam group selection”).  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `-`

**Interpretation in practice:** only the specified beam groups via GRP1/GRP2/GRP3 receive loading; by default all beam groups are used.

### 2) Explicit structured-area definition (triangular/quadrilateral meshes)
A block of fields becomes relevant when **neither NAR nor GRP is specified**:

- **M**: *Partitions of N1–N2 or N3–N4*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `*` (use asterisk meaning: depends on other input or is not fixed)
- **N**: *Partitions of N2–N3 or N4–N1*.  
  - Unit: none  
  - Default: `*`  
- **T**: *Application range of the load distribution*.  
  - Unit: `*` (table indicates flexibility/parameter)  
  - Default: `0.0`  

If **no M/N** is provided or the mesh is **too coarse**, **SOFiLOAD generates a mesh automatically**.

### 3) Geometry input for the explicit load distribution area corners
The record then specifies the **corner points** of the explicit LAR area via coordinates or reference points (**GPT points**):

- **X1, Y1, Z1**: *Coordinates of first point OR input of GPT point number for each coordinate dimension*.  
  - Unit: `[m]1001` for X1/Y1/Z1  
  - Default: `0.0`  
- **X2, Y2, Z2**: *Coordinates of second point OR input of GPT point number for X2/Y2/Z2*.  
  - Unit: `[m]1001`  
  - Default mapping shown: `X2 default = X1`, `Y2 default = Y1`, `Z2 default = Z1`
- **X3, Y3, Z3**: *Coordinates of third point OR input of GPT point number*.  
  - Unit: `[m]1001`  
  - Default mapping shown: `X3 default = X2`, `Y3 default = Y2`, `Z3 default = Z2`
- **X4, Y4, Z4**: *Coordinates of fourth point*.  
  - Unit: `[m]1001`  
  - Default mapping shown: `X4 default = X3`, `Y4 default = Y3`, `Z4 default = Z3`

**Triangle vs quadrangle:**  
- For **triangles**, the fourth point is specified but must effectively **repeat the third point** (as stated in the table: “For triangles the fourth point must be the same as the third point.”).

## Notes linked to the record semantics
- Each load distribution area gets a **local z direction**, derived from the **sense of rotation in analog mode to QUAD elements**. This enables usage of free loads in the local z direction (PZ-type).
- Large LAR extents can cause unintended **deductional loads**; therefore, LAR should be sized appropriately (often per span in multi-span bridges).
- The table complements the larger concept of LAR generation and usage, including guidance to verify areas visually (e.g., via an animator).

The goal of the parameters is to define *what reference the load targets*, *where it acts*, and *in which direction/magnitude*.

### REF / NO / TITL (reference identification and naming)
- **REF (reference type)** selects the category from which the load point/area will be derived. Supported values include:
  - **AUTO** (automatic)
  - **MOVE** (automatic moving load)
  - **LAR** load distribution area
  - **SLN** structural line

  - **GFA** surface number of B/RICs

  Default is **AUTO**.
- **NO (reference or group number)** provides the numeric identifier for the chosen REF type. If a reference is **NODE** with an explicit number, coordinate defaults are taken from that node; eccentricities then create **moments at the node**.
- **TITL (short title of loading)** is a label for the load definition. Default is blank.

### PROJ / WIDE / NREF (projection setup for choosing where the load lands)
These parameters control projection of the load point onto a reference area/direction:
- **PROJ (projection of load point)** determines the projection method:
  - **N** = projection normal to the reference area (SAR)
  - **XX/YY/ZZ** = projection in global X/Y/Z direction

- **WIDE (range in direction of projection)** sets an additional search/selection range **only when a specific PROJ is selected**. Default is **0.0 m** (shown with an example unit format like \[m\]1001).
- **NREF (reference node for coordinate values)** optionally supplies a node whose coordinates are used as reference for coordinate interpretation. Default is **–** (not set).

### TYPE (load type and direction) and P / X / Y / Z (magnitude and coordinates)
- **TYPE (load type and direction)** specifies the load kind (in the context of this table it corresponds to the POIN load definition) and its direction coding. Default is **PG**.
- **P (load value)** gives the magnitude. Unit follows **LIT** with a default of **0.0**.
- **X, Y, Z (global coordinates of the loading)** define where the point load is placed in global space. Each has units of **\[m\]1001** and defaults to **0.0**.

The program searches points/lines/regions to place the load, and the influence area can manifest as a **dirac-delta-like strain at element centers**, with the mesh deformation smoothing the theoretical singularity. If the mesh is refined around the load location, the singular character becomes more pronounced. The table therefore provides mechanisms (REF/PROJ/WIDE/NREF and coordinates) to control where this equivalent load is mapped onto the model.

Overall, the table is a concise schema for configuring a POIN load: choose **reference target (REF/NO)**, optionally **project and constrain placement (PROJ/WIDE/NREF)**, and then define **load type/direction (TYPE)** and **position/magnitude (P, X, Y, Z)**.

## Columns / fields
- **REF (Reference type, Unit: LIT, Default: AUTO):** Selects what the reference identifier points to.
  - **AUTO**: automatic moving/reference behavior.
  - **MOVE**: automatic (moving) load.
  - **LAR**: load distribution area.
  - **SAR**: structural area.
  - **GFA**: surface number of BRICs.
  - **BGRP**: group of beam elements.
  - **QGRP**: group of QUAD elements.
- **NO (Reference or group number, Unit: –, Default: –):** The identifier associated with REF.
- **TITL (Short title or ident, Unit: LIT12, Default: –):** Human-readable label for the loading.
- **PROJ (Projection of loading area, Unit: LIT, Default: N):** How the load polygon is projected into a calculation plane.
  - **N**: use normal of the reference area (SAR).
  - **XX / YY / ZZ**: project in global X/Y/Z direction.
  - **XXL / YYL / ZZL**: like XX/YY/ZZ but with the *sign* interpreted as a local component direction (used when local orientation matters).
  - **LOAD as N, without eccentricities**: special mode suppressing eccentricity handling.
- **WIDE (Range in direction of projection, Unit: [m]1001, Default: 0.0):** Extension allowed along the projection direction; used to control which elements are considered “hit” by the projected load region.
- **NREF (Reference node for coordinate values, Unit: –, Default: –):** Node used as a basis for interpreting coordinate values.

## Load definition fields
- **TYPE (Load type and direction, Unit: LIT, Default: PG):** Defines the physical kind/direction of the load (e.g., pressure, moment, distributed forces) and ties direction to projection rules. (The narrative context indicates available load types such as **MX** and various P*/component types.)
- **P1 (Load value of first point, Unit: *, Default: 0):** Scalar value at the first defining point.
- **X1, Y1, Z1 (Coordinates of first point, Unit: [m]1001, Default: 0):** 3D coordinates of point 1, defining where the load value applies.
  - **X1** may also accept special **GPT/GP literal** formats: the description indicates “GPT for X1 and the point number for Y1” (i.e., coordinate inputs can be literal values or references to points/GPT constructs).
- **P2 … P6 / X2..Z2 … X6..Z6:** The table allows up to **six defining points** per record, each with:
  - a load value (**P2 … P6**),
  - and coordinates (**X2,Y2,Z2 … X6,Y6,Z6**).
  If more than six points are needed, the input must use **continuation records (CONT)**.

## Interpretation rules embedded in the surrounding context
- **Interpolation / degree:** Up to **4 points** can define a **bilinear** (4-coefficient) distribution; more points enable **quadratic** (6-coefficient) or **bicubic** (10-coefficient) distributions, provided points exist in at least two directions to solve all coefficients. If insufficient directional coverage exists, the solver automatically reduces to the highest degree that yields unique coefficients.
- **Kinks:** Non-smooth changes must be modeled using **separate load areas**.
- **Element association:** For non-nodal distributed types, the solver determines target elements by projecting the polygon; for irregular meshes, “100%” matching of area to elements may deviate because selection uses element-center “hits”.
- **Reference uniqueness:** If an explicit area number is given, it is unique; if not, the program may search all areas, but only those completely inside the volume are used.
- **Continuation constraint:** When using **CONT**, records must not contain generation/list expressions; points beyond 6 require continuation.

If coordinates for a direction are omitted, the program attempts to use the **maximum extent in the gravity direction** and fills missing perpendicular directions automatically, interpreting the missing parts as increments.

For **BRIC-elements**, **partial loading is not implemented**: either an element is loaded if its **center point** lies within the body, or it is not loaded at all.

The input table defines an **“EVAL” evaluation block** used to compute scalar quantities from results stored in the model database (e.g., load vectors, displacements, velocities, accelerations, eigenform data, or equivalent temperature loading). The computed value(s) are then provided to **CADINP** as variables for subsequent input after the **END-record**. The table is organized as a list of parameters controlling what type of evaluation is performed and which database data it uses.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter name/label for each row (e.g., TYPE, NO, NAME).
- **Description**: Human-readable explanation of that parameter, including accepted options.
- **Unit**: Unit field for the parameter (mostly not applicable for enumerations/indices, so shown as “—” or similar).
- **Default**: Default value if the parameter is not specified (examples shown as “RU”, “!”, and numeric defaults like 0).

### Parameters / Rows
1. **TYPE (Type of evaluation)**  
   Controls the mathematical operation applied to the vector(s) in the database. The default is **RU**. Supported TYPE keywords include:
   - **RR**: norm of the load vector \(R\) (i.e., load-vector magnitude).
   - **RU**: scalar product \(R \cdot U\) (displacement-weighted load).
   - **RUU**: scalar product \(R \cdot U^2\) (displacement squared weighting).
   - **RV, RVV**: operations involving velocities \(V\) (e.g., \(R \cdot V\), and possibly \(R \cdot V^2\) depending on the exact keyword interpretation in the code).
   - **RA, RAA**: operations involving accelerations \(A\) (analogous to velocity forms).
   - **RP, RPP**: operations involving support forces \(P\).
   - **RI, RII**: operations with displacement increments.
   - **TEQV**: equivalent linear temperature load.
   - **TEIG**: TEQV plus *eigen stress* contribution.
   - **WCOH / WCOU / WCOV**: coherent spectral density terms for different response components (u-, v-, w-components or total w-component depending on naming).

2. **NO (Second load case number: (U, V, A, …))**  
   Selects the relevant **secondary load case** identifier used by the evaluation. It specifies which stored result case (e.g., displacement case number, velocity case number, acceleration case number, depending on TYPE) is used in the operation.  
   - Default shown: **“!”** (meaning the program expects this to be provided; “!” typically flags *required* or *not defaulted*).

3. **NAME (Name of a CADINP variable)**  
   Names the output variable that will receive the evaluation result. The table notes the name is given **without the trailing “#”** (CADINP variable naming convention).  
   - Default shown: **LIT8** (example default variable name).

4. **IND (Index for array-variable)**  
   Used when the target CADINP variable represents an array; selects which element/index receives the computed value.  
   - Default: **0**.

5. **LEIG (load case number of first eigenform)**  
   Specifies the load-case number corresponding to the **first eigenform** referenced in the evaluation (relevant for eigenform-related types such as those involving eigen stress).  
   - Default: **0**.

6. **NEIG (number of eigenforms)**  
   Specifies how many eigenforms are included in the evaluation.  
   - Default: **0** (so eigenform-dependent behavior requires nonzero NEIG).

### Contextual meaning (from the provided description)
The surrounding text explains that **EVAL evaluates expressions using actual load vectors with displacements from other load cases**, supplying the computed scalars to the next CADINP input block as variables. Conceptually, it supports:
- **Influence-area/integral evaluations**: e.g., if a constant area load of value 1.0 is used, the result of **RU** corresponds to the **integral of that area over the loaded region**.
- **Fast influence-line re-evaluation**: by using the evaluation machinery to quickly test different loads on a precomputed influence line.

Overall, the table parameterizes *what* is computed (**TYPE**) and *which* stored model data it uses (**NO**, eigenform selectors), and it defines *where* the result is stored for subsequent processing (**NAME**, **IND**).

The input table is a compact parameter specification matrix that defines how to provide **CTRL control options** for an analysis load generation workflow. It has four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Each row describes a required field that can be combined into a CTRL record.

1) **OPT** (Item): Represents the **name of a control option**. The table indicates the data type as **LIT** (likely a string/literal identifier). The **Default** for OPT is **FULL**, meaning the option identifier is expected to be fully specified (i.e., the user must choose from the defined option names/keywords rather than relying on a partial value).

2) **VAL** (Item): Represents the **value** assigned to the selected control option. The **Unit** column shows **–/LIT**, indicating the value type depends on the chosen OPT and may be numeric or literal. The **Default** is **!**, which implies “no default available/mandatory” (i.e., the value must be provided explicitly for the option to be meaningful). This aligns with the context that *CTRL is evaluated sequentially and values must be entered before load cases*.

3) **V2** (Item): Provides an **additional value** for the selected control option. Unit is shown as **–** (type not fixed at the table level; depends on OPT). The **Default** is **-** (no default). This supports options that require multiple parameters (e.g., direction components, thresholds, sub-options, or angles).

4) **V3** (Item): Provides **another additional value** for the selected control option. Like V2, Unit is **–** and Default is **-**, indicating it is optional and only needed for certain CTRL options.

5) **V4** (Item): Provides **yet another additional value** for the selected control option. Unit is **–** and Default is **-**; used only when the chosen OPT requires up to four parameters.

Overall, the table functions as a schema: for each CTRL control option record, the system expects **OPT** (required selector) and **VAL** (required option value), plus **V2–V4** when the specific control option’s definition needs extra numeric inputs. This structure supports the many option behaviors described in the accompanying text (e.g., COPY behavior modifiers, distribution rules, WIND patterns, SUML factors/angles, HYDRA/CFD pressure selection parameters).

The table is a command-option specification for controlling what information the system prints in an “ECHO” (print/verbosity) style interface. It contains four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Each row defines a configurable parameter (“Item”) and how it affects the output, including its default behavior.

### Column meanings
- **Item**: Name of the option/parameter (e.g., OPT, VAL, VAL1).
- **Description**: Allowed values and what each value does.
- **Unit**: Display/format category; in this table it shows the likely default “level” group (mostly **LIT**).
- **Default**: The default selection for that option when not explicitly set (commonly **FULL**).

### Rows / options

#### 1) **OPT**
**Purpose:** Selects a “literal” subset of elements to include in the output. The value is a literal from a predefined list.

**Allowed values in the Description:**
- **FULL**: “Set all options” (enables everything under OPT).
- **LANE**: “Lane geometries” (print lane geometry information).
- **ACT**: “Actions” (print actions section).
- **LOAD**: “Loadings” (print loadings section).
- **WIND**: “Wind parameters” (print wind parameter information).
- **COPY**: “Load case combinations” (print combinations generated by COPY).
- **LTD**: “Load take down” (print the LTD-related load processing output).
- **TAG**: “Loadings with tags from GUID record” (print loads associated with tags sourced from a GUID record). The note in the surrounding context clarifies that multiple TAG records can be used to obtain tables for several tags, and that TAG is not enabled with the **OPT FULL** command.

**Default:** **FULL** (as shown in the Default column).

**Unit column:** **LIT**.

#### 2) **VAL**
**Purpose:** Controls the overall **volume of printout** (verbosity / print level).

**Allowed values:**
- **NO**: no printout at all.
- **YES**: standard printout.
- **FULL**: enhanced printout.
- **EXTR**: extended printout.

**Default:** **FULL**.

**Unit column:** **LIT**.

#### 3) **VAL1**
**Purpose:** Filters output by **tag value** associated with a **GUID record**.

**Meaning in context:**  
- If **VAL1 is left empty**, all loads with a tag are printed.
- The table row specifies: “Filter for tags from **GUID** record,” with default **–** (none stated) and **Unit** shown as **LIT32**.

**Default:** “-” (no explicit default value shown).

### Overall intent
Together, **OPT** determines *what categories* of information to print (lane, actions, loadings, wind, combinations, etc.), while **VAL** determines *how much detail* to print (none/standard/enhanced/extended). **VAL1** adds a targeted filter mechanism for tag-based load selections using GUIDs. This structure is designed to support precise control over printed load-related tables for later inspection or ingestion into a downstream knowledge base.

The image is a single, landscape schematic figure (Figure 4.1) illustrating a multi-stage workflow for pushover analysis in seismic performance-based design. The overall layout is divided into four consecutive panels from left to right, each labeled with a stage name: **“AQUA + SOFIMSH Mat./Hinges + System”** (left), **“SOFILOAD Push Load”** (second panel), **“ASE Push Anal…”** (rightmost panel; partially visible but clearly “ASE”), with arrows showing progression through the process.

**Left panel (AQUA + SOFIMSH):**  
A simplified structural model is depicted at the top as a vertical element (a black line) with a small red marker near its upper end, suggesting a controlled point or hinge location. In the lower-left corner, there is a diagram with two curved lines resembling capacity or displacement-shape concepts plotted against axes labeled **M** (mass) and **P** (load). A green and a red curve form a stylized backbone/capacity envelope, and a red arrow indicates an upward or increasing load direction. Next to these curves is a green arrow labeled **ϕ** (phi), representing the **assumed displacement shape vector** used for defining non-linear behavior and equivalent system properties.

**Second panel (SOFILOAD – Push Load):**  
This section shows a **multi-degree-of-freedom** representation: a grid-like arrangement of **rectangular masses or nodes** (alternating black outlines with small red/green dashed accents). Beneath the grid are short vertical supports drawn in black, indicating the base support conditions. A large **blue arrow** on the left side of this panel points to the structure from left-to-right, symbolizing the application of a lateral pushover load pattern. Small black base nodes appear under the supports, implying the structure is being pushed laterally under a defined load case pattern.

**Third/final panel (ASE – Push Analysis):**  
The rightmost diagram shows a similar frame/grid structure but in a state of **progressive pushing**, indicated by a red arrow at the top pointing rightward-to-downward and a red **labeled displacement** symbol **u_cnod** (control node displacement). Near the bottom-left of this panel, a blue/black arrow indicates the direction of increasing lateral force. The structure’s boxes and internal lines appear to represent stiffness degradation or nonlinear response as the displacement increases, consistent with incremental monotonic loading during pushover analysis. A red arrow labeled **V** (base shear or lateral force) appears pointing left, suggesting base shear development as the load is increased.

**Global visual logic:**  
Thick white arrows between panels indicate that the workflow proceeds sequentially: first define material properties/hinges and the system (AQUA + SOFIMSH), then define the pushover lateral load pattern (SOFILOAD), and finally perform the incremental nonlinear static analysis up to the target displacement (ASE). The figure is conceptual and schematic rather than to scale, focusing on illustrating how displacement control (control node), load pattern definition, and incremental analysis relate to each other in pushover-based seismic performance assessment.

The image is a schematic figure illustrating the concept of a **pushover curve** for a structural system, specifically the relationship between **base shear** and **displacement**.

On the left side, there is a simplified elevation view of a multi-story structure drawn as a rectangular frame with several evenly spaced horizontal levels (representing floors). The **overall building** is shown in side view, with the left side conveying **lateral force application** through a series of **blue arrows** pointing toward the building from the left. The arrows have varying lengths and are arranged vertically along the height, indicating that the lateral loads are distributed along the structure (consistent with using a displacement-shape or mode-proportional lateral load pattern in pushover analysis). The building is simplified to vertical members and floor lines, without detailed element geometry.

At the top of the structure, a **red dot** marks the **control node** (the key point used for tracking displacement). Above this dot, a red horizontal arrow labeled **u_cnrod** (or similarly denoted as control node displacement) indicates the **horizontal displacement** of the control node. A black line at the top level serves as a reference position, and the red arrow shows the displacement direction.

A second red arrow at the bottom indicates the **base shear direction**: a red double-ended arrow labeled **Vb** runs along the base, emphasizing that base shear is the lateral force measure at the foundation level, with the sign indicating direction.

On the right side of the figure, there is a graph with the vertical axis labeled **Vb** (base shear) and the horizontal axis also labeled **u** or **displacement** in a generic sense (the axis ticks are not shown, focusing attention on the curve shape). The curve starts near the origin and rises quickly, then **flattens and gradually saturates**, forming a **concave downward** nonlinear shape. This curvature visually represents progressive inelastic behavior during the pushover procedure: the structure initially offers stiffness (steep slope), and as yielding occurs, stiffness degrades (shallower slope), while base shear increases more slowly until a maximum or plateau-like response is reached.

The caption at the bottom reads: **“Figure 4.2: Pushover curve (Vb-u diagram)”**. Overall, the figure conveys that as lateral loads increase incrementally, the structure’s control-node displacement increases, and the corresponding base shear follows a nonlinear capacity/pushover relationship.

The image is a schematic figure illustrating the conversion of a structural pushover curve into an equivalent capacity diagram in ADRS (spectral displacement–spectral acceleration) format. The layout is a three-panel left-to-right flow, with arrows indicating transformation steps, and annotated axes and equations to clarify the mapping between different coordinate systems.

**Left panel (MDOF pushover curve):**  
A plot shows a red, nonlinear, monotonically increasing curve that starts near the origin and then levels off, indicating yielding/strain-hardening behavior typical of a pushover (base-shear vs. control-node displacement) relationship. The vertical axis is labeled **\(V_b\)**, representing base shear. The horizontal axis is labeled **\(u_{cnod}\)**, representing the control-node (roof) displacement of a multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) system. The curve rises steeply at first and then approaches a plateau-like shape, implying a gradual reduction in incremental stiffness.

**Middle panel (ADRS capacity diagram):**  
The middle plot shows another red curve in a different coordinate system. The vertical axis is labeled **\(S_a = V_b / (\Gamma^2 \cdot m)\)**, explicitly relating spectral acceleration to the original base shear via factors involving \(\Gamma\) and \(m\) (conversion constants from MDOF to equivalent SDOF). The horizontal axis is labeled **\(S_d = u_{cnod} / (\Gamma \cdot \phi_{cnod})\)**, relating spectral displacement to the control-node displacement through the same transformation and the displacement shape coefficient **\(\phi_{cnod}\)**. The red curve again increases nonlinearly and shows a similar “flattening” trend, indicating that the capacity information from the pushover analysis is transferred into the spectral coordinates.

An arrow points from the left panel to the middle panel, signifying the **conversion** from the MDOF pushover curve \(V_b\)–\(u_{cnod}\) to the SDOF capacity diagram \(S_a\)–\(S_d\).

**Right panel (equivalent SDOF system):**  
A simple single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) mechanical model is drawn. The mass block labeled **\(m^*\)** sits on a base representing the ground motion input. A dashpot/spring element is shown with an attached force–displacement resistance labeled **\(f_s^*(D)\)**, where **\(D(t)\)** is the relative displacement of the mass. The diagram includes a horizontal arrow labeled **\(\ddot{u}_g(t)\)** (ground acceleration time history). A stiffness/damping element is depicted with **\(c^*\)** and resistance behavior, emphasizing that the system response under seismic excitation is modeled as an inelastic SDOF with an equivalent force–deformation relationship.

Overall, the figure communicates that by using scaling relationships (involving \(\Gamma\), \(m\), and \(\phi_{cnod}\)), the nonlinear capacity from a pushover analysis of the MDOF structure can be represented as an ADRS capacity diagram for the equivalent inelastic SDOF oscillator, which can then be used in performance-point determination workflows.

The image is a cropped, text-heavy page from a technical book/manual about seismic performance-based analysis, specifically pushover (nonlinear static) procedures and the conversion between multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) and equivalent single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) representations using spectral displacement/acceleration diagrams (ADRS format).

At the top portion, the page contains dense paragraphs describing how seismic demand estimation tools range from response spectrum analysis (RSA) to nonlinear response history analysis (RHA), and why engineers increasingly rely on performance-based seismic design using nonlinear static procedures (NSP/pushover). The text outlines the conceptual relationship between structural capacity and seismic demand, emphasizing that pushover analysis compares available capacity with estimated demands.

The core of the content lists the pushover procedure stages in an enumerated manner. These include (1) defining material properties and nonlinear link elements/plastic hinges (AQUA + SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHC), (2) defining the pushover lateral load pattern (SOFILOAD), often proportional to a chosen displacement shape vector ϕ (commonly the fundamental mode), (3) incrementally applying monotonically increasing lateral forces to obtain structural capacity (ASE), and (4) transforming/combining capacity with seismic demand to determine structural performance.

Beneath the textual explanation, the page includes multiple mathematical equations formatted in LaTeX-like notation, such as the equation of motion of the nonlinear MDOF system and its approximation/transformation into an equivalent inelastic SDOF system. Variables like mass, damping, resisting force, base shear Vb, control node displacement cnod, spectral displacement Sd, and pseudo-acceleration spectral response Sp are explicitly referenced. The equations include expressions relating MDOF pushover outputs (Vb–cnod) to SDOF capacity/demand curves in spectral coordinates (Sp–Sd), and show how pseudo-acceleration and spectral relationships are used in the analysis.

A “Hint” section appears with bullet points describing key assumptions for converting MDOF to SDOF, including that the displacement shape remains constant during the response and that the distribution of pushover loads is proportional to mass times displacement shape.

Near the bottom, a final equation is visible stating a relationship for spectral displacement in terms of spectral acceleration and period, shown as:  
Sd = Sa / ω² = Sa · (T / 2π)² (labeled as equation 4.19).  
This suggests the page is discussing the conversion of elastic response spectra from traditional spectral acceleration vs. period (S–T) format into spectral acceleration vs. spectral displacement (A–D/ADRS) format.

Overall, the image functions as a technical reference page: it conveys methodology, assumptions, and mathematical transformations used to build capacity and demand diagrams for determining a performance point (target displacement) and back-transforming SDOF results to the original MDOF structural model.

The image is a schematic two-panel diagram illustrating a transformation of an elastic seismic demand representation from the standard acceleration–period format to an acceleration–spectral-displacement (A–D) format (ADRS).

**Left panel (traditional elastic response spectrum):**
- Axes are drawn in a Cartesian style.
- The vertical axis is labeled **Sa** (spectral acceleration).
- The horizontal axis is labeled **T** (structural period).
- A black curve shows a typical response spectrum shape: starting at a higher value for small periods, remaining approximately flat over an initial region, then decreasing monotonically as period increases.
- A dashed vertical guide line drops from a point on the curve at some **T = const** region to the **T** axis. Near that guide, a small label indicates **T = cons** (i.e., a constant period).
- The panel includes an arrow pointing from left to right, indicating conversion/mapping from this representation into the right panel’s representation.

**Right panel (A–D / spectral displacement format):**
- A new coordinate system is drawn.
- The vertical axis is still labeled **Sa** (spectral acceleration).
- The horizontal axis is labeled **Sd** (spectral displacement).
- The same black decreasing curve appears in the right panel, but now the axes correspond to **Sd** instead of **T**. The curve location/shape relative to the vertical axis is consistent with a transformation: the curve decreases as moving right along **Sd**.
- A dashed straight diagonal line originates at the origin and rises, corresponding to the relationship used in the conversion.
- Another dashed vertical guide line indicates **T = const** in this transformed domain as well.
- There is an explicit formula near the right conversion:  
  **Sd = Sa · (T / 2π)²**  
  This formula visually emphasizes that the horizontal-axis variable **Sd** is computed from **Sa** and **T** (or equivalently, from the same constant-period point used in the left panel).
- The diagonal dashed line visually represents how points at a fixed **T** map from the Sa–T curve into the Sa–Sd coordinate plane.

**Overall purpose:**  
The diagram serves as a conceptual guide for converting an elastic response spectrum from **Sa vs. T** to **Sa vs. Sd (A–D format)**, which is commonly needed for capacity spectrum / performance-based procedures (e.g., for intersection with a capacity diagram).

The image is a schematic diagram illustrating how to determine the **performance point** in performance-based seismic design using **capacity** and **demand** curves in an **ADRS-type** (spectral displacement \(S_d\) on the horizontal axis, spectral acceleration \(S_a\) on the vertical axis) format.

### Layout and axes
- The plot shows a coordinate system with:
  - **Horizontal axis:** labeled \(S_d\) (spectral displacement). It increases to the right.
  - **Vertical axis:** labeled \(S_a\) (spectral acceleration). It increases upward.
- There are no grid lines; the presentation is diagrammatic and intended for conceptual understanding.

### Curves and labels
- A **blue curve** (labeled **“Demand Diag”**) slopes downward from left to right, starting relatively high and bending toward lower \(S_a\) values as \(S_d\) increases. This blue shape represents the reduced inelastic demand relationship used to estimate the seismic demand.
- A **red curve** (labeled **“Capacity Diag”**) is drawn as a nonlinear curve rising quickly from the origin, reaching a peak/rounded top, and then slightly leveling or declining. This red curve represents the structure’s capacity (monotonic maximum force–deformation relationship transformed into spectral coordinates).
- The blue and red curves intersect at a key point on the graph.

### Performance point and guides
- The **performance point** is marked with a **black dot** located at the intersection of the red and blue curves.
- A **vertical dashed line** drops from the black dot to the horizontal axis, and the bottom corresponds to \(S_{dp}\), labeled on the x-axis as **\(S_{dp}\)** (demand/control spectral displacement at the performance point).
- A **horizontal dashed line** extends from the black dot to the left-side level, indicating \(S_{ap}\), labeled on the vertical direction as **\(S_{ap}\)** (performance spectral acceleration).
- The label **“Performance Point”** points toward the intersection region (near the black dot).

### Additional annotations
- Near the upper left, the text **“El. Demand Diagram”** (elastic demand diagram) is shown with a dark/black downward curve segment distinct from the blue inelastic demand. This implies the elastic demand is reduced to obtain the inelastic demand diagram used for the intersection.
- A black arrow-like axis marking appears at the origin region, emphasizing directionality of \(S_d\) (to the right).
- There are colored annotations:
  - “Capacity Diag” in **red**
  - “Demand Diag” in **blue**
  - The performance point itself is highlighted in black, with red text **“Performance Point”** near the marker/region.

Overall, the diagram communicates the core method: **plot capacity and (reduced) seismic demand in \(S_d\)-\(S_a\) coordinates and read the intersection to obtain \(S_{dp}\) and \(S_{ap}\)**, which together define the structural performance state.

The image is a schematic diagram illustrating the conceptual flow of pushover/capacity-spectrum transformation from an SDOF representation back to a structural displacement target. The left side shows a simplified structural “base” idealization: a vertical column or single-degree-of-freedom oscillator element sitting on a ground support (a gray base rectangle). At the top of the element is a circular “lumped” mass. A black vertical arrow indicates displacement response (downward from the circular mass toward the base). Near the top, a horizontal double-headed arrow labeled **Sd,p** (spectral relative displacement at the performance point) indicates the target displacement for the control degree of freedom.

A large rightward black arrow connects the left idealization to the right portion of the figure, emphasizing that the process transforms the SDOF spectral demand into equivalent quantities for the original structure’s control node.

On the right, the diagram shows a stylized multi-story building: a rectangular structural frame with multiple horizontal “story” lines (several tiers) and vertical grid lines. Above the frame, a small dashed or stepped representation indicates an upper target displacement level. Seismic design of structures is a challenging and demanding task for a structural engineer and the tools at his disposal range from a relatively simple multimodal response spectrum analysis (RSA) which has been incorporated into almost all modern seismic design codes to a rather complex and expensive direct nonlinear response history analysis (RHA). Despite its accuracy and rigorousness in estimating the seismic response of structures, direct nonlinear response history analysis still remains impractical for a wide range of problems encountered in earthquake engineering practice. On the other hand, the multimodal response spectrum analysis with its use of the estimated average ductility capacity based mostly on the type of the structure often provides a too crude estimation of the nonlinear seismic demand. In recent years, a turn from RSA towards performance-based seismic design based on the nonlinear static procedure (NSP) or pushover analysis has been evident. This procedure recognizes the fact that the capacity of the structure and a seismic demand are two inseparable parts of the performance-based design.
 Pushover analysis is a procedure whose purpose is to evaluate the performance of the struc- ture under a specified earthquake hazard by comparing the available capacity and estimated
 structural demands.
 Pushover analysis procedure comprises of the following stages (Figure 4.1):
 1. AQUA + SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHC: First stage is the definition of the material properties, or what is more common in the pushover analysis definition of non-linear link elements, or plastic hinges (see AQUA: SMAT). Next the system is defined, with appropriate non-linear links assigned to e.g. ends of the beams.
 2. SOFILOAD: Next stage is the definition of the pushover lateral load case pattern. Choice of the load case pattern is an important point in the pushover analysis since these lateral forces should be able to represent the inertial forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake ground motion as accurately as possible. The load pattern is usually assumed to be proportional to some assumed displacement shape vector ϕ. Most commonly, the chosen load pattern is proportional to the fundamental eigenmode of the structure. However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (e.g. constant or linear distribution of forces, etc.). Instead of a load driven pushover analysis, a displacement driven analysis might also be required (Figures 4.11 and 4.12). For more details about the definition of the pushover load see ACCE: Pushover Load.

However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (e.g. constant or linear distribution of forces, etc.). Instead of a load driven pushover analysis, a displacement driven analysis might also be required (Figures 4.11 and 4.12). For more details about the definition of the pushover load see ACCE: Pushover Load..
 3. ASE: Pushover analysis is performed by subjecting the structure to a monotonically in- creasing load pattern of lateral forces defined in stage 2. As aforementioned, these lateral forces represent the inertial forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake excitation. The goal of this incremental nonlinear static analysis is to obtain the capacity of the structure.
 4. SOFILOAD: Based on the previous stages the structural capacity can be analyzed to- gether with the seismic demand and the structural seismic performance can be deter- mined.

The table defines parameters for an earthquake response spectrum (“RESP”) used in structural seismic design. It is organized into two main groups: (1) spectrum shape/control parameters and (2) site/zoning factors and labeling metadata. Each row specifies an *Item* (keyword/field), a brief *Description*, the *Unit* type, and a *Default* value.

**1) Spectrum type and governing parameters**
- **TYPE (Default `*`)**: Selects the *type of spectra*. The field references additional documentation (“see remarks / follow links on top of the page”), implying that the chosen code/type determines the relevant spectral formulation.
- **CLAS (Default `*`)**: Specifies the *soil class* (or similar classification). The remarks indicate that subsequent spectral values depend on soil/ground conditions (e.g., stiffness categories such as A–E in the accompanying context).
- **MOD (Default `0.05` and/or `1.5` shown in the table)**: Represents the *damping or behaviour factor*. The description clarifies it can be used as either:
  - modal damping ratio **ξ**, or
  - reduction/behaviour factor **q** for design spectra (notably tied to “EC8 Design spectra” in the context).
  The defaults shown suggest two typical settings: a damping ratio default of **0.05** (5%) and a behaviour factor default of **1.5** (for design spectra).
  
**2) Spectral acceleration definition and shape controls**
- **SA (Rigid acceleration at T=0) (Default `*`)**: Defines the plateau/rigid-body spectral acceleration corresponding to period **T = 0**. The default is not fixed, indicating it is determined by the chosen spectrum type/parameters.
- **SB (Constant acceleration) (Default `*`)**: Defines the constant-acceleration region level (dimensionless/unitless as “−” in the table, implying consistent normalization with the rest of the spectrum definition).
- **SMIN (Minimum acceleration threshold) (Default `*`)**: Sets a floor value below which the spectrum will not drop.
- **TB, TC, TD, TE (time breakpoints and cut-off) (Units: `sec`) (Defaults `*` except TE listed as `*`)**:
  - **TB**: start/end transition for the early spectral region,
  - **TC**: next transition point,
  - **TD**: later transition point,
  - **TE**: cut-off time beyond which spectral ordinates reduce or terminate.
- **K1 (Exponent for TC < T < TD) (Default `*`, unit `−`)**: Exponent controlling the decay slope in the intermediate long-period region.
- **K2 (Exponent for T > TD) (Default `*`, unit `−`)**: Exponent controlling the decay after TD.

**3) Seismic zone and acceleration scaling**
- **ZONE (Default `(NORM)`)**: The *seismic zone* identifier. Default indicates a “normal” or standard value mapping, likely derived from code requirements.
- **AG (Free field basic acceleration) (Unit: `m/sec^2`, Default `(NORM)`)**: Defines the basic site acceleration **ag** used to scale the spectrum. The context notes this acceleration must be specified (e.g., via record **ACCE** in the full loading definition).
- **AH (Horizontal acceleration factor) (Unit `−`, Default `1.0`)**: Factor applied to horizontal spectral parameters. The context explains that for codes with separate vertical/horizontal spectra (e.g., Eurocode), only one should be defined; if **AH = 0.0**, **AV** may default to the design-code value.
- **AV (Vertical acceleration factor) (Unit `−`, Default `-`)**: Factor for vertical spectral parameters. Its default is not set explicitly in the table, consistent with conditional code behaviour.

**4) Metadata**
- **TITL (Default `*`)**: “Title of response spectrum,” used as a label for identification. The table shows unit type `LIT32`, implying a limited-length text field.

Overall, the table captures both the *parameterization of the spectral curve* (SA/SB/SMIN, TB–TE, exponents K1/K2) and the *code/site scaling logic* (TYPE, CLAS, ZONE, AG, AH/AV) needed to compute response spectra for different design assumptions (serviceability vs ultimate limit states) as described in the provided context.

 RESP
 Earthquake loading is defined in most design codes as a basic acceleration dependant on the importance of the building and the seismic zone. The response of the structure is then defined as a response spectra depending on soil classes and the magnitude. RESP allows not only the selection of the standard spectra, but also variants with explicit parameters. For special cases even an individual curve may be defined with succeeding FUNC records.
 For the complete loading definition you need the direction of the acceleration specified with the
 record ACCE. Please note that the spectra may be defined in absolute accelerations or as a fraction of the gravity acceleration g or a base acceleration g. The second approach is more straight, as we have the theoretical value of 1.0 for T = 0 (perfect rigid structure). Thus this approach is chosen for all spectra beside the UBC and the Chinese and Japanese spectra. It might happen that SA is less than 1.0 for some design codes due to soft soils.
 In general you are using only one spectra, but it is possible to define multiple spectras with different modal damping ratios. The response is then interpolated between the adjacent curves for any eigenmode.
 For those design codes using different spectra for vertical and horizontal response (Eurocode), two factors AH and AV are provided. However only one of these factors should be defined, but a definition of AH 0.0 will preset the value AV to the default of the design code.
 In general there are two cases to be distinguished for the design:
 Limit state of serviceability
 This is normally a request for deformations and constructional rules.
 • Ultimate Limit design
 This requires the stability of the structure. The most severe case would be the elastic response, but in general it is justified to use reduced design spectras taking into account the ductility of the structure with a reduction behaviour factor q. The selection of an appropriate behaviour factor is within the responsibility of the designing engineer.

• Ultimate Limit design. This requires the stability of the structure. The most severe case would be the elastic response, but in general it is justified to use reduced design spectras taking into account the ductility of the structure with a reduction behaviour factor q. The selection of an appropriate behaviour factor is within the responsibility of the designing engineer..

### Table structure and meaning
- **Rows**:
  - **a/g**: a normalized acceleration value (i.e., the characteristic ground acceleration expressed as a fraction of g) associated with each intensity. This acts as the base intensity-related scaling input.
  - **αmax (frequently)**: the maximum spectral acceleration factor for the *frequent* earthquake type.
  - **αmax (rarely)**: the maximum spectral acceleration factor for the *rare* earthquake type.
- **Columns**:
  - **Intensity**: four discrete intensity levels labeled **6**, **7.7a**, **8.8a**, and **9**. (The “a” suffix indicates the standard intensity labeling convention used in the document.)

| 6 | 0.05 | 0.04 | 0.28 |
| 7.7a | 0.10 | 0.08 | 0.50 |
| 8.8a | 0.15 | 0.12 | 0.72 |
| 9 | 0.20 | 0.16 | 0.90 |

### How to interpret for design-spectrum use (context)
This table fits into the standard workflow described in the surrounding text: earthquake action for the **frequent** and **rare** cases corresponds to different design earthquakes (e.g., GBF* vs GBR* types). The **αmax (frequently)** values correspond to the frequent design spectrum’s maximum level, while **αmax (rarely)** corresponds to the rare event’s maximum.

In the text, the spectrum maximum is referenced using relations like **SB = η2 · αm** (frequent/rare handled through corresponding coefficients and period adjustments such as increasing the characteristic period by **0.05 s** for rare actions). This table therefore serves as a **lookup** translating **intensity → acceleration scale (a/g) → αmax maxima** for frequent/rare spectra.

### Key RAG-relevant relationships captured
- Higher intensity increases **a/g** monotonically: **0.05 → 0.10 → 0.15 → 0.20**.
- **αmax (frequently)** follows the same proportional increase but stays below **a/g**.
- **αmax (rarely)** is substantially larger than **αmax (frequently)** at each intensity, representing the stronger rare-earthquake action level used for design spectra.

The table defines the parameters used to specify a time-dependent load function for dynamic response analysis (keyword **FUNC** / load function concept). Each row corresponds to an input item that controls either the time definition, amplitude scaling, periodicity settings, or specialized “function types” used for modeling pedestrian/excitation intensity patterns.

- **T (Time value / type or mode number)**: Primary time reference. Depending on context it can represent a discrete time point for polygonal interpolation, or a coded “type/mode number” for harmonic/Fourier-based representations. **Unit: sec**. **Default: !** (required/mandatory).

- **F (Amplitude F1)**: Function value (amplitude) associated with **T** (first harmonic or first data point, depending on function definition mode). **Unit: –**. **Default: (not specified)**.

- **T1 (Phase for periodic function)**: Initial phase offset used when the function is periodic. **Unit: sec**.

- **TMIN (Start time for periodic function)**: Lower time bound that activates the periodic behavior. For times earlier than **TMIN**, the function value is **zero**. **Unit: sec**.

- **TMAX (End time for periodic function)**: Upper time bound that deactivates the periodic behavior. For times later than **TMAX**, the function value is **zero**. **Unit: sec**.

- **S (Function type / impact factor pedestrians)**: Selector that determines how the time function is generated and interpreted. **Unit: –/LIT**. **Default: 0.0**. The table lists supported **subcodes**:
  - **0.0** = *Fourier series*
  - **< 0.0** = *Pedestrian acceleration: Bachmann*
  - **> 0.0** = *Pedestrian acceleration: Seiler/Hüttner*
  - **WALK +0.4** = walking at **2.0 Hz** (i.e., frequency implied by code)
  - **RUN +1.6** = running at **2.4 Hz**
  - **JUMP +3.0** = jumping at **2.0 Hz**
  - **FRUN** = running modeled as *Fourier series*
  - **FJMP** = jump modeled as *Fourier series*
  - **COMP** = *Compound intensity function*
  - **EXPO** = *Exponential intensity function*
  
  This row is central because it determines whether the function is treated as Fourier/harmonic, pedestrian kinematics-based, or a specialized intensity model.

- Harmonics support (for Fourier-like definitions):
  - **F2 (Amplitude for T/2)**: amplitude of the harmonic at period ratio 2. **Unit: –**. **Default: * (asterisk)** meaning typically required/optional depending on chosen S/type.
  - **T2 (phase of that harmonic)**: phase associated with **F2**. **Unit: sec**.
  - **F3 / T3**: amplitude and phase for **T/3** harmonic. Units: **–** and **sec**.
  - **F4 / T4**: amplitude and phase for **T/4** harmonic. Units: **–** and **sec**.
  
  The presence of **F2–F4** and **T2–T4** implies the function may be built from a finite set of harmonics (likely Fourier series truncated to 4 components).

- **TBLC (time for base line correction)**: timing parameter used to apply a baseline correction to the generated intensity/load function. **Unit: sec**. **Default: –**.

- **TITL (Title of function)**: descriptive label for the function. **Unit: Lit32** (a string length/type). **Default: –**.

Overall, the table provides a comprehensive parameter schema to define how a dynamic load function evolves over time—either as discrete/periodic data-driven signals (via **T, F, TMIN, TMAX, T1**) or as harmonic/pedestrian-intensity models (via **S** plus harmonic amplitudes/phases **F2–F4** and **T2–T4**, and optional baseline correction **TBLC**).

This table defines the parameters of a function/result object used by **FIMP**, which creates (or imports) a function by referencing a **transient result in the database (HIST)**. It is particularly intended for **response spectrum evaluation for local components** (see also SIMR), but can be used for other function-generating tasks. The table describes how to define what kind of quantity is being imported, over what set (nodes/elements), under which load case, and with what scaling and time-averaging behavior.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter name/key.
- **Description**: Meaning and allowed forms.
- **Unit**: Physical units or dimensionless markers.
- **Default**: Default value if not specified.

### Parameters (rows)
1. **TYPE**  
   Specifies the **type of results** to be imported/used as a function. Options are categorized by quantity:
   - **U-X, U-Y, …, U-RZ** → *Displacements*  
   - **V-X, V-Y, …, V-RZ** → *Velocities*  
   - **A-X, A-Y, …, A-RZ** → *Accelerations*  
   - **U, V, W** → *Fluid velocities*  
   It also notes that **most literals** for this item are definable in the **HIST** definition, meaning the exact mapping of components can depend on the HIST setup.  
   Default: `!` (mandatory/special value).

2. **NO**  
   Defines the **number of nodes or elements** to which the result applies, or the special string **"FUNC"** to indicate that values come from an **existing load function**.  
   Unit: `LIT/-`  
   Default: `1`  

3. **LC**  
   The **load case** from which the results are taken.  
   Unit: `–` (load case identifier)  
   Default: `1`

4. **FACT**  
   A **multiplication factor** applied to the imported function values.  
   Unit: `[-]` (dimensionless)  
   Default: `1.0`

5. **TEFF**  
   Averaging time value, i.e., an effective time window over which imported time-dependent values are averaged.  
   Unit: `[sec]`  
   Default: `-` (no default shown; likely optional/depends on usage)

6. **TBLC**  
   Time for **base line correction**, indicating an offset or correction interval used in processing.  
   Unit: `[sec]`  
   Default: `-` (optional/unspecified)

7. **TITL**  
   Title of the function (for identification/documentation).  
   Unit: `Lit32`  
   Default: `-`

### Overall meaning
Together, these fields configure **what signal** (TYPE), **where it is sampled** (NO or FUNC), **under which scenario** (LC), and **how it is transformed** (FACT scaling plus optional TEFF/TBLC time processing) to produce a named function object via **FIMP** from **HIST** transient results.

The table documents parameters for the **ACCE** load definition, which creates **translational and rotational accelerations** (including centrifugal effects for uniform rotation). Depending on the chosen output type, these accelerations are converted into **nodal loads** and/or **element loads** applied to **all masses currently defined in the database** (e.g., beam, cable, and truss element contributions). The parameter set primarily controls (1) what acceleration components are used, (2) how rotation reference/axes are treated, and (3) how the excitation is spatially limited, scaled, and mapped via influence lines.

### Key parameter meanings
- **TYPE (default: NODA)**: Determines how the acceleration is stored/converted. The broader documentation indicates options such as:
  - **NODA**: nodal accelerations (for DYNA),
  - **NODE**: pure nodal forces from mass × acceleration,
  - **NODC**: nodal forces including moments,
  - **ELEM**: element loads for beam-type elements,
  - additional variants for direction-only specification (DIRN/DIR etc.), and **DISP** for prescribed displacements (pushover).
- **NO (default: -)**: Node number; **NO = 0** corresponds to **base acceleration** (i.e., used as the excitation reference point).
- **AX, AY, AZ (default 0.0, units m/sec²)**: Global acceleration components in X, Y, Z.
- **AXX, AYY, AZZ (default 0.0, units rad/sec²)**: Rotational acceleration components about global axes.
- **WXX, WYY, WZZ (default 0.0, units rad/sec)**: Rotational velocity components used to represent **uniform rotation** (angular velocity formulation).
  
### Rotation reference handling
- **REF (unit: /LIT, default “*”)**: Reference node for the rotations.
- **REFX, REFY, REFZ (unit: m, indexed default 0.0)**: Additional offsets defining the rotation point in x/y/z. Together with the reference definition, these parameters control the pivot point for computing the resulting torsional effects. The surrounding text notes that specifying an eccentricity for translational acceleration generates an additional torsional moment through acceleration variation about the center of mass.

### Spatial restriction via selection
- **GRP (default -)**: Group selection; limits where loads are applied (group/box-based mechanism is also referenced for SSI and earthquake-soil interaction).
- **XMIN/YMIN/ZMIN, XMAX/YMAX/ZMAX** (units m, defaults -): **Selection box limits** used to apply loads only to nodes inside the box. The table notes **ZMIN** is “only for NODE/DIR” (consistent with special handling for certain output types).

### Acceleration depth reduction (ARED)
- **ARED (default -)**: Reduction factor for acceleration with depth (used for underground structures per specific design-code logic).
- **AH (default 30)**: Z-coordinate where the factor equals **ARED**.
- **GH (default 0.0)**: Z-coordinate of the ground surface where the factor becomes **1.0**.
  - Intermediate depths use **linear interpolation** between GH and AH.
- **Important modeling note from text**: discrete loading should be used for this reduction option.

### Influence mapping / load distribution (LINF)
- **LINF (default “*” in table)**: Number of an **influence line** used to distribute base excitation into effective nodal/element forces. The text explains that influence lines can incorporate soil–structure interaction effects, multiple footing excitation differences, and that **LINF** may be used together with special negative LINF conventions to pass displacement shape vectors for pushover analyses.

Overall, this table is a parameter reference for configuring how **base/global accelerations and rotations** are transformed into **distributed loads** through **reference-axis definitions**, optional **selection boundaries**, **depth scaling**, and **influence line-based distribution**.

The acceleration will act on all masses defined in the database and will create nodal loads or loads on beam, cables and truss elements. This feature can be used

The defined values AX to AZ will be multiplied then with the horizontal and vertical acceleration components defined with the last RESP before.

The value ARED (e.g. 0.5) is the factor to be applied at a depth of AH, i.e. where the coordinate of the gravity direction has this value.  In order to perform the pushover analysis the pushover load must be defined first. Pushover load case must contain additional information (e.g. participation factor, modal mass, displace- ment shape vector, etc.) which needs to be saved in the database.  The pushover static load should be able to represent the inertia forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake ground motion as accurately as possible. The load pattern is usually assumed to be proportional to some assumed displacement shape vector ϕ. Most commonly, the chosen load pattern is proportional to the fundamental eigenmode of the structure. However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (Figure 4.12).

The table defines configuration parameters for a transient (nonlinear) dynamic analysis “time history” setup, specifically controlling how an input block’s selected load cases and time functions are combined into transient loading over discrete time steps.

**Overall purpose and workflow**
- It states that for a general dynamic analysis, all selected load cases and time functions within an input block may be combined to generate transient loading for all time steps.
- The resulting transient loading is then used in a loop for **ASE and DYNA** (implying automated execution per time step/load case combination).
- It also indicates that all load cases for the **nonlinear dynamic analysis** are created and saved to the database.

**Table structure**
- Columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, **Default**.
- Each row specifies a single parameter used to build the transient history.

**Row descriptions**
1. **N — “Number of time steps or divisor”**
   - **Meaning:** Controls the discretization of time. The parameter is interpreted in two ways:
     - **If N > 0:** Represents a *time discretization scheme* using a **time interval of N time steps** with **time step size DT**, yielding a total duration **N·DT**.
     - **If N < 0:** Indicates an alternate scheme where **a total time interval DT is divided into N·DT time steps** (the table’s text notes this selection occurs with **N < 0**, so the sign is used to select interpretation).
   - **Unit:** “–” (unitless).
   - **Default:** **1**.

2. **DT — “Time step or total time”**
   - **Meaning:** Provides either:
     - the **time step size** (when N is used as number of steps), or
     - the **total time duration** that will be subdivided (when N < 0 triggers the divisor mode described above).
   - **Unit:** **sec**.
   - **Default:** shown as **“!”**, meaning the default is unspecified/required or determined elsewhere.

3. **LCST — “First load case of explicit history”**
   - **Meaning:** Specifies the starting identifier for a sequence of load cases generated for the explicit history.
   - In practice, the system will likely create multiple load cases representing the history progression, with this value marking the first one.
   - **Unit:** “–” (identifier/code).
   - **Default:** **1000**.

4. **TITL — “Title of history”**
   - **Meaning:** A human-readable label assigned to the generated history, aiding identification in outputs or database entries.
   - **Unit:** shown as **Lit32** (implying a 32-character text literal field).
   - **Default:** “–” (no explicit default provided in the table).

**Key interpretation for RAG usage**
This table should be retrieved when documenting: how transient loading is discretized in time (N/DT dual interpretation), how generated load cases for explicit nonlinear dynamics are indexed (LCST), and how the analysis history is named (TITL). It directly links to the mechanism described in the accompanying context: combining selected load cases and time functions to produce time-step-based transient loading used by ASE and DYNA.

See also: RESP, FUNC, ACCE
 STEP
 For a general dynamic analysis all selected load cases and time functions within an input block may be combined to generate the transient loading for all time steps to be used then in a load case loop for ASE and DYNA. Possibilities are:
 • A time interval of N time steps of size DT with a total length of N·DT
 • A total time interval of DT divided into time steps N·DT. This case is selected with a value of N < 0.
 All the load cases for a nonlinear dynamic analysis are created and saved to the database.

The input table lists configurable parameters for **SIMQ** (artificial earthquake accelerogram generation) that control which target spectra are used, how the intensity function and discretization are defined, and how the iterative fitting to the target response spectra is performed.

### Table structure
Each row has:
- **Item**: parameter name used in the input file
- **Description**: meaning of the parameter in SIMQ
- **Unit**: physical or logical unit (or “–” if not applicable)
- **Default**: the default value if not specified

### Parameters and roles
1. **LSPE**  
   - **Case number of target spectrum**  
   - **Unit:** –  
   - **Default:** `!` (must be provided/depends on file setup)  
   LSPE selects the target spectrum dataset that the generated accelerogram should match. This aligns with the workflow described in the context: starting from a given target spectrum (powerspectrum/velocity/acceleration form), SIMQ generates an accelerogram whose response spectra are adjusted iteratively.

2. **LINT**  
   - **Case number of intensity function**  
   - **Unit:** –  
   - **Default:** `0`  
   Chooses the intensity function case used to shape the spectrum via an intensity function, combined with random phases to synthesize the time history.

3. **DT**  
   - **Time step of the resulting function**  
   - **Unit:** sec  
   - **Default:** `0.01`  
   Defines the temporal resolution of the produced accelerogram.

4. **TMIN**  
   - **Smallest period**  
   - **Unit:** sec  
   - **Default:** `0.01`  
   Lower bound of the period range for the target/derived spectral content.

5. **TMAX**  
   - **Largest period**  
   - **Unit:** sec  
   - **Default:** `10.0`  
   Upper bound of the period range for spectral matching.

6. **NFRE**  
   - **Number of frequencies**  
   - **Unit:** –  
   - **Default:** `100`  
   Determines discretization density in the frequency domain used during spectrum construction and fitting.

7. **ITER**  
   - **Number of iterations**  
   - **Unit:** –  
   - **Default:** `1`  
   Controls how many iterative updates SIMQ performs to adjust the generated accelerogram to better match the target damping response spectra.

8. **AG**  
   - **Base acceleration**  
   - **Unit:** `[m/sec^2]`  
   - **Default:** `*` (not explicitly fixed; typically depends on scaling behavior)  
   In the provided context, **AG** is the base acceleration multiplier used to scale the synthetic accelerogram; default is often **9.81 m/sec²**, but a key control is:
   - if **AG is negative** (e.g., `AG -1`), scaling of the accelerogram is switched off
   - if **AG = 0.0**, SIMQ generates the **power spectra function** instead of acceleration time histories

9. **D**  
   - **Target damping for spectra**  
   - **Unit:** –  
   - **Default:** `0.05`  
   Specifies the damping ratio used when comparing the response spectrum of the generated record to the target spectrum.

10. **TITL**  
   - **Title of history**  
   - **Unit:** (not specified; shown as a label)  
   - **Default:** `Lit32`  
   Provides a descriptive identifier for the output accelerogram history.

### Overall interpretation for RAG use
Collectively, these parameters define (1) which spectral target and intensity shaping are used (LSPE, LINT), (2) the discretization and period range (DT, TMIN, TMAX, NFRE), (3) the iterative spectral-matching control (ITER, D), and (4) scaling/synthesis mode (AG). The context further recommends validating the generated record by computing its response spectrum using **REVA**, comparing it to **LSPE**, and generating accelerograms according to NISEE SIMQKE procedures.

See also: RESP, FUNC, ACCE, REVA
 SIMQ
 The generation of artificial accelerograms for earthquakes follows the procedures published by the NISEE in 1976 for the software SIMQKE. From a given target spectra, defined as:
 - Powerspectra in [m?/sec?]
 • Velocity spectra in [m/sec]
 - Acceleration spectra in [ m/sec? |
 random phase values (based on the load case number) will be generated and with the help of an intensity function will yield an accelerogram, adjusted with a target damping D to the response spectra with an iterative process. The base acceleration AG has to be selected to match the spectra. The default is 9.81 [m/sec?]. However the most common case is to switch off the scaling of the accelerogram altogether. This can be achieved by specifying the negative value for AG (e.g. SIMQ ... AG -1) (see sofiload.dat/english/simg.dat). If the value AG is specified as 0.0, the function of the power spectra is created instead of the accelerations.
 Hint
 It is strongly recommended, as a way of checking the validity of the generated accelel- ogram, to always calculate a response spectrum from a generated accelerogram and compare it with a target spectrum (LSPE). This can be achieved with the help of the command REVA (see sofiload.dat/english/simq.dat).

The input table defines parameters for the **REVA** response analysis, specifically controlling how a response spectrum (or power density spectrum) is computed and displayed from an excitation/load time history and one or more load functions.

### Core representation settings
- **TYPt (representation in dependence from)**: Selects the axis representation type for the spectrum. Allowed values in the table are:
  - `TIME` (time domain)
  - `FREQ` (frequency domain)
  - `LOGT` (logarithmic time)
  - `LOGF` (logarithmic frequency)
  - `DFT` (discrete Fourier transform)
  - `LDFT` (DFT with logarithmic frequency)
  - `PDS` (logarithmic power density spectra)
  - `PDSN` (normalized logarithmic power density spectrum)  
  **Default:** `TIME`.  
  This field affects how **TMIN/TMAX/TDIF** are interpreted and how intermediate sampling along the spectrum axis is constructed.

- **TYPE (result to be presented)**: Chooses the output quantity plotted for each natural period/frequency and damping value. Table options are:
  - `P` force
  - `S` displacement
  - `V` velocity
  - `A` relative acceleration
  - `AA` absolute acceleration
  - `AS` acceleration as a function of S
  - `AAS` AA as a function of S  
  **Default:** not specified explicitly in the table body; the overall parameter section implies `LIT` for TYPt and `TYPE` remains flexible.

### Load function selection
- **LFUN (number of the load function)**: Identifies which excitation/load function is used for the spectrum. The table notes the syntax conceptually as:
  - `loadcase.function_number` (written as `= load_case.sequencenumber` conceptually in the surrounding text).  
  **Default:** `1`.  
  In the broader description: load cases may contain multiple functions, and REVA can select them accordingly.

### Frequency/period range and discretization
- **TMIN (lowest natural period/frequency)**: Defines the start of the spectrum evaluation range. **Default:** `0`.  
- **TMAX (highest natural period/frequency)**: Defines the end of the spectrum range. **Default:** `!` (marked as unspecified/required in typical documentation style).  
- **TDIF (step size of natural periods/frequencies)**: Controls the increment between points on the spectrum axis. Unit: `sec, 1/sec`. **Default:** `*` indicating computed value in the text: `(TMIN - TMAX) / 50` (the table header indicates TDIF is derived unless explicitly given).  
  The text further clarifies special interpretations: if TYPt is logarithmic (LOGT/LOGF/LDFT etc.), TDIF acts as a **subdivision factor** relative to 1.0 for generating intermediate values; if `TYPE FREQ` is used, TMIN/TMAX/TDIF of RESP are treated as frequencies.

### Damping values (multiple simultaneous curves)
- **D1–D5 (modal damping values)**: Up to five damping cases can be evaluated and marked simultaneously:
  - **D1** marked with `.`, **default 0**
  - **D2** marked with `+`
  - **D3** marked with `*`
  - **D4** marked with `o`
  - **D5** marked with `x`  
  Each is dimensionless (“modal damping value”), and their specific numerical values determine where each response spectrum curve is computed.

### Optional reference curves
The table continues to support overlaying up to **two** reference curves (while surrounding text mentions three total reference curves overall):
- **REF1 / RID1**: reference curve number and its color/line type.
  - **Default curve configuration:** `RID1 = 2001` (color/line style ID), while **REF1** has no fixed default.
- **REF2 / RID2**:
  - **Default style:** `RID2 = 2001`  
  **Note:** The table excerpt ends after REF2/RID2; the provided narrative indicates that REVA can show three external reference curves when configured via FUNC or as constant limits.

Overall, this table specifies **(1)** what spectrum domain/scaling to use, **(2)** which response measure to output, **(3)** which excitation function drives the single-degree-of-freedom oscillator response, **(4)** the period/frequency evaluation range and discretization, **(5)** up to five damping ratios for multiple curves, and **(6)** optional reference curves with styling.

 REVA allows the calculation of a response spectra for a given load or acceleration function. Any load case may contain more than one function. The input selection can be done for LFUN or REF1 to REF3 with the syntax loadcase.sequencenumber.
 This is done by the response analysis of a single mass oscillator within a given frequency range. Then the maximum results depending on the frequency or period are visualized.
 If the LFUN has been established by a transient analysis with DYNA, it is strongly suggested to use the total accelerations. These can be only obtained if the loading is defined as accel- eration. (see ACCE) A transient analysis with eqvivalent forces will not allow to add the base accelerations to the results.
 For TYPE one can also enter P+, S+, V+, A+, AA+ as well as P-, S-, V-, A-, AA-. Then only the positive or negative components are evaluated. In the case of excitation through an acceleration, TYPE AA can be used to plot the total acceleration (ground+oscillator). This is usually the desired value. Without a specification for TYPE the original function is shown.
 The duration of the evaluation is determined by the highest time value of the excitation value. A somewhat longer time range with exciting function 0.0 should thus be defined in the case of high frequency excitation.
 For a FFT or PDS evaluation TDIF is required as constant time value for a genral time function. The default is the first time step of the selected function. It can be also specified with a negative number of the time steps. TMIN and TMAX will be the frequencies of visualized range of the resulting spectrum.
 Up to five different damping values can be examined simultaneously. The damping values D1 through D5 can be used arbitrarily according to the desired marking.
