TMIN and TMAX will be the frequencies of visualized range of the resulting spectrum.. Up to five different damping values can be examined simultaneously. The damping values D1 through D5 can be used arbitrarily according to the desired marking..
 Three external reference curves may be shown. These functions have to be defined either via FUNC or may be selected as a constant limit value specified by a number and an attached unit specification.
 For wind spectra two factors are needed. The first factor is to convert the natural frequency to the spectral ordinate (x = f*L/U or similar). The second factor is to denormalize the spectra and is obtained from the standard deviation σ. These values will be passed from WGEN over FIMP to REVA, but may be specified also at D1 and D2 explicitly.
 The use of the generated responsespectrum of type A and AA as a load is only possible if no reference curve has been selected!
 When TYPE FREQ is input, the values TMIN, TMAX and TDIF of the RESP input are inter- preted as frequencies too.
 If LOGT, LOGF or LDFT are defined, a TIME, FREQ or DFT with a logarithmic time or frequency scale will be performed. If LLGT, LLGF or LLFT are defined, a TIME, FREQ or DFT with a double logarithmic scale will be performed. TDIF defines then a subdivision factor relative to 1.0 for the number of intermediate values (e.g. TDIF 0.05 = 20 intermediate values). However if PDS0 or PDS1 is defined, none or only the frequency axis will be selected as logarithmic for a PDS:

The table defines the configurable inputs for a “PUSH” (pushover) analysis module, i.e., a nonlinear static procedure used to estimate seismic demand/response by progressively applying lateral forces or displacements to a structural model. The surrounding context notes that the general workflow and theoretical background are provided elsewhere (Section 4.1), while this table enumerates the specific parameters exposed to the user.

### Layout and columns
- **Item**: Short parameter identifier used in configuration interfaces or input files.
- **Description**: Human-readable meaning of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Engineering units associated with the parameter (where applicable).
- **Default**: The default value or indicator if a value is required to be provided by the user. An asterisk “*” denotes a default or behavior that is not a fixed literal value (i.e., it must be determined/selected).

### Analysis type selection (Item: TYPE, OPT)
**TYPE (Analysis Type)** selects the computational method or representation used for the pushover workflow. The **Unit** column shows **LIT**, indicating the field is literal/choice-based rather than dimensional.
- **VB-U**: “Base Shear – Control Node Displacement diagram”
- **A-D**: “Spectral Acceleration – Spectral Displacement diagram”
- **ATC**: “ATC-40 Procedure”
- **EC8**: “Eurocode 8 Procedure”

**OPT (Additional Option)** provides additional modeling/behavior classification options, also marked with **LIT**.
- **SBTA**: Structural Behavior Type A
- **SBTB**: Structural Behavior Type B
- **SBTC**: Structural Behavior Type C  
This suggests the analysis can be aligned with different nonlinear capacity/demand assumptions typical of code-based approaches.

### Capacity curve load case definition (LCC fields)
These parameters determine how the capacity curve (monotonic nonlinear pushover backbone) is constructed.
- **LCC0**: “Basis load case for capacity curve” (no unit; default is “-” meaning no preset)
- **LCC1**: “First load case of the capacity curve” (no unit; default is “-”)
- **NLCC**: “Number of load cases of the capacity curve” (dimensionless). Default shown as **1**, implying at least one load case increment/step is used unless specified otherwise.

### Control and damping parameters (CNOD, DSTR)
- **CNOD (Control node)**: Specifies which node’s displacement drives the pushover control variable. This is nondimensional in terms of the table schema; default is “-” (must be defined).
- **DSTR (Viscous structural damping)**: Represents viscous damping ratio used in response calculations or spectrum matching. Unit is “-” and default is “*”, indicating the damping value is typically required/selected rather than hard-coded.

### Demand load case and performance limits (LCDM, SPL fields)
- **LCDM (Demand load case)**: Identifies the load case representing the seismic demand side (e.g., selected from spectral/target demand construction). Default “-” implies required configuration.
- **SPL1–SPL5 (Structural Performance Limits 1 to 5)**: Define up to five performance thresholds used to classify structural response states (e.g., damage/limit states).  
  - Unit: **[mm] × 10^3** (the table shows **[mm]1003**, i.e., millimeters with an indicated scaling factor \(10^3\)).  
  - Defaults for SPL1–SPL5 are “-” (user-defined values).  
These limits likely correspond to displacement-based criteria that map the computed pushover/control responses to performance levels.

Overall, the table centralizes key choices for pushover formulation (TYPE/OPT), defines capacity curve generation (LCC0/LCC1/NLCC), sets the nonlinear control and damping basis (CNOD/DSTR), links to demand definition (LCDM), and establishes displacement-based performance interpretation (SPL1–SPL5).

See also: ACCE, RESP
 PUSH
 General workflow and theoretical background behind the pushover analysis are described in Section 4.1.

The table defines the **input parameter schema** for a SOFiLOAD command that creates a **capacity/demand “pushover curve” basis (VB-U) and its subsequent transformation** into other capacity-spectrum formats. It is presented as a two-sided specification listing, for each keyword/field, a short description, the expected unit (or none), and a default value where applicable. The table’s header indicates the columns: **(1) Parameter**, **(2) Description**, **(3) Unit**, and **(4) Default**.

### Columns
- **PUSH**: Command/function context (the section is about parameters under a `PUSH` input block).
- **Description**: Human-readable meaning of each parameter.
- **Unit**: Engineering unit type for the parameter; if the parameter is an index/identifier, the unit is “–”.
- **Default**: Value used if the parameter is omitted.

### Rows / Parameters
1. **TYPE**
   - **Meaning**: Analysis/format type of the pushover conversion.
   - **Values shown**: Default is **VB-U** (explicitly stated in the “Default” column).
   - **Unit**: `LIT` (literature/enum-like token).
   - **Interpretation in context**: Determines whether the result remains in **VB–U** format or is converted later to other formats (A–D, ATC, EC8 conversions are discussed in the surrounding text).

2. **LCC0**
   - **Meaning**: “Basis load case for capacity curve”.
   - **Unit**: `–` (load case identifier).
   - **Default**: none shown (must be provided for capacity curve definition).
   - **Role in context**: Supplies the **control DOF displacement basis** used to scale/select the control-node displacement for subsequent load cases (also referenced as the basis capacity load case in the narrative).

3. **LCC1**
   - **Meaning**: “First load case of the capacity curve”.
   - **Unit**: `–` (load case identifier).
   - **Default**: none shown.
   - **Role in context**: Starting index for the incremental load cases that form the capacity curve.

4. **NLCC**
   - **Meaning**: “Number of load cases of the capacity curve”.
   - **Unit**: `–` (count).
   - **Default**: **1**.
   - **Role in context**: Together with `LCC1`, defines the load case range used for the curve (e.g., `LCC1` through `LCC1 + NLCC − 1`).

5. **CNOD**
   - **Meaning**: “Control node”.
   - **Unit**: `–` (node identifier).
   - **Default**: none shown.
   - **Role in context**: The **base shear and displacement** are referenced to the control node (e.g., “node 4” in examples), and displacement may be taken component-wise or via an Euclidean norm unless `LCDM` is used.

6. **LCDM**
   - **Meaning**: “Control direction (optional)”.
   - **Unit**: `LIT` (enum/direction selector).
   - **Default**: `–` (not provided by default).
   - **Direction sub-options**:
     - **X**: Global X direction
     - **Y**: Global Y direction
     - **Z**: Global Z direction
   - **Role in context**: Allows explicit selection of how the control components are taken (directional base shear/displacement). Without it, the method uses the **Euclidean norm of dominant components** determined from the control-node displacement in the basis case.

Overall, the table encodes how to **select the load case range** (`LCC0`, `LCC1`, `NLCC`), **identify the structural response point** (`CNOD`), and optionally **fix the directionality** (`LCDM`), with `TYPE` controlling the output representation (defaulting to **VB-U**).

The table is a compact parameter reference for the **PUSH** command used in a pushover-capacity/demand workflow (e.g., converting a pushover curve into an ATC-40, A-D, or EC8 capacity spectrum representation). It lists the **field names**, a short **description** of each field, and two metadata columns: **Unit** and **Default**. The table has 6 columns: **PUSH**, **Description**, **(right-side) Unit**, and **Default**.

### Row/field meanings

- **TYPE**  
  - **Description:** Selects the analysis/output format for the pushover-to-spectra conversion and capacity spectrum method. In the surrounding context, supported formats include **A-D**, **ATC**, and **EC8** (and other variants may exist).  
  - **Unit:** LIT (treated as a literal/enum field rather than a physical quantity).  
  - **Default:** **A-D**.

- **LCC0**  
  - **Description:** **Basis load case for the capacity curve**. This is the load case used to obtain the base/reference quantities needed for capacity curve construction and performance-point-related properties (e.g., displacement DOF of the control node, assumed displacement shape vector, modal/participation information).  
  - **Unit:** “–” (no physical unit).  
  - **Default:** “–” (not given; required).

- **LCC1**  
  - **Description:** **First load case of the capacity curve**. Together with **NLCC**, it defines the sequence of incremental capacity/control values that form the capacity curve. In the text examples, these are load cases 2301…(2301+NLCC−1).  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** “–” (required).

- **NLCC**  
  - **Description:** **Number of load cases of the capacity curve**. Determines how many load cases starting from **LCC1** are used to build the capacity curve.  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **1**.

- **CNOD**  
  - **Description:** **Control node**. The base shear and displacement are extracted using the response of this node (denoted as the control node displacement). The narrative emphasizes that base shear/displacement can be taken using either component selection (**LCDM**) or Euclidean norms of dominant DOFs derived from the control-node displacement in **LCC0**.  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** “–” (required).

- **LCDM**  
  - **Description:** **Demand load case**. Used as the input for the seismic demand spectrum; the selected demand load case is converted into the appropriate demand coordinate system depending on **TYPE** (A-D/ATC/EC8). Also, in the earlier explanation, it can define the control direction/component-wise selection (depending on the chosen convention), thereby affecting the global direction of base shear and displacement in the converted curve.  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** not specified in the table (implied required).

### Overall structure intent
This table documents the **essential scalar inputs** required by the PUSH command to (1) define the **capacity curve** from a set of load cases (**LCC0/LCC1/NLCC**) and (2) define the **demand representation** from a spectrum load case (**LCDM**), using a specified **control node** (**CNOD**) and a specified **conversion/solution TYPE** (**TYPE**).

The table defines the input parameters for the SOFiLOAD **PUSH** command segment that constructs a **pushover-based capacity spectrum / performance point** according to different analysis formats. It is organized into five columns: **“PUSH”**, **“Description”**, **“Unit”**, and **“Default”**. Each row specifies a keyword used in the command and explains its role in forming the capacity and demand curves.

**Row groups and meaning**
- **TYPE**: Selects the analysis procedure and thus the overall method used to compute the performance point from the capacity and demand diagrams.
  - Values: **ATC** (ATC-40 Procedure) is shown, with **Default = ATC**. Unit is “LIT” (literals/choice rather than physical unit).
- **OPT**: Specifies an additional option, mainly used to select the **structural behavior type**.
  - Default is **SBTA**.
  - Options:
    - **SBTA**: Structural Behavior Type A (Default shown as SBTA)
    - **SBTB**: Structural Behavior Type B
    - **SBT C**: Structural Behavior Type C
  - Unit column again indicates “LIT”.
- **LCC0**: The **basis load case for the capacity curve**. This provides key deformation information (e.g., the basis displacement shape / control DOF displacement) used to define the capacity coordinates (notably referenced in the accompanying text as basis load case used to determine control-node displacement and participation information). No physical unit; Default “-”.
- **LCC1**: The **first load case of the capacity curve**. Together with LCC0 and NLCC it defines the sequence of computed incremental load cases used to sample the pushover curve. Default “-”.
- **NLCC**: **Number of load cases of the capacity curve**. The Default is **1**. In typical usage (from the context), NLCC specifies how many consecutive load cases starting at LCC1 are included.
- **CNOD**: The **control node** whose displacement is used to represent the system response in the pushover and subsequent transformations (e.g., base shear vs. control node displacement curve). Default “-”.
- **DSTR**: **Viscous structural damping** (inherent viscous damping of the structure). Unit is not physical here but implied as damping ratio; Default is **0.05** (i.e., 5%).
- **LCDM**: The **demand load case** defining the elastic response spectrum (e.g., via RESP) that will be converted into the demand representation compatible with the selected PUSH TYPE/option (A-D / ATC / EC8). Default “-”.

Overall, the table captures how a user parameterizes the transformation pipeline: **capacity curve assembly** from {LCC0, LCC1, NLCC, CNOD} and **demand spectrum selection/formatting** from LCDM, while TYPE/OPT determine the **ATC-40 method** and the assumed **hysteretic behavior class** used in damping and energy-based links.

The image is a single multi-panel figure (Figure 4.16) on a white background, with a SOFiSTiK/Dynamic Loads header at the top-right. It contains three side-by-side/stacked subplots labeled (a), (b), and (c), each depicting the derivation of the effective viscous damping parameter \( \xi_{\mathrm{eff}} \) for an equivalent linear SDOF system using energy relationships from an inelastic capacity diagram.

**Panel (a): “Capacity diagram” (top-left).**  
Axes are shown in an \(S_a\) (vertical) versus \(S_{d}\) (horizontal) format (ADRS-like). The horizontal axis is labeled \(S_{d}\) with tick/marker points \(S_{d,p}\) (performance-point displacement) and the larger \(S_d\) direction arrow. The vertical axis is labeled \(S_a\). A red concave capacity curve rises from the origin to a black point labeled **PP** (performance point) at coordinates \((S_{d,p}, S_{ap})\). Dashed projection lines indicate the PP coordinates: a vertical dashed line down to \(S_{d,p}\) and a horizontal dashed line to \(S_{ap}\). The area under the red curve up to the PP is shaded light pink and labeled **\(E_c\)**, representing deformation/combined strain energy (capacity energy).

**Panel (b): “Bi-linear approximation of capacity” (top-right).**  
The same \(S_a\) vs \(S_d\) axes are used. The red curve is now overlaid with a black, idealized bilinear capacity approximation. Two key black points appear: **PY** (yield point) at \((S_{d,y}, S_{ay})\), and **PP** at \((S_{d,p}, S_{ap})\). A gray shaded region is bounded by the bilinear idealization and the red curve segment, and it is labeled **\(E_b\)**. A dashed line indicates \(S_{ay}\). Additionally, the effective stiffness term \( \omega_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}\) appears near the upper right, and a dashed horizontal line at \(S_{ap}\) indicates the performance acceleration level. A dashed vertical/horizontal construction provides the yield displacement \(S_{d,y}\) and performance displacement \(S_{d,p}\).

**Panel (c): “Hysteretic dissipation energy \(E_D\) and maximum strain energy \(E_S\)” (bottom).**  
This panel combines both the inelastic hysteretic and elastic energy concepts in the same \(S_a\)–\(S_d\) coordinate system. A red “capacity”/envelope curve (with black outline) reaches the black **PP** point at \((S_{d,p}, S_{ap})\). The gray shaded region extends from the origin to the PP along a black envelope, labeled **\(E_D\)** (hysteretic dissipation energy). A green shaded triangular region on the upper side is labeled **\(E_S\)** (maximum strain energy). Dashed construction lines project from PP to the axes: a dashed horizontal line at \(S_{ap}\) and a vertical dashed line down to \(S_{d,p}\). The yield displacement \(S_{d,y}\) is marked on the \(S_d\) axis, and a dashed/outlined boundary indicates the yield level and the transition in the bilinear idealization. The labels \(S_d\), \(S_a\), and specific symbols \(S_{dy}\), \(S_{ap}\), and **PP/PY** provide coordinate landmarks needed for energy-based calculation of equivalent damping.

Overall, the figure visually communicates how the effective damping \(\xi_{\mathrm{eff}}\) can be derived by comparing capacity-related energies (area under the curve \(E_c\), bilinear energy \(E_b\)), and separating the hysteretic dissipation energy \(E_D\) from the maximum strain energy \(E_S\) at the performance point.

The table is titled **“Table 4.12: Values for damping modification factor, K (ATC-40)”**. It provides numerical **parameters for the ATC-40 capacity spectrum method** that are needed to account for how real hysteretic (inelastic) behavior can be represented by an equivalent linear viscous damping model.

### Structure
- The table has **three columns**:
  1. **SBT**: a categorical label describing the **structural behavior type** (as defined in ATC-40) of the hysteretic force–displacement loops.
  2. **ξ0 [%]**: a threshold/value condition for the **initial equivalent viscous damping** (expressed in percent), used to choose the correct K expression for certain SBT categories.
  3. **K**: the corresponding **damping modification factor** value or formula.

### Rows / Meaning of Entries
- **SBT = A**:
  - Condition: **ξ0 ≤ 16.25%**
  - K = **1.00**
  - Condition: **ξ0 > 16.25%**
  - K = **1.130 − 0.510·(ξ0/π/2)**  
  (the table expresses the correction term in terms of ξ0 scaled by π/2; effectively ξ0 is inserted into the linear expression with that normalization).

- **SBT = B**:
  - Condition: **ξ0 ≤ 25.00%**
  - K = **0.67**
  - Condition: **ξ0 > 25.00%**
  - K = **0.845 − 0.446·(ξ0/π/2)**

- **SBT = C**:
  - Condition: **Any value**
  - K = **0.33**

### Interpretation for RAG / Retrieval
This table is not a dataset of structural results but a **lookup rule** used during ATC-40 calculations. Given:
- the structural behavior type (**A, B, or C**), and
- the damping parameter **ξ0** (equivalent viscous damping representing hysteretic damping),
the table yields **K**, which later affects the **effective damping of the equivalent linear SDOF system**, via an equation of the form **ξeƒƒ = ξstr + κ·ξ0** (where κ corresponds to this table’s K).

In summary, the table defines **piecewise constants/formulas** for K that depend on both **hysteresis quality (SBT)** and **magnitude of ξ0**, with constant values for low-damping regimes and linear corrections for higher ξ0 for types A and B, while type C uses a single constant for all ξ0.

### Table description (for RAG indexing)

**Table 4.13: “Minimum allowable \(SR_a\) and \(SR_v\) value”** provides lower-bound limits for **spectral reduction factors** used in seismic analysis, specifically when converting elastic response spectra to equivalent reduced (highly damped/effective) demand spectra within ATC-40/related capacity-spectrum formulations.

The table has a compact structure with **three columns**:

1. **Hysteretic behavior type (SBT)**: a categorical index describing the quality of hysteretic loops and their expected cyclic degradation. The table includes:
   - **A**: stable, reasonably full hysteresis loops.
   - **B**: moderate reduction of loop area.
   - **C**: poor hysteresis behavior with substantial reduction of loop area (pinched and/or degraded loops).

2. **\(SR_a\)** (minimum): the **minimum allowable spectral reduction factor** associated with **spectral acceleration**. Values reflect the floor beyond which \(SR_a\) must not be reduced further, depending on behavior type.
   - For **Type A**: \(SR_{a,\min} = 0.33\)
   - For **Type B**: \(SR_{a,\min} = 0.44\)
   - For **Type C**: \(SR_{a,\min} = 0.56\)

3. **\(SR_v\)** (minimum): the **minimum allowable spectral reduction factor** associated with **spectral velocity** (or the corresponding reduction factor used in the velocity-domain relationship of the spectrum reduction scheme).
   - For **Type A**: \(SR_{v,\min} = 0.50\)
   - For **Type B**: \(SR_{v,\min} = 0.56\)
   - For **Type C**: \(SR_{v,\min} = 0.67\)

**Interpretation:** As the hysteretic behavior degrades from **A → B → C**, the minimum allowable reduction factors **increase**. This means the method enforces less aggressive spectrum reduction (i.e., larger retained demand modifiers) when hysteretic performance is poorer, consistent with higher uncertainty or reduced energy dissipation effectiveness from pinching/degradation.

**Key takeaway for usage in workflow:** When calculating spectral reduction factors (e.g., using equations like Newmark & Hall relations), the computed \(SR_a\) and \(SR_v\) must be checked against these tabulated minimum values to ensure the reduction does not fall below the prescribed thresholds for the selected behavior type.

The performance point is used to compare the global response of structure and individual component deformations to limit values in context of the specific performance objectives for the building in question. The performance objective represents the desired building perfor- mance level under a given seismic hazard (earthquake ground motion). The performance levels are defined by the performance limits (ATC-40 [5]). The structural performance limits can be categorized as:
 • Local element and component acceptability limits. Each component (beam, column, slab, connections, etc.) of the structural elements (frames, seismic walls, diaphragms, foundations, etc.) should be checked to verify if its response under a given seismic demand (level of forces and deformations corresponding to the performance point) is within the acceptable limits (performance limits). Local performance limits for beam plastic hinges can be defined in AQUA (see AQUA: SFLA).

Train loads for bridges are ruled by the fact, that the most unfavourable position of the loading is different for every single element and reaction and not known in advance.
 The base of the moving load process is a lane geometry, described in the plan view by straight, circular or clothoid segments and in the elevation as straight or quadratic parabola. This can be taken from the database as defined by SOFiMSHB or explicitly input with the record GAX. Each axis may have up to 99 separate lanes defined via LANE. For the dynamic impact coefficients an effective length may be specified and the extra width of the traffic area may be defined.
 Each lane has two coordinate systems. There is a local system (x) at the lane axis for real distances. However, the inputs for the positions along the lanes are entered in a global system of stations (s) which defines an alignment of the lanes to each other.
 There are three principal approaches for the problem of finding the most unfavourable load position:
 • One can generate numerous load cases with the train load at distinct positions and search for the maximum with the superposition tool MAXIMA. For some load definitions this ap- proach is not possible with acceptable effort however.
 • More general one can establish the influence lines for the forces and moments of all or selected locations within the structure. In a second step these influence lines may be eval- uated with the load trains. The result are direct extreme values of all forces and moments. This is performed with the program module ELLA, highly optimized for this task.
 Last not least a transient analysis of the load coursing the structure with the program DYNA is possible. For the animation of this process the record TREX is very helpful.
 •
 Depending on the system and the loading, the one or the other method will be better. Spe- cial effects like a load which is not bound to the lane in transverse direction (EC) or having independent wheels (DIN) may increase the number of needed load cases considerably.

For the animation of this process the record TREX is very helpful.. •. Depending on the system and the loading, the one or the other method will be better.  The commands available for the load train definition are:
 TRAI Specifying the load train
 TRPL, TRBL Explicit loading of a load train
 With this commands no loading will be applied to the structure yet. The load definitions are saved under a load case number which should not be used otherwise. It is the SOFiLOAD / COPY command that will transform the train to individual loading. With a reference to a geometric line (GAX) and an associated lane (LANE) the following transformations will take place:
 • The load train will be adopted to the geometry of the lane.
 • Centrifugal loading will be created based on the speed of the train and the curvature of the lane.
 • Variable eccentricities will be applied automaticallly in an unfaourable way.

This table defines **load group (“gr”) selections for traffic-induced actions** and maps each group to the **participation of vertical load components (LM1 variants and LM4)** and the **participation of horizontal load components (braking and centrifugal)**. It is intended to be used inside a *load-train / combination* framework where different parts of a complete train may require different combination coefficients (e.g., based on DIN FB / EN 1991-2 / other standards).

### Table structure
- **Column “type”**: names the load group (gr0…gr6). These are the selectors used by the software/combination engine.
- **Vertical loads**:
  - **LM1(TS)**: LM1 with traffic surface / “TS” coefficient set.
  - **LM1(UDL)**: LM1 with uniform distributed load (“UDL”) coefficient set.
  - **LM4**: a separate vertical load term acting on an area or specified location.
- **Horizontal loads**:
  - **braking**: braking action coefficient status.
  - **centrifugal**: centrifugal action coefficient status.

### Meaning of coefficient labels
- **“Charact.”** indicates characteristic-value participation (ψ = 1 at the reference action level).
- **“frequent”** and **“non frequent”** indicate reduced design combinations using frequency-based factors.
- **“permanent”** indicates the most reduced (long-term) participation level.
- **“(*)”** means a special case/conditional coefficient is used (not fully specified by this table alone; likely depends on external parameters or rules).
- **Numeric entries like “0.5 Charact.”** indicate a fixed multiplier of the characteristic value (here, 0.5×).

### Group-by-group mapping
- **gr0**: vertical LM1(TS) is **characteristic**; no LM1(UDL), no LM4; no braking/centrifugal.
- **grU**: vertical LM1(UDL) is **characteristic** only; no LM1(TS), no LM4; no horizontals.
- **gr1**: LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) are both **characteristic**; braking and centrifugal are **conditional** (**(*)**).
- **gr2**: LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) are **frequent**; braking is **characteristic**; centrifugal is **characteristic**.
- **gr2n**: LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) are **frequent**; braking and centrifugal are both **non frequent**.
- **gr2f**: LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) are **permanent**; braking is **frequent**; centrifugal is **frequent**.
- **gr3**: LM1(UDL) is **characteristic** but specified as **“on sidewalks”**; no braking/centrifugal; LM1(TS) and LM4 are not applied here.
- **gr4**: LM4 is **characteristic UDL on total area**; no LM1(TS), no LM1(UDL) entries; no horizontals.
- **gr5**: LM1(TS) is **“LM3 characteristic in main lane”**; LM1(UDL) is **“LM1 frequent on other lanes”**; no LM4; no horizontals.
- **gr6**: LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) are both **0.5× characteristic**; braking and centrifugal are both **0.5× characteristic**. This group is referenced as relevant for **exchange of supports according to DIN FB**.

### Use within broader combination logic (context)
In the surrounding framework, load group selection determines which **PSI coefficients** are applied to components of a traffic load train. For “other than characteristic” combinations, PSI1 coefficients from **EN 1991-2 / BS EN 1990** (or standard-specific defaults) are used, unless overridden by special train load cases via **PSI1(TS)** and **PSI2(UDL)**. Additionally, for road bridges, DIN FB Appendix C imposes restrictions on **combining LM2/single pathway loads with other life loads**, and on relationships between **snow/wind**, **braking**, and specific load groups (e.g., gr2/gr3, gr1/LM1 thresholds, and wind vs temperature mutual exclusivity). For railway bridges, groups 11–31 (DIN FB 101 table 6.6) are better handled with dedicated evaluation methods (ELLΑ/MAXIMA) rather than by explicit combined loading; wind and life load are coupled by position and threshold.

Overall, this table provides the **component-level coefficient participation map** needed to construct the correct combination of vertical and horizontal bridge actions for each predefined **load group**.

The table defines the **parameter schema for a SOFi/SoFiLOAD/ELLА/TENDON general geometric axis (GAX) / lane axis**. Each record represents one geometric axis segment or point on the axis, depending on how the axis definition is authored. Columns specify identifiers, stationing, spatial coordinates, curvature parameters, and orientation vectors that are needed to generate the axis in 3D. The table is structured with fields for name, description, unit, and default value.

### Fields and meaning

- **NO (Axis identifier)** (`LIT4`, default **A1**)  
  A label for the axis definition. It allows multiple axes (e.g., B1, B2, A1…) to coexist in a data set.

- **S (Total arc length / station)** (`—`, default **0**)  
  Represents the stationing/arc-length along the axis. In the provided context, this aligns with the “length resp. station in the plan view” concept used for axis segments: the first record establishes starting conditions and includes an initial segment length; subsequent records typically add only incremental segment lengths and/or curvature-related parameters.

- **X, Y, Z (Real-world coordinates of point)** (`[m]1001`, default **0** each)  
  Define the 3D coordinates of the axis element reference point. In the context text, for definitions using 3D points along a curve, **coordinates are required for all records**.

- **R (Radius of the lane axis)** (`[m]1001`, default shown as **“–” / not set**)  
  Curvature parameter representing circular arc radius. The sign convention matters: **positive R curves to the right-hand side**, negative R curves to the left-hand side. If R is not given, the system can compute it automatically from the provided geometry/length; if R is provided together with A, the curvature at the start point is derived differently.

- **A (Transition curve parameter / clothoid parameter)** (`[m]1001`, default **“–” / not set**)  
  Used to create curvature transitions, described as **transition curve R·L = A²** (i.e., linking radius, transition length, and A). The context further states:  
  - **A > 0**: curvature increases through the transition (clothoid spiral)  
  - **A < 0**: curvature decreases  
  - **A = 0.0**: indicates **piecewise constant curvature** (basket arches / pure circular segments)

- **NX, NY, NZ (Direction vector for curves in 3D)** (`—`, default `*`)  
  These define the **local z-axis direction**. The context clarifies: the given direction (NX, NY, NZ) is the local z-axis and therefore the defined circular arc rotates around this vector. The defaults are marked `*`, implying these values are required/meaningful depending on the axis type or authoring mode (e.g., 3D curve definition).

- **TYPE (Type of axis)** (`LIT`, default **AXIS**)  
  Governs interpretation of the axis:
  - **AXIS** = general axis  
  - **LANE** = traffic lane  
  - **BGER0 / BGEO** = bridge geometry line  
  The table’s default indicates the general case is **AXIS**.

- **TITL (Designation of lane / axis title)** (`LIT32`, default **–**)  
  Human-readable designation used to label the axis. In the context text, titles like **“SPIRAL AND CIRCLE”**, **“THREE CENTER CURVE”**, and **“CENTER GEOMETRY”** appear.

### Overall interpretation for RAG ingestion
Each row/record in this table contributes to constructing a 2D/3D alignment: stationing (**S**), spatial anchor (**X/Y/Z** when required), curvature definition (**R**, **A**), and orientation (**NX/NY/NZ**). The axis may be defined by a simplified segment-chain approach (first record carries start point and direction, then subsequent records provide segment lengths and curvature parameters) or by a full 3D point approach (coordinates required for all records). After definition, the described elements are intended to be imported/adopted as **dynamic axes** (e.g., via WinGRAF), with graphical verification recommended.

The table defines the **input data structure for a SOFiLOAD/ELLА lane load definition**. It lists parameters grouped into (a) lane identification and predefined lane layouts, (b) curbstone geometry and lane boundaries at the start/end of a segment, (c) longitudinal segmentation and effective loading length, and (d) vertical road/track geometry and railway-specific effective parameters.

## Lane identification and predefined type
- **NO (Lane number, `lane_ident.nummer`)** *(Unit: LIT; Default: `*`)*  
  Identifies the lane within an axis, e.g., “A1.3” = third lane of axis A1. A note indicates `lane_ident only = all/total lanes`.
- **TYPE (Predefined type)** *(Unit: LIT; Default: `*`)*  
  Selects a standard lane layout literal. Remarks in the surrounding text indicate available standards/lane schemes (e.g., EN 1991-2 / DIN-Fachbericht 101, BS, TMH7, Canadian, Indian, Japan, Australian). For many “RQ…” types, **curbstone coordinates are required** and constant along the total lane.

## Curbstone coordinates (right/left edges)
- **WR (Ordinate of right curbstone)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `-`)*  
- **WL (Ordinate of left curbstone)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `-WR`)*  

These establish the lateral extent of the traffic load area used for lane generation (notably for certain predefined types where total width is derived from these curbstone coordinates).

## Longitudinal stationing (start/end)
For a lane definition that is possibly piecewise along the structure:
- **SA (Coordinate along lane axis for start)** *(Unit: —; Default: `!`)*  
- **SE (Coordinate along lane axis for end)** *(Unit: —; Default: `!`)*  

The table segment runs from **SA to SE** along a defined geometrical lane axis.

## Lateral lane centre offsets and boundaries (start/end)
Offsets and boundary positions are defined separately at start and end to allow varying lane widths and eccentricities:
- **YCA (Offset of centre of lane at start)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `*`)*  
- **YCE (Offset of centre of lane at end)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `YCA`)*  
- **YRA (Right value at start)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `*`)*  
- **YLA (Left value at start)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `*`)*  
- **YRE (Right value at end)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `YRA`)*  
- **YLE (Left value at end)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `YLA`)*  

This supports lane widening/narrowing by station, and the surrounding notes clarify that **edge intersections must be treated only at distinct points** to enable correct torsional loading.

## Effective loaded length / impact segmentation
- **L (Effective length of segment for impact coefficients and loaded length dependencies)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `*`)*  
  Used when the effective loaded length differs from the geometrical segment.  
- **CONT (Literal “add to last segment”)** *(Unit: —; Default: —)*  
  Used when combining multiple lane-definitions into a single longitudinal segment: **L is given only for the first definition**, while others specify `CONT` to avoid resetting the effective length.

## Vertical geometry and railway-specific effective parameters
The table includes parameters affecting moments (and railway ballast stress modeling):
- **HSA (Height of deck or rail above lane at SA)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `0.0`)*  
- **HSE (Height of deck or rail above lane at SE)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `HSA`)*  
- **INCA / INCE (Cross fall at SA / SE)** *(Unit: [mm]; Default: `0.0` and `INCA` respectively)*  
  Represents cross fall `dz/dy` or `Δh[mm]`, influencing additional moments.
- **HEFF (Effective height of rail and sleeper)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `-`)*  
- **BEFF (Effective length of sleeper)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `-`)*  
- **DEFF (Effective width of sleeper)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `0`/`-` as shown; purpose: rail/wall effective geometry)*  
- **INCD (Spread angle for stresses)** *(Unit: —; Default: `0.25`)*  
  Used for calculating spread of stresses (railway).

- **ASL (Distance between mounting points)** *(Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default: `-`)*  
  Railway-specific parameter related to mounting/stress distribution.

## Interpretive notes linking to the broader lane concept
The surrounding text explains that:
- Up to **99 lanes** can be defined relative to an axis, and lanes must be **defined together** because redefining deletes prior lane definitions.
- **Lane 0** is mandatory and acts as the basis for residual/pathway inclusion (pathways only included in lane 0; gaps between lanes are not treated as residual loading).
- Predefined lane types may auto-create secondary lanes; for certain standards, curbstone coordinates are required and total width is constant along the lane.

Overall, this table specifies all parameters needed to fully characterize **lateral lane geometry (centre, boundaries, curbstone limits), longitudinal extent (SA/SE with impact-effective length L), and vertical/railway properties (HSA/HSE, cross fall, and railway effective dimensions)**.

The table defines **parameters for a “load train”** in a structural loading context (e.g., road/rail traffic, wind, braking, centrifugal effects, and fatigue/relevant train models). Each row lists an **Item** (parameter name), its **Description** (what the parameter controls), the **Unit** (where applicable), and a **Default** value. The parameters are grouped conceptually into: load train type/values, special loading regions (spare/wind), geometry (width/eccentricity/heights), scaling factors, dynamic/impact-related factors, and direction/sequence controls.

### Core identification and load definition
- **TYPE**: Selects the **type of load train** (parameter corresponds to a predefined loading model). Default shown as **CONS** (constant/required setting rather than a numeric default).
- **P1–P4**: Up to four generic **load values** for the train definition. They share unit **kN,m** and are marked with default “*”, meaning the actual default is type-dependent (often taken from the chosen train definition or left to be specified).
- **P5**: Load applied to **spare areas** (unit **kN/m²**). Default “*” indicates train/type-dependent usage. Context text clarifies that residual area loading P5 is applied **without dynamic impact factors and without centrifugal forces**, only to specified area portions (based on train constant width vs polygon/lane bounds; and for certain load groups such as pedestrian-bridge-like GR4 total lane area).
- **P6**: **Wind loading** parameter (unit marked as “*”, i.e., type/definition-dependent).
- **P7**: **Height of wind attack area / height of wind load** (unit **[m]1001**; default “*”).
- **P8**: Parameter for **brake load** (unit marked “*”). The context explains that the **sign/direction logic** for P8 is handled relative to train motion direction, with special handling options in ELLA/SOFILOAD.
- **P9**: **Height of mass center** used for **centrifugal load and crossfall** effects (unit **[m]1001**; default “*”).

### Scaling and geometry
- **PFAC**: Multiplier for **the total load train** (dimensionless). Default **1.0**.
- **PFAV**: Multiplier for **favorable effects within load trains** (dimensionless; train-dependent default is discussed in the context). Context indicates defaults differ for railway vs road trains and for LM71 vs other load cases; PFAV may apply only to **wheel loads** for road train loadings.
- **WIDT**: **Width of the load train** (unit **[m]1001**; default “*”). Context links WIDT to residual area loading: if **WIDT = 0**, there will be **no residual area P5** for railways.
  
### Dynamic/impact and speed
- **PHI**: Explicit **impact factor for bending** (dimensionless; default “*”).
- **PHIS**: Explicit **impact factor for shear** (dimensionless; default “*”).
- **V**: **Speed of load train** (unit **[km/h]1203**; default “*”). Speed influences dynamic-related effects.

- **FUGA**: Factor for masses of total train used for **centrifugal forces** (dimensionless; default **1.0**).

### Repeated-convoy spacing and eccentricity
- **XCON**: **Minimum distance for repeated load trains** (convoy) (unit **[m]1001**; default **0**). Context: if a convoy distance is given (XCON), the specified train is applied **multiple times**, maintaining that minimum distance between the last load ordinate of one train and the reference point of the next.
- **YEX**: **Eccentricity** of the train within the lane (possible sign ±) (unit **[m]1001**; default **0.0**). Context: for railway, default eccentricity corresponds to **±r/18** in any direction; for road, it offsets the total train to the right/left.

### Direction and loading suppression
- **DIR**: Controls **direction of the train** and influences braking/velocity/wind sign handling (unit/type **LIT**, default **B**). Options:
  - **B** = in both directions
  - **R** = only to the right (positive)
  - **L** = only to the left (negative)
  - **N** = do not apply  
  Context: if **DIR N** is specified, **no impact factor** is applied and **brake, velocity, and wind** are preset to zero; filters may still be available. DIR can control sequence of standard trains but cannot flip a user-defined train sequence.
- **DIRT**: Direction for **transverse loading** (e.g., cross-direction wind/transverse effects) (unit/type **LIT**, default **B**). Options:
  - **B** = both directions
  - **R** / **L** = only right/left (sign convention follows direction)
  - **N** = suppress this loading  

Overall, the table is a parameter schema enabling detailed, type-specific construction of loading actions (including special cases like residual spare-area loading, wind/combined wind+traffic definitions, braking direction logic, and optional multi-body-dynamics mass/beam/spring/damper generation via related records such as TREX).

### Table description: **TRAI — Parameters for multibody dynamics / load train definition**

This table entry describes the parameter record **TRAI** (a configuration section used to generate “load trains” for structural loading). It is heavily focused on how a predefined traffic/loading pattern is applied to a structure—particularly when combined with lane geometry, dynamic/impact effects, braking and wind actions, eccentricity, and (optionally) multi-body-dynamics generation.

#### Core concepts covered
- **FRB**: A frequency parameter for a body spring (**Spring Cb**) with units **1/sec**. The value can be **∞** (indicating no oscillatory behavior / effectively rigid response).
- **XCON (convoy distance)**: If a convoy distance is specified, the selected train is **repeated multiple times** along the travel direction, keeping the given **minimum distance** between the last load ordinate of one train and the reference point of the next train.

#### Residual area loading behavior
- The **residual area load P5** is applied **without dynamic impact factors** and **without centrifugal forces**. It is applied only within specific area regions:
  - Between the **constant width** of the load train and the **polygonal bounds** of the lane.
  - For cases where the load train has **no width** (**WIDT = 0**), residual area loading is **not applied** (notably for railways).
  - Between the borders of **lane 0** and **all other lanes** (e.g., pathways).
  - Across the **total lane area** for load group **GR4** (e.g., pedestrian bridges).

#### Load scaling and favorable-load factors
- **PFAC**: A global **multiplier** for **all load elements** in the load train. Intended for classified loadings such as **LM71** or **SW/0**, using factors like: **0.75, 0.83, 0.91, 1.00, 1.10, 1.21, 1.33, 1.46** (from **EN 1991-2 6.3.2(3)**).
- **PFAV**: A factor for **favorable loadings** (referencing **EN 1990-2 GRP 13/14 and 23/24**). For road train loadings, it is applied **only to wheel loads**. Defaults differ by railway vs road:
  - Railway: **0.0** for **LM71**, **1.0** for all other railway load trains.
  - Majority of other road trains: default **0.0**.
  - Road train note: PFAV for road trains may only be specified with individual load train definitions.

#### Eccentricity / offset definition
- **YEX**: Represents eccentricity within the lane.
  - Should only be defined **when applying the loading**.
  - Wide heavy trains (e.g., **LM3, HB**) may allow an **explicit eccentricity** predefinition.
  - For **railway loadings**, YEX is aligned with **EN 1991-2 6.3.5**, with a default of **± r/18** in either direction.

#### Direction, braking, impacts, and wind
- **Moving direction** is crucial:
  - **Positive** load values correspond to **braking loads** in traveling direction.
  - **Negative** values correspond to **accelerating loads** in reverse direction.
- **DIR N**: If specified, **no impact factor** is applied and brake/velocity/wind load are **preset to zero**. Also, ELLA includes available filters in this case.
- **DIR**: Controls the **sequence** of generated loads for a standard train, but **cannot be used to flip** user-defined load train sequences.
- **Wind loading**:
  - Defined via a wind **attack area** with section definition.
  - May act as a combined traffic-and-wind load (P6 acting horizontally on a traffic band of height P7), or a line load variant for **AASHTO**.
  - Wind sign convention: **positive** when wind comes from the **right** in moving direction.
  - **DIRT**: allows a more specific definition and ELLA can apply wind in the **most unfavorable direction** if enabled; both mechanisms combine via logical **AND**.
- **P8 meaning**: Dependent on loading type. Braking load sign follows moving direction. **DIR B** can change sign, but only ELLA can manage this. ELLA and SOFILOAD may deactivate/change direction; combined via logical **AND**.

#### Multi-body dynamics extension
- When using multi-body dynamics, masses/beams/springs/dampers can be generated via record **TREX**.
- Bogie and wheel mass can be entered as:
  - a **positive absolute value**, or
  - a **negative fraction** of total mass.
- For more details, the table directs to **TREX**.

#### Supported load train families
The table text enumerates available predefined load types, including (non-exhaustively):
- Canadian **CSA** pedestrian loads (HA)
- **BS 5400 / BD 37-01**: HA, HB, and centrifugal loading
- **Indian Road Congress** (IRC) classes AA/A/B and Appendix I
- **Japan Road Association** train types (T and L)
- Multiple **Swedish BRO** train types (1, 2/3/4, 5), plus fatigue-relevant BRO
- **French** Fascicule 61 (area loading, lorry, tandem) and **Cerema/Leclerc** heavy load trains
- Australian **AS 5100** (single wheel/axle, M1600, S1600, heavy load platform)
- **LM71** and railway variants (UIC 71 / RU of BS 5400)
- **SW/0** and **SW/2** heavy load trains (DS 804 / EC)
- **EC railway fatigue** (RFAT)
- **EC 1 Annex 2** (HSLM)
- Railway loadings: **BS 5400** (RL) and **AS 5100** (ASRT)

#### Extensions and user-defined load behavior
- Standard load trains can be extended using **TRPL** and **TRBL**.
- If standard elements shouldn’t be used but other properties (e.g., impact factors) should remain, literal **USER** may be defined for **P1**.
  - The table warns the user to:
    - deduct default live load **P5** from areas covered by the defined loading,
    - verify spacing to the last load of a standard train due to potentially **automatically generated loads**.

#### Notes on extended eccentricity usage
- Load application may include variable eccentricity **YEX**:
  - Railways: additional moments are generated.
  - Roads: the total train has an offset (default **0.0**) to the **right or left**.

Overall, **TRAI** acts as a comprehensive specification mechanism for selecting a traffic/load train, scaling it, positioning it in lanes, applying direction-dependent braking and wind actions, optionally repeating it as a convoy, and interfacing with multi-body dynamics via **TREX** and extensions via **TRPL/TRBL**.

The table defines parameters for a multibody-dynamics based load train model (record **TRAI**, with optional coupling to **TREX** for generating masses/beams/springs/dampers). Each row lists an **Item** (parameter name), a human-readable **Description**, its **Unit**, and a **Default** value. The parameters shown focus on dynamic characteristics and per-component load magnitudes for **bogies** and **wheels**, including associated spring frequencies and modal damping.

### Parameters in the table

- **DAB** — *Modal Damping of body support*  
  - **Unit:** “–” (dimensionless or non-specified damping unit)  
  - **Default:** **0.0**  
  - **Meaning:** Damping applied to the supporting body support in a modal damping sense. This controls how oscillations are attenuated in the body support subsystem.

- **BOGI** — *Load value of bogie*  
  - **Unit:** “–/kN”  
  - **Default:** **0.0**  
  - **Meaning:** The applied load carried by the bogie. The unit notation “–/kN” indicates the value is given in kN, but may be interpreted relative to other mass/load definitions (consistent with the surrounding context that masses can be specified as absolute or negative fractions).

- **FRBO** — *Frequency for bogie spring Cbo*  
  - **Unit:** **1/sec**  
  - **Default:** **∞**  
  - **Meaning:** Natural/oscillation frequency of the bogie spring (Cbo). A default of **infinity** implies an effectively rigid or non-dynamic spring behavior (no compliant spring effect).

- **DABO** — *Modal Damping of bogie support*  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **0.0**  
  - **Meaning:** Modal damping for the bogie support element, governing energy dissipation at the bogie support interface.

- **WHEE** — *Load value of wheel*  
  - **Unit:** “–/kN”  
  - **Default:** **0.0**  
  - **Meaning:** Applied load on each wheel (or wheel element, depending on how the train is instantiated). As with **BOGI**, the unit suggests the value is expressed in kN and may be used in absolute or scaled forms depending on the model setup.

- **FRWH** — *Frequency for wheel spring Cwh*  
  - **Unit:** **1/sec**  
  - **Default:** **∞**  
  - **Meaning:** Natural/oscillation frequency for the wheel spring (Cwh). Again, **∞** suggests the wheel spring is non-compliant by default.

- **DAWH** — *Modal Damping of wheel support*  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **0.0**  
  - **Meaning:** Modal damping associated with the wheel support subsystem, reducing oscillatory response.

### Overall role in the system
Collectively, these parameters allow the load train to be represented not just as static wheel/bogie forces, but as a dynamic system with spring-like compliance (via **FRBO**, **FRWH**) and damping (via **DAB**, **DABO**, **DAWH**), while also defining the load magnitudes on bogies and wheels (**BOGI**, **WHEE**). The defaults indicate a “no additional damping” configuration (0.0) and “non-compliant spring” configuration (∞ frequency), with zero bogie/wheel loads unless explicitly set.

The table lists “standard load trains” (types of vehicle/rail/pedestrian loading) that can be selected by name within the application’s loading definition workflow. The header indicates the first column is the load train identifier (e.g., **USER**, **LM1**) and the second column describes the corresponding loading model/type (e.g., “double axle load model 1 according Eurocode…”). The table is intended to provide a compact catalog for choosing a predefined loading scheme without manually constructing individual wheel/axle elements.

## Column 1: Load Train Key (String Codes)
This column contains short mnemonic identifiers. **USER** is a special option indicating that the loading uses a constant area loading **P5** divided by (or combined with) a user-defined load train, implying that some default constant-area behavior remains while the train geometry/content is user-specified. All other keys represent predefined standard trains or subtypes (e.g., **LM1–LM4** for Eurocode 1 line/axle models, **FLM1–FLM4** for fatigue variants, **SLW** for heavy load truck, etc.).

## Column 2: Description (Standard/Source and Intended Use)
This column specifies the governing standard and the semantic meaning of the load train. Examples shown include:
- **LM1–LM4**: Eurocode 1 (EN 1991-2 / “Eurocode 1 part …”) simplified axle/load models, with **LM3** noted as a “special case load model 3.”
- **SV, SOV**: “Special vehicles” according to **BS EN 1991-2**.
- **FLM1–FLM4**: fatigue load model variants corresponding to **Eurocode 1** parts, labeled “Fatigue relevant load model …”.
- **SLW**: heavy load truck according to DIN/ÖNORM/IANORM (the standard reference is truncated in the capture).
- **SLW/LKW/LKWA**: variants of trucks depending on country/standard practice (“LKW” is standard truck; “LKWD” for German truck in Austria; “LKWA” Austrian truck).
- **NBR**: “Brazilian load trains NBR 7188 / NB6 similar to SL…” (truncated), indicating an equivalent heavy loading definition.
- **HS** and **HT**: AASHTO highway load and highway truck respectively.
- **CAN**: Canadian highway load according to CSA.

The table itself complements that by enumerating the allowable **named choices** that those parameters will act upon. For example, once a user selects **LMx** or **FLMx**, the system can then apply transport-direction sign conventions, load multipliers, eccentricity/moments creation, and potentially fatigue behaviors per the selected standard.

The table defines selectable **AASHTO/HL-93 load train parameters** using four key input fields: **P1 (load train class/type)**, **P2 (HS total/axle-related load term in the selected system)**, **P3 (lane/traffic band load intensity)**, and **P4 (axle spacing or variant distance override)**. The model context indicates that the **HL-93** live load can be used in **SI** and **US** versions, and that the **old AASHTO 1944** model uses three loading classes (10, 15, 20). It also notes that uniform loading can be represented (in HL-93) as two stripes due to the **train width limit of 10 ft (3.048 m)** (or 3.000 m for SI), though the table itself focuses on the parameter presets.

### Columns and meaning
- **P1 – Load train selector**
  - Values **10, 15, 20** correspond to **HSxx-44**, i.e., the **AASHTO 1944** shear/local loading classes.
  - Values **US** and **SI** correspond to the **HL-93** model in **US** or **SI** units.
- **P2 – HS total load (unit depends on system)**
  - For **AASHTO 1944** classes, P2 is given as a pair **(kip)** values, denoted like **(13.0/9.0) kip**, reflecting the HS load distribution parameters used for the older definition (the context states that the old-load P2 must be chosen explicitly for shear).
  - For **HL-93**:
    - **US:** **P2 = 24.0 kip**
    - **SI:** **P2 = 110 kN**
- **P3 – Lane load intensity**
  - **AASHTO 1944**:
    - **Class 10:** **0.32 klf**
    - **Class 15:** **0.48 klf**
    - **Class 20:** **0.64 klf**
  - **HL-93 alternate/basic traffic band**:
    - **US:** **0.64 klf**
    - **SI:** **9.3 kN/m**
  - Context indicates that in the 2002 HL-93 formulation, traffic band loading can be turned off by setting **P3 = 0**, but this table provides active defaults.
- **P4 – Distance override / spacing control**
  - For **HSxx-44**, **P4 = 0**, implying no override (i.e., default/implicit spacing behavior for that older model).
  - For **HL-93**:
    - **US:** **P4 = 4 ft** (approx. 1.2 m)
    - **SI:** **P4 = 1.2 m**
  - The wider modeling context explains that **P4** can overwrite the variable distance between the two axles; **P4 = 0** would create a simplified model.

### Row-by-row presets
1. **P1=10 (HS10-44):** P2=(13.0, 9.0) kip, P3=0.32 klf, P4=0  
2. **P1=15 (HS15-44):** P2=(19.5, 13.5) kip, P3=0.48 klf, P4=0  
3. **P1=20 (HS20-44):** P2=(26.0, 18.0) kip, P3=0.64 klf, P4=0  
4. **P1=US (HL-93):** P2=24.0 kip, P3=0.64 klf, P4=4 ft  
5. **P1=SI (HL-93):** P2=110 kN, P3=9.3 kN/m, P4=1.2 m  

Overall, this table serves as a **preset mapping** from the user’s **load train selection (P1)** to the numerical defaults for **HS load magnitude (P2)**, **traffic band/uniform lane intensity (P3)**, and **axle spacing/override (P4)** for both **AASHTO 1944 HS classes** and the **HL-93 US/SI variants**.

This table defines the selectable parameters for modeling the **HL-93/legacy AASHTO 1944 lane load train**. The columns are **P1, P2, P3, and P4**, which are program parameters used to generate different bridge traffic loading cases and their geometry.

### Column meanings (implied by the surrounding context)
- **P1 (Load Train selector):** Chooses the load definition type/class. It distinguishes between the **legacy AASHTO 1944 three-class system** and the **HL-93** family, including special compact-truck variants and fatigue/local-design options.
- **P2 (Total load train weight / axle group total):** Provides the total weight associated with the chosen load train class. For legacy cases it is given in **kip**; for HL-93 it is also expressed as **kip** (US) or **kN** (SI).
- **P3 (Lane/traffic band load intensity):** A distributed load (kLF per lane width or line load), given as **kif/klf** for the legacy entries and as **kN/m (SI)** or **klf (US)** for HL-93. Notably, the context states that **setting P3 = 0 can produce an alternate loading** (and that for the HL-93 model the traffic-band loading can be active along the full longitudinal length).
- **P4 (Variable axle spacing / distance parameter):** Defines the spacing between axles (or between the two vehicles/axle groups depending on the chosen variant). It may be a range (for variable spacing) or a fixed distance for simplified or fatigue/local variants.

### Rows: what each P1 option corresponds to
#### Legacy AASHTO (1944) three loading classes
- **P1 = 10 → H10-44:** **P2 = 20 kip**, **P3 = 0.32 klf**, **P4 = “-”** (no spacing parameter required for this legacy class definition in the table).
- **P1 = 15 → H15-44:** **P2 = 30 kip**, **P3 = 0.48 klf**, **P4 = “-”**.
- **P1 = 20 → H20-44:** **P2 = 40 kip**, **P3 = 0.64 klf**, **P4 = “-”**.

These are three “loading classes” under the older AASHTO approach.

#### HL-93 (SI/US) and derived variants
- **P1 = US → HL 93:** **P2 = 72 kip**, **P3 = 0.640 klf**, **P4 = 14 to 30 ft** (variable spacing).
- **P1 = SI → HL 93:** **P2 = 325 kN**, **P3 = 9.3 kN/m**, **P4 = 4.30 to 9.00 m** (variable spacing in SI).
- **P1 = US2 → HL 93 (special):** **P2 = 72 kip**, **P3 = 0.640 klf**, **P4 = 14 ft** (compact-vehicle selection; fixed spacing).
- **P1 = SI2 → HL 93 (special):** **P2 = 325 kN**, **P3 = 9.3 kN/m**, **P4 = 4.30 m**.
- **P1 = USF → HL 93 (fatigue):** **P2 = 72 kip**, **P3 = 0.640 klf**, **P4 = 4 ft**.
- **P1 = SIF → HL 93 (fatigue):** **P2 = 325 kN**, **P3 = 9.3 kN/m**, **P4 = 1.20 m**.

**Interpretation consistent with the context:** the model uses a train width limited to **10 ft (3.048 m)** (or **3.000 m for SI version**). Uniform loading is represented by **two stripes** with fixed width (because the train width limit is fixed). For HL-93, the variant distance between the two axles/axle groups is selectable via **P4** (either variable 14–30 ft or fixed for US2/SI2 and fatigue/local variants). The table therefore encodes both **unit system differences (US vs SI)** and **design scenario differences (base, compact special, fatigue/local)** through P1–P4.

The Loadtrain HL-93 may be selected in a SI and an US Version, as the load values are not completely equivalent. There is the one/two axle load train (HS) and a three axle load train (HT) with a variant spacing. A uniform loading will be added if appropriate.

The Canadian standards define a truck load in several variants. The type CAN is used for the default load train according chapter 14.9.
 The value P1 defines the level of the load train (CL, CL4 = only 4 axles, CL3 = only 3 axles) The definitions ON, ON4 and ON3 select the variants for Ontario according Annex A14.4. The definitions BC, BC4 and BC3 select the variants for Britisch Columbia. The definition MV selects the maintenace vehicle according 3.8.11.
 The value P2 defines the class of the load train (default 625).
 If the value P3 is defined ( 9.0, 8.0 or 7.0 for class A, B or C and D) a constant lane load will be defined with reduced load values of the load train without any dynamic allowance. For this loading a braking load P8 of min(700,180+0.1*L) will be applied. So P8 should become zero for secondary lanes.
 The height of the wind attack area P7 is 3.0[ m] , the zentrifugal force is acting at P9=2.0[ m] aove the lane.
 The value P4 defines the fixed distance to the 4th load of the vehicle, it is 6.6 in general, but up to 18 m in British Columbia.
 Further wit Literals EP1 and EP2 the special load trains EPLL1 and EPLL2 may be selected.
 The value P8 defines a factor on the braking load which is applied as 180+0.1*P3*L but not larger than 700 kN distributed along the total length. P8 0.0 deactivates this type of loading.

The table defines parameters (“Item”) used to model a freely defined load train / moving loads, including their vertical, longitudinal, transverse and torsional (moment) components, as well as optional impact/special treatment and optional multi-body-dynamics properties (masses, springs, damping). It is organized into two main blocks: (1) general load component and placement parameters, and (2) wheel/area-contact and multi-body-dynamics parameters.

**General load components and geometry (top block)**  
- **P**: Vertical load value (unit kN, default 0.0).  
- **PB**: Longitudinal braking load component (kN, default 0.0). Positive acts in travelling direction (braking); negative represents acceleration in the opposite direction.  
- **PW**: Transverse load component (e.g., bumping/wind) (kN, default 0.0).  
- **PF**: Vertical load value specifically for centrifugal loading (kN, default equals P).  
- **PFAC**: Factor for favourable components (dimensionless, default 0.0). Intended to modify favourable/unfavourable combinations of load components (as controlled by OPT; exact combination logic not in table).  
- **DIST**: Minimum/absolute distance mode parameter; described as “A is Minimum (MIN) / absolute (ABS) distance”. Default uses **ABS**.  
- **A**: Distance to the last load of the train (m, default 0.0). Together with an initial reference at x=0, successive loads are positioned relative to each other using A (constant or variable depending on DIST/DPOS logic).  
- **DPOS**: Minimum distance to load reference point (point) (m, default 0.0). Used when the distance to the last load point may be variable with a minimum.  
- **DMIN / DMAX**: Influence region extents before and behind the load (m, default 0.0). These are intended for special cases where influence-line evaluation needs a restricted region.  
- **Y**: Eccentricity to lane axis (m, default 0.0). Positive means to the right. (Context notes that for symmetric load trains, Y may need a complemented negative position; Y2 is not supported.)  
- **HW**: Total height of wind attack area (m, default 0.0).  
- **ZW**: Height of horizontal force (m, default HW/2). Used to generate torsional moments: centrifugal moment depends on height **hs** (from context), and horizontal force height **zw** defines torsional lever arm.  
- **HF**: Height of mass center (m, default 0.0). Used for dynamic/mass distribution effects in multi-body contexts.

- **PHI**: Impact and special options (dimensionless, default 1). The remarks provided in the prompt describe how OPT/PHI-encoded options can apply impact factors, split loads transversely, force centric loading, convert to area load distribution, etc.

**Wheel/area-contact and multi-body dynamics (lower block)**  
- **NW**: Number of wheels on an axle (0–7) (default is marked with “*”, meaning required/variable depending on use). Context: if **NW=0**, the load is converted to a distributed load across the train width **WIDT** and then clipped by lane width; alternatively certain code-specific cases distribute over lane width controlled by **PHI**.  
- **B**: Distance of wheels across the lane (m, default 0.0). Used to define transverse spacing; if **B < WIDT**, the model forms a pair of wheels across the lane.  
- **BW**: Width of wheel contact area (m, default 0.0). Used to create area loadings on the wheel contact.  
- **LW**: Length of wheel contact area (m, default 0.0). Complements BW to define area loading dimensions.

**Animation and multi-body dynamics parameters**  
- **SNO**: Section number for animation/which load train section is visualized (default “-”, unitless).  
- **FRB**: Frequency for body spring **C_b** (1/sec, default “*”).  
- **DAB**: Modal damping of body support (dimensionless or “-”, default “*”).  
- **BOGI**: Load value of bogie (unit shown as “−/kN”, default “*”). Context suggests bogie mass/load can be specified as positive absolute or as negative fraction of total mass.  
- **FRBO / DABO**: Frequency (FRBO) for bogie spring and modal damping (DABO) of bogie support (1/sec and “-”, respectively; both default “*”).  
- **WHEE**: Load value of wheel (displayed as “−/kN”, default “*”).  
- **FRWH / DAWH**: Frequency for wheel spring (FRWH) and modal damping of wheel support (DAWH) (1/sec and “-”, respectively; both default “*”).

Overall, the table specifies **how to locate and decompose a moving load into resultant forces** (vertical PB transverse components, torsional lever-arm heights), **how to discretize it** into wheels or distributed/area loading using NW/B/BW/LW and lane-width clipping rules, and **how to optionally expand it into dynamic multi-body elements** (bogie/wheel/body springs and damping) via TREX/SNO-related parameters.

 A freely defined loading by the user comprises an arbitrary number of loads defined relative to
 each other. The first load determines the load reference point (x=0.0). Each further loading is defined with a distance to the previous one.The distance of the point load to the last load point may be either constant or variable with a minimum value. In the latter case and additional minimum distance to the load reference point may be defined with DPOS. For the evaluation in ELLA two additional values DMIN and DMAX may be specified for special cases describing an influence region before and behind the load.
 For the evaluation of the load trains in ELLA symmetric load trains are expected. Thus, any definition of Y should be complemented with a second definition at the same position (A 0) with a negative Y-value. Thus, a second value of Y2 is no longer supported. An eccentricity may be specified with YEX with the load train. NW allows to specify directly a number of wheels with a distance B for that load element. They loads with the same load value will then add up to a total axle distributing the loading on all wheels of that axle.
 If NW = 0 the load values will be converted to a distributed load based on the width of the load train WIDT. (120kN distributed on 3m yield 40kN/m) and will be then clipped at the boundary of the the current lane width. But there are also cases (KEL of HA in BS), where the load is distributed over the lane width, which is controlled via PHI.
 A definition of BW and LW will allow to create also area loadings for every wheel.
 The loading has a vertical component P, a longitudinal component PB and two components in transverse direction. The load may be defined either as single point load, as a pair of wheels (Definition of B < WIDT) or as distributed load (Definition of BW only or B equal to WIDT) The true dimension of the wheel contact area is only used for COPY within SOFiLOAD, ELLA uses only the resultant forces for the evaluation of the influence lines.

 The centrifugal loading acts in the height hs, the constant horizontal force in the height zw, thus creating torsional moments. If the load has a width B, this moment will be applied as a pair of forces on the lane surface, a torsional moment along the lane axis will be generated otherwise.

 Multiply vertical load value with UDL-value of design code (eg.BS)
 Multiply longitudinal load value with value of design code (eg. EN),
 8 split load in transverse direction if unfavourable,
 the load is an area load, the total load value will be adopted to the lane width
 32 load is always centric, YEX is not applied
 For an analysis with multi-body-dynamics it is possible to generate masses, beams, springs and dampers via the record TREX. The mass of bogie and wheel may be specified either as a positive absolute load value or as a negative fraction of the total mass. The default values are specified with the record TRAI. For more information see record TREX.
 As an alternate method, it is possible to associate a load train to a user defined structural model of the load train. In that case CONT specifies the number of a node of the structural system, which is located at the current position of the load train. If CONT is specified with a positive number, the node will get the deformations of the structure at this point. If defined negative, the node will get only the offset of the current position for the visualization however. This has to be done for all nodes of the train model having no direct contact to the bridge.

content:
The table defines input parameters for **free-form load trains in record TRBL (related to TREX multi-body dynamics)**. It lists each configurable **Item** (parameter name), a short **Description**, the **Unit** used by the input, and the **Default** value. Most parameters control how a vertical load train is converted into one or more **line loads, distributed loads, wheel/track line loads, or area loads** along a lane, including eccentricity and wind-related geometric data.

## Core vertical and directional load parameters
- **P**: vertical load value, unit **[kN/m]**, default **0.0**.
- **PB**: braking load value, unit **[kN/m]**, default **0.0**.
- **PW**: transverse-direction load value, unit **[kN/m]**, default **0.0**.
- **PF**: vertical load for **centrifugal load**, unit **[kN/m]**, default **P** (i.e., inherits P).
- **PFAC**: factor for “favourable components” (dimensionless factor), default **0.0**.

## Load discretization / arrangement control
- **DIST**: interpretation mode for the area/length relation: “**MIN / absolute**” selector. The value is **LIT** with default **ABS**.
- **A**: distance to the last load of the train, **[m]**, default **0.0**.
- **L**: fixed or minimum length of the load, **[m]**, default **0.0**. The sign is meaningful: positive/negative indicates fixed vs minimum behavior, **0 means unlimited**.
- **LMAX**: maximum length of the load train segment, **[m]** (no default shown explicitly in the table).
- **LDEL**: discrete variable length defined as **L + n·LDEL**, **[m]**, default **0.0**.

## Lane eccentricity and wind-geometry parameters
- **Y**: eccentricity to the lane axis (**>0 to the right**), **[m]**, default **0.0**.
- **HW**: total height of the wind attack area, **[m]**, default **0.0**.
- **ZW**: resulting force height corresponding to PW, **[m]**, default **HW/2** (derived from HW).
- **HF**: height of the mass centre, **[m]**, default **0.0**.
- **PHI**: impact and special options flag/settings (dimensionless), default **1**.

## Multi-lane / wheel/track contact modeling parameters
- **NW**: number of tracks on an axle (**0–2**), default “*” (i.e., not fixed; depends on context).
- **B**: distance of tracks across the lane, **[m]**, default **0.0**.
- **BW**: width of track contact area, **[m]**, default **0.0**.

The accompanying context states how these are interpreted in TRBL:
- For **freely defined loading**, an arbitrary number of loads can be specified relative to each other (general parameters/remarks are in TRPL).
- Load values are generally treated as **line loads**.  
- If **NW = 0**, load values are converted to a **distributed load** using the load train width (**WIDT**): e.g., 12 kN/m distributed over 3 m yields 4 kN/m², then **clipped to the current lane width**.
- If **NW > 0**, one or more **line loads for wheels/tracks** are created with separation **B**. If **BW** is defined, an **area load** can be created instead of a line load.
- If only **HW** is specified, **PW** can be evaluated from the wind load defined for the load train.
- Multi-body-dynamics input values for line loads in TRBL (referenced under TREX) “**will not be used currently**”.

## Animation / multi-body dynamics (currently not used for line loads)
The table also includes parameters labeled for multi-body dynamics, each with default marked “*” (meaning required/depends on runtime logic):
- **SNO**: section number for animation.
- **FRB**: frequency for body spring (**1/sec**).
- **DAB**: modal damping of body support.
- **BOGI**: load value of bogie (**−/kN**).
- **FRBO**: frequency for bogie spring.
- **DABO**: modal damping of bogie support.
- **WHEE**: load value of wheel (**−/kN**).
- **FRWH**: frequency for wheel spring (**1/sec**).
- **DAWH**: modal damping of wheel support.

Overall, this table provides a compact parameter schema for how TRBL constructs spatially distributed loads (line/distributed/area) across lanes, accounts for eccentric placement, and optionally supports advanced multi-body dynamics settings (though those dynamics parameters are currently stated as not used).
