The table defines the **TREX** input record parameters for a *load train* used in **DYNA** as a movable load (CONT). TREX is responsible for generating the appropriate **beam elements** representing the bogie and wheels (when configured), with the generated elements assembled under a special analysis group. The record is closely tied to other records such as **TRAI** (defines bogie/wheel dynamic model parameters) and **TRPL** (defines each load/contact position), and is treated collectively at the **end of the program run**—meaning old TREX element definitions are removed for the same specified load case.

### Field-by-field description (as in the table)

- **NO (Item: NO)**  
  Specifies the **load case number** of the load train.  
  - **Unit:** “–” (not a physical unit; it is an identifier)  
  - **Default:** **not set** (“!” indicates mandatory or user-defined)

- **GRP (Item: GRP)**  
  Specifies the **group number** under which the generated TREX elements (separate nodes for the created beam/bogie/wheel representation) will be organized for inclusion in the analysis.  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **900**

- **SNO (Item: SNO)**  
  Specifies the **section number** to be used by the generated elements (i.e., the cross-sectional/structural section properties reference).  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **900**

- **NODE (Item: NODE)**  
  Specifies the **smallest node number** used for the generated elements. The program will allocate consecutive nodes beginning from this value for the TREX-generated representation.  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **\*** (typically meaning “automatic/required by system logic,” i.e., not fixed)

- **OPT (Item: OPT)**  
  Specifies the **bitpattern/options** controlling how the TREX elements are created. The default is **3**, which combines multiple behaviors depending on the option interpretation. Listed options are:
  - **1:** Real Run / Stargate Run  
  - **2:** Beam elements with hinges  
  - **4:** Generate Bogies and wheels  
  - **8:** without artificial rigidities  
  - **Unit:** “–”  
  - **Default:** **3** (i.e., option bits **1 + 2** enabled unless changed; bogie/wheel generation via option 4 is not included in the default)

### Contextual implications
To model trains in a more complex way, the text notes that TREX may be avoided and a classical finite-element train (beams/springs/dampers/masses) can be built instead, using user-defined TRAI and proper contact node assignment in each TRPL. For pure visualization in the Animator, the text advises selecting a section with **no self weight or stiffness** (via GRP-record settings **FACS 0.0** and **FACM 0.0**) while allowing arbitrary contour shape.

The image is a schematic diagram (Figure 5.41) illustrating a **bogie and wheel subsystem of a coach** for a dynamic “load train” model. The graphic shows two identical vertical stack assemblies positioned left and right, representing a bogie–wheel arrangement along a rail line.

Across the bottom, there is a thick **horizontal base line** symbolizing the **track/rail**. Above it, each assembly contains several repeating blocks connected vertically to indicate mechanical elements. On both sides of the figure, small orthogonal components at the top of each stack suggest **connections/constraints** between the vehicle elements (illustrating springs/dampers or coupling components typical of multibody dynamic representations).

### Left assembly (labeled components)
- A bracket-like label on the far left reads **Pbo** near the upper stack, where **“Bogie”** is explicitly written next to the assembly.
- A second label reads **Pwh** at the lower region, where **“Wheel”** is written.
- The text **Bogie** appears near the middle of the left stack, while **Wheel** appears closer to the lower part of the same assembly.

### Right assembly (dynamic parameters)
On the right side, the same mechanical stack is annotated with stiffness/damping-related terms:
- **Cb** is placed near the upper portion of the right stack (associated with the bogie).
- **Cbo** is placed around the mid-upper portion (associated with the coupling between bogie and wheel).
- **Cwh** appears near the lower portion (associated with the wheel).
These “C” terms visually correspond to the modeled coefficients (commonly stiffness-like or damping-like constants) for each axis/component, consistent with the contextual equations shown above the image (references to TRAI/TRPL and parameters like Mb, Mh, and damping coefficients).

Overall, the diagram emphasizes that the coach’s bogie and wheel system can be modeled as a set of elements with **separate nodes and grouped properties**, where bogie and wheel components receive distinct parameter definitions (Cb, Cbo, Cwh) and apply to the contact interaction with the track.

 A load train may be used within DYNA as movable load (CONT). For a multibody dynamic analysis it is possible to create beam elements from any load train including peoperties for Boogie and wheels. The generated elements with separate nodes will be assigned to a special group to be included in the analysis.
 All nodes may be defined along the global x-axis with the real distances of the loads or col- lapsed to the origin (0,0,0). In the latter case the load elements will appear and disappear near the structure just before usage.
 The properties of the bogie and the wheel are specified with a general model for each axis based on the mass, the frequency and the modal damping as specified with the TRAI record.

 All TREX-definitions are treated together at the very end of the program run, old definitions of those elements will be removed for the same specified load case.
 For more complex cases the load train may be modelled with finite elements in the classical way (beams, springs, dampers, masses). Then TREX needs not to be used, but the train and all its loads should be specified with a user defined TRAI and each single TRPL should have its contact node properly assigned.

For more complex cases the load train may be modelled with finite elements in the classical way (beams, springs, dampers, masses). Then TREX needs not to be used, but the train and all its loads should be specified with a user defined TRAI and each single TRPL should have its contact node properly assigned..
 Hint
 For a pure visualisation within the Animator the selected section should have no self weight or stiffness, but may have any shape of the contour. Thus the group should be selected with FACS 0.0 and FACM 0.0 in the GRP-record in DYNA

Wind is a randomly non deterministic dynamic loading. The flow of the air induces a velocity pressure on the structure. Dynamic effects of natural wind are mainly introduced by a variance of wind speed and thus wind pressure within time and space.
 The complex action of wind is a combination of mutually influencing effects like:
 • Wind climate (the global wind)
 • Topology and roughness of terrain (the local wind)
 • Aerodynamics, aeroeleasticity (drag coefficients and wind force derivativa)
 • Structural dynamics (response of the structure)
 • Design of the structure
 The program SOFiLOAD allows to take into account and to simulate most of the above effects. To use these features two extra licences are needed: SOFILOAD-W for the static wind loading and SOFILOAD-WH for the dynamic wind loading (especially WGEN) and NONL-DYN for the interaction analysis in DYNA.
 As basic safety concept for the wind loaded structure it will be specified in the design codes or especially for large projects in the submission that within a given time (e.g. 50 or 100 years) the failure of the structure will be avoided with a given safety factor. The analysis itself will be based on shorter interval - in Europe: 10 minutes - which includes the maximum wind speed of the 50-year-wind but is long enough to allow a considerable dynamic response for all resonance frequencies. The wind speed within that interval may be described as the sum of
 a timely constant, but spatial variant basic mean wind speed (10-minute-wind) and
 •
 a superimposed timely and spatial variant part of turbulence.
 •
 The treatment of dynamic wind effects is governed by the fact that turbulences may be only described by statistical means: The real time-spatial wind speed is within the statistical limits purely random. The usual analysis methods use probabilistic analysis with power spectras (Ruscheweyh [15], Dyrbye and Hansen [16], Rosemeier [17], and Davenport [18]). As these methods do not use the time but the energy content of the wind speeds, they yield clear and re- liable basics for the analysis. Several steps then provide the power spectra of the deformations and forces within the structure. The probabilistic peak value will be the result of an extremal analysis of the spectras. At the time being, most of wind loaded structures will be analyzed via this approach. And all modern design codes for wind use these methods to obtain wind pressures.

Several steps then provide the power spectra of the deformations and forces within the structure. The probabilistic peak value will be the result of an extremal analysis of the spectras. At the time being, most of wind loaded structures will be analyzed via this approach. And all modern design codes for wind use these methods to obtain wind pressures..
 National and international Design codes nowadays however use strongly simplified methods (ECCS [19, 20]) [ 11, 12, 13]. The total map will be subdivided with 3 or 4 wind zones with step-wise wind speeds. To facilitate the usage, several wind parameters will be set up on the safe (unfavourable) side naturally. The complex structure is reduced to a simple single one degree of freedom oscillator. Even then working with wind loads is still difficult. Compared to the efforts, the results will be unsatisfactory in numerous cases: The total dynamic effects will
 be accounted for with a constant gust factor for the total structure which might be rather faulty for individual elements. Structures with several sensible frequencies (skeletons, towers with antennas, pedestrian and other types of bridges) are not applicable for this simplified approach. The same holds for structures with tuned damping elements and many more cases.
 The complete spectral design - the so called stochastic analysis - is rather complex and costly, it is thus applied only for very sensitive structures (cable stayed bridges with large spans). On the other side the stochastic analysis is still underestimating the ultimate load, because the spectral methods are purely linear for the structure and especially for the wind loads and do not account for any nonlinear effects. The linear relation between the angle of attack and the wind force coefficients are seldom admissible. The stochastic analysis is further unprecise for systems with close eigenfrequencies (e.g. tuned damper systems). Further more it has only limited possibilities to account for interactivity (dynamic response of the structure and its effect on the wind pressures or forces).
 SOFiLOAD has been created to cope with more detailed and thus more economic wind loading for the design of structures, overcoming the above limitations. Two of the benefits of the new method to be stated are:
 • SOFiLOAD uses the ESDU procedure to generate wind profiles accounting for the envi- ronment of the structure - roughness, elevations - similar as but more precise than it is foreseen partially in the most recent design codes like EN 1991-1-4.

Two of the benefits of the new method to be stated are:. • SOFiLOAD uses the ESDU procedure to generate wind profiles accounting for the envi- ronment of the structure - roughness, elevations - similar as but more precise than it is foreseen partially in the most recent design codes like EN 1991-1-4..
 • DYNA evaluates more precise forces and moments via transient analysis, accounting on one side for nonlinear effects like changes of the wind forces when the cross section rotates and on the other side for interactive behaviour like aerodynamic damping, potential flutter, galloping and torsional galloping or discrete damping elements.
 The second method is based on a mathematical turbulence generation which creates a se- ries of random transient wind histories. The structure will be imposed via program DYNA to that wind history and the development of deformations and forces will be recorded and su- perimposed by statistical means to get the extreme values along the time interval. The total methodology has been developed in the years 1992 to 1994 (Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21], Kovács and Andrä [22], and Kovács [23]) and has been applied since then to many large buildings, bridges and towers.

The wind in great heights is coherent and will be dominated only by global meteorological conditions. Near the surface the roughness of the terrain will induce an atmospheric boundary layer, where the wind speed is zero at the ground and will approach the limit asymptotically. In SOFiLOAD this limit value is called "atmospheric wind" which is not in correspondence with the general literature.
 The basis is the boundary layer model from Deaves and Harris, which is also part of the ISO 4354:2009. It is combining a logarithmic profile with extra terms in larger heights accounting for Coriollis effects. By the effect of the Coriollis forces we have a rotation of the wind direction by 10 to 45 degrees over the height, which will be neglected here.
 The SOFiLOAD-user may create the wind profile - as the first method - by defining the appro- priate atmospheric wind speed. To facilitate this we have provided a a global wind map for
 the 10 min wind with a return period of 50 years. This wind map has been established by us using older wind maps and meteorological measurements. It allows a smooth interpolation of the atmospheric wind and is therefore more elaborate than the rough subdivision of staggered wind pressures of the older design codes.
 As the newer design codes are based on a continuous wind profile, it is recommended to use as a second method the reference mean wind profile to specify the wind profile.
 For special applications like large and sensitive structures, bridges and towers it is also possible to define explicit wind profiles.
 The transformation of the atmospheric wind speed defined for a 50 year return period to an- other time value - as it might needed for large bridges - has to be performed by the user if needed. A rather good estimate is given by:
 1 + 0.12 · lnN

 The distribution of the wind speed over the height is depending on the terrain roughness and topology. Within SOFiLOAD it is possible to define a distribution of roughness (WROU), along the wind luv direction up to 200 km and geometric simplified elements like a hill, edge or ridge. For the latter there are estimates given in the literature, especially in Eurocode 1991-1-4, and in the newest EDIN 1055-4, having been implemented in SOFILOAD.

The image is a technical diagram illustrating how wind force coefficients depend on the wind angle of attack, α, for aerodynamic loading on a structural element/plane section.

At the top, there are two small graph panels labeled **CD** and **CA**, respectively.

A vertical line in the center indicates a force or reference axis. The wind is drawn as a **blue arrow** pointing toward the structure at an angle; adjacent to it is the **angle of attack symbol α**, showing the wind approaching obliquely rather than head-on. The shaded **area** beneath the vertical reference line is labeled **A**, indicating the projected/loaded area (or width/attack area for the element) used in the aerodynamic loading relation.

 The elements to be loaded with wind are selected via the GRP record. A purely steady loading without any dynamic effects may be also created via SOFiLOAD.
 The wind force coefficients for the element types beam, cable and truss may be defined within AQUA for any section depending on the angle of attack. This definition is strongly recom- mended for all dynamically sensitive structures or elements sensitive for galloping or flutter. To obtain those values it is common practice to perform wind tunnel tests or use a CFD (Compu- tational Fluid Dynamics) analysis.
 For standard steel shapes or buildings there are values given in the literature or the design codes. AQUA generates for steel shapes simple functions depending on the angle of attack but without any information about galloping. SOFiLOAD has all values for rectangular and circular sections available. The latter are dependent on the roughness and the Reynolds num- ber. Without any specification an enclosing rectangle is assumed or in special cases only the component in wind direction is considered with a coefficient of 2.0.

AQUA generates for steel shapes simple functions depending on the angle of attack but without any information about galloping. SOFiLOAD has all values for rectangular and circular sections available. The latter are dependent on the roughness and the Reynolds num- ber. Without any specification an enclosing rectangle is assumed or in special cases only the component in wind direction is considered with a coefficient of 2.0..
 SOFiLOAD has also the possibility via records BEAM, TRUS and CABL to define additional factors to the defined force coefficients selectively for for those type of elements individually. Further there is the record GRP with additional factors available to define shadowing, influence ordinates etc.
 For areas it is possible to define in SOFiLOAD via AREA or QUAD explicit wind pressure or uplift values perpendicular to the area. For cylindrical shapes according to many codes and for planar standard roofs and walls according to DIN 1055 Teil 4 values may be selected. If no such values are defined, all coefficients are taken to be 1.0.
 If the pressures are defined in several data points from a wind tunnel test, the record WIPT allows a comfortable method with an external FE-mesh of the data points to generate the required loading data. Especially in case of transient loadings, this method is strongly recom- mended.

The natural wind is the sum of the mean wind velocity and the variances due to turbulence which might be decomposed in three directions within the wind coordinate system:
 longitudinal (= parallel to the mean wind velocity)
 lateral (horizontal inclined to the wind direction) and
 •
 • vertical
 The turbulence is then the sum of an infinite large number of small harmonic velocity frequen- cies. Their distribution along the axis of frequencies is characterized by a power spectra.
 The power spectra are the deterministic part of the wind load, the real kernel as the Fourier- Integral of the turbulence time history. The power spectra of the natural wind may be described by simple formulas according to the general pattern of the Karman spectra definition. If one chooses then a random phase distribution for all the frequencies, it is possible to reconstruct the Fourier-Integral of a clearly defined random time history and thus the time history itself. This is exactly what SOFiLOAD does when generating a wind history.
 The ratio between the turbulence in different locations in space are characterized by special similarity or coherence functions. These functions define in a coarse sense the relation be- tween gust wind velocity, the duration of the gust and the size of the gust. It is clear that the spatial distribution of the gust has a large influence on the forces within the structure. SOFiLOAD works with natural sizes of the gust which are otherwise overestimated in most design codes considerably. (Davenport’s model with constant size of the gust in all heights).
 The coherence algorithm of the wind history generation has to reflect that the similarity between two natural wind histories in two points must become smaller with larger distances. This decay of correlation is described in the literature in different ways depending on the author of the publication, but may be generalized by the use of the half value distance (Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21]), where the square root of the coherence of the stochastic process has reduced from the full value of 1.0 ( full coherence with distance zero) to a value of 0.5. Each turbulence along any of the axis has the same function of similarity. Thus the coherence of the natural wind is described by a 3 by 3 matrix of the half value distances. For more details see notes for the record WSPE.

SOFiLOAD generates from the wind profile, the turbulence spectra, the coherence and some random numbers artificial random wind histories, based on the theoretical considerations in Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21] , to be used then within the program DYNA with a transient dynamic analysis of the structure. By applying a sufficiently large number of such histories it is possible to establish a statistically based proof of the ultimate state limit or a serviceability state limit including any material or geometric nonlinear effects available.
 Such a design based on transient analysis facilitates the design process of a structural sys- tem against wind loading to a great extent. Instead of a simple dynamic gust factor we have dynamic forces and stresses available for all points of the structure which might be introduced into the design process directly. By repeating the process for a reworked structure it is possible
 to optimize it for the wind loading criteria.
 The first step of a wind analysis is always a static wind load (basic load case), introducing all values needed for the wind history generation. Based on this data the random time histories will be generated in a second step within time and space.
 The transient analysis in DYNA is nonlinear by using the nonlinear wind force coefficients de- fined within AQUA. The analysis is interactive as it is considered that the structure will move within the wind field and will thus modify the relative wind speed in all cases by a vectoral su- perposition of the structural and the wind velocity. Only by this feature important aerodynamic effects may be simulated like aerodynamic damping or the bending galloping excitation.
 The aerodynamic damping is introduced into the simulation with the den-Hartog formulas, i.e. as a stationary approach automatically. (It should be noted here, that despite the important effect it is hardly accounted for in German design codes) Also the bending galloping excitation is automatically introduced in the analysis if the wind force coefficients have been properly defined in AQUA.
 The more enhanced possibilities to check for torsional galloping and general flutter are only available with the inclusion of the Scanlan derivativa.

(It should be noted here, that despite the important effect it is hardly accounted for in German design codes) Also the bending galloping excitation is automatically introduced in the analysis if the wind force coefficients have been properly defined in AQUA.. The more enhanced possibilities to check for torsional galloping and general flutter are only available with the inclusion of the Scanlan derivativa..
 Last not least it should be pointed out, that the treatment of critical wind effects is also a complicate matter of safety definitions (see e.g. Kovács and Andrä [22]). This manual will not state any rules for that, the user will need to find its own demands for that purpose.

The table defines the **input parameters for generating a wind profile** (mean wind and, where needed, gust/turbulence characteristics) in the record **WIND**. It is organized by *Item*, *Description*, *Unit*, and *Default*. Many defaults are marked with “*”, meaning the value is determined internally or depends on the selected design code/zone (or that the parameter is optional and only required in certain configurations).

### Wind selection and governing model
- **CODE** (Unit: LIT, Default: ATMO) selects the wind formulation / design code:
  - **ATMO** atmospheric wind (default)
  - **EN** Eurocode 1991-1-4
  - **ISO** ISO 4354 (2009)
  - **DIN** DIN 1055-4 (2006)
  - **SIA** SIA 216 (2003)
  - **VGB** VGB-BTR (1997/2005)
  - **SP** SP 20.13330.2011 (SNIP 2.01.07-85)
  This choice governs whether the profile is derived from atmospheric logarithmic theory or from classical design-code formulations (static profiles are adapted for transient dynamic use by internally selecting missing gust/turbulence/coherence parameters).

### Wind zone / terrain / reference height
- **ZONE** (Default: *) represents wind zone or base wind speed selection (windzone vs. speed depends on CODE).
- **CLAS** (Default: *) sets the **terrain category** (1 to IV or A to C depending on design code). It also supports code-specific mixed coast/inland options:
  - **K** mixed profile for coast (DIN)
  - **B** mixed profile for inland (DIN)
- **GH** (Groundlevel in system coordinates, Default: 0 m) defines the **origin of the wind coordinate system**, i.e., heights for profile generation are measured relative to this terrain level (not necessarily the structural coordinate system).

### Air and atmospheric parameters
- **RHO** (density of air, Unit: kg/m³, Default: 1.25) converts between velocity and pressure; assumed constant over the structure.
- **LAT** (latitude for ATMO, Unit: °, Default: “-”) influences the atmospheric boundary layer via Coriolis/Ekmann spiral effects; default nominally yields **f ≈ 0.0001** (per surrounding context).

### Reference speed/pressure and roughness definition
The table provides multiple ways to set the intensity level:
- **VB0** optional reference wind speed (Unit: m/s, Default: *), *or* it can act as a factor for season/wind direction corrections depending on design code.
- **VP0** optional explicit gust wind speed (Unit: m/s, Default: *).
- **QP0** optional explicit reference pressure (Unit: kN/m², Default: *).
- **Z0** optional explicit roughness length/height (Unit: m, Default: *).

If explicit profile details are supplied via another record (**WPRO**), **NORM/CODE selection may be ignored** for certain parts (as described in the narrative text).

### Near-ground behavior
- **HMIN** (height with constant wind speed, Unit: m, Default: *) sets the lower part of the wind profile where velocity is held constant and turbulence development is suppressed; if the design code doesn’t specify it, **10.0 m** is used.

### Wind direction and dynamic reference geometry
The remaining entries define the wind direction in the building coordinate system and the reference plane used for dynamic wind histories:
- **DX, DY, DZ** (Unit: –, Defaults: 0.0) define the wind direction vector; the table notes that at least one component is required.
- **XREF, YREF, ZREF** (Units: m, Defaults: 0.0/0.0/0.0) specify the **point in the reference plane** for dynamic wind generation (used with coherence requirements).
- **DXR, DYR, DZR** (Direction of the reference plane, Unit: –, Defaults: DXR: *, DYR: *, DZR: *) define the plane orientation; if not given, **DYR/DZR defaults enforce perpendicularity to the wind direction** (per context).

Overall, the table is a parameter schema enabling: (1) selection of a wind model/design code, (2) mapping to wind zone and terrain roughness conditions, (3) choosing reference intensity (speed/gust/pressure/roughness) and near-ground profile behavior, and (4) defining wind direction and spatial coherence reference geometry needed for dynamic simulations.

The input table provides an overview of how the **wind profile generation** (record **WIND**, including the selection of **NORM**) maps to different **design codes** and which **zone/roughness classification schemes** they use. It is organized into four conceptual rows: **Design code**, **Wind zones**, **Roughness classes / terrain category**, and **No. of edges/ridges**. The table primarily communicates which categorical inputs the software expects for each standard.

### 1) Design code row
This row lists supported standards as columns:
- **EN 1991-1-4**
- **ISO 4354**
- **DIN 1055**
- **VGB** (German guideline)
- **SIA 261**
- **SNI P 2.01.07** (shown as “SNI P 2.01.07”)

These indicate the wind modeling basis. In the text context, this selection is tied to choosing a **wind profile type** (logarithmic vs. code-specific), including how missing parameters for dynamic/transient analysis (gusts, turbulence, coherence) are auto-selected.

### 2) Wind zones row (default definition scheme)
Each column specifies the allowed **wind zone format** and/or default behavior:
- **EN 1991-1-4:** zones **1–9(2)** with default selected from a **country annex** (written as “country”).
- **ISO 4354:** zone specified as **VGB0** (the table cell indicates **VGB**-related naming; in the broader text, wind speeds can be defined via reference values like **VB0**).
- **DIN 1055:** zones **1–4(2)** (with “(2)” implying an indexed/alternative meaning per the DIN scheme).
- **VGB:** zones **1–4(2)**.
- **SIA 261:** zones **1–4(2)**.
- **SNI P 2.01.07:** zones **Ia–VII** (and also shows an additional default detail: “II”); meaning the code uses broader labeled categories (Ia…VII) but the default is **II**.

### 3) Roughness classes / terrain category row
This row defines the permitted **terrain roughness classification** for each design code:
- **EN:** **0, I–IV** plus “etc.” (implying additional code-defined options, with 0 as a special case; “etc.” suggests extended categories).
- **ISO:** **1–4**.
- **DIN:** **I–IV** with an additional mapping indicated as **K, B** (reflecting DIN’s terrain-dependent roughness/terrain parameter grouping).
- **VGB:** **I, II** and **II, IIIa** (shows that VGB distinguishes multiple terrain categories, including a subcategory “IIIa”).
- **SIA:** **II, IIIa** and **III, IV** (two-tier grouping; includes **IIIa** explicitly).
- **SNI P:** **A–C** (with a parenthetical **(B)**), indicating categories A/B/C and default likely **B**.

This row is crucial because the surrounding text explains that the wind profile height distribution depends strongly on **roughness height z0**, either explicitly or via a categorical terrain model (and that more detailed changing-terrain support exists via **WROU**).

### 4) No. of edges/ridges row
The final row specifies the number of edges/ridges supported/used for terrain influence:
- **EN:** 1  
- **ISO:** 1  
- **DIN:** 1  
- **VGB:** 0  
- **SIA 261:** 0  
- **SNI P:** 0  

This implies that only some codes (EN/ISO/DIN) model or require edge/ridge effects in the profile generation, while VGB/SIA/SNI P do not.

Overall, the table acts as a compact compatibility map: it tells a user (or system configuration logic) which **zone numbering scheme** and **terrain roughness categories** are valid when selecting a specific **NORM/design code** for generating the wind profile in **WIND**.

This table defines the parameters for the **WPRO wind profile** records (up to 9 individual height points) used to prescribe a wind profile within the broader WIND definition set. It lists each **Item** (parameter name), a concise **Description**, the associated **Unit**, and a **Default** indicator. The parameters together determine how wind speed and turbulence characteristics vary with height.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter identifier used in the input.
- **Description**: Meaning of the parameter in the wind model.
- **Unit**: Physical unit for the parameter (with internal numbering tags like 1001/1201/1006).
- **Default**: Whether a default value exists (`*`) or whether it must be explicitly provided (`!`).

### Parameters
1. **H** — *Height above ground*  
   - Unit: **[m]**  
   - Default: **`!` (mandatory for all WPRO-records)**  
   - Interpretation: Each WPRO record is anchored at a specific height. All specified WPRO records must provide **H** and the records must be **sorted by increasing H**.

2. **V** — *Mean value of wind speed (10-minute wind)*  
   - Unit: **[m/sec]**  
   - Default: `*` (optional depending on input completeness)  
   - Interpretation: The mean wind speed at the corresponding height. If only some parameters are provided, the system fills gaps using SOFiLOAD.

3. **VBOE** — *Gust wind peak value (5-second wind)*  
   - Unit: **[m/sec]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Peak gust speed corresponding to the height. The guidance states that, per Karman, **VBOE should equal**:  
     **VBOE = V + ψ · TLON**, where ψ depends on **LLON** and **V**. This ties gust formulation to turbulence/length scale parameters.

4. **TLON** — *Longitudinal turbulence*  
   - Unit: **[m/sec]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Turbulence intensity in the wind direction. Used especially in gust prediction (via TLON in the VBOE relation) and possibly dynamic generation.

5. **TLAT** — *Lateral turbulence*  
   - Unit: **[m/sec]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Turbulence intensity transverse to the wind direction.

6. **TVER** — *Vertical turbulence*  
   - Unit: **[m/sec]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Turbulence intensity in the vertical direction.

7. **LLON** — *Effective longitudinal wave length \(L_w^x\)*  
   - Unit: **[m]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Turbulence length scale longitudinally; influences the ψ term and thus gust-speed relation.

8. **LLAT** — *Effective lateral wave length \(L_w^x\)*  
   - Unit: **[m]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Lateral turbulence length scale.

9. **LVER** — *Effective vertical wave length \(L_w^x\)*  
   - Unit: **[m]**  
   - Default: `*`  
   - Interpretation: Vertical turbulence length scale.

### Practical implications for RAG use
- The **WPRO mechanism overrides** recent **NORM** or **ATMO** definitions: once any WPRO record set is provided, only explicit WPRO values are used thereafter.
- Input may be **sparse and incomplete**: partial specification such as only **H + V** or **H + VBOE** per record is allowed; missing values and gaps are filled by **SOFiLOAD**.
- **Dynamic wind generation** requires turbulence parameters (TLAT/TVET and corresponding wavelengths LLAT/LVER etc.), whereas **pure static wind design** can ignore their detailed importance.

See also: WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WSPE, WGEN
 WPRO
 Enables the definition of individual wind profiles by up to 9 WPRO records. The value of the height H must be specified for all WPRO-record and the list must be sorted by increasing H values.
 Any single WPRO-definition will invalidate all recent NORM or ATMO definitions. Only the explicit WPRO definitions will be used from then.
 The input of the values does not need to be complete or consist of uniform types of values. A simple value of H, V or VBOE will be sufficient. Gaps will be filled by SOFiLOAD on its own as reasonable as possible. Physically contradictions will be corrected as far as possible. Thus the following input definitions are possible:
 LC 100
 WIND DY 1
 WPRO 50 V 52.5
 defines a logarithmic profile with a prescribed wind velocity at a height of 50 m for a terrain roughness of 0.050 m (farmland); or
 LC 8200
 WIND DY 1 WPRO 15 V 30 WPRO 30 VBOE 58 WPRO 45
 WIND DY 1
 TLON 5.55 TVER 2.22 LLON 250
 enforces a not really sound or even matching set of all characteristic parameters.
 In such a case with not really clear definitions, which might be a real case if only sparse data is available for the site of the structure, it is strongly recommended to check the diagrams created by SOFiLOAD (especially picture No 3.) and modify the input in such a way until a reasonable
 smooth wind profile is obtained. According to Karman, the value VBOE should be equal to V + ψ · TLON, where ψ is 2.65 – 0.433 * 1-0.5772*ln(LLON/V)**2.
 The lateral and vertical turbulences as well as the corresponding wave length will be needed only in case of a dynamic wind generation. Their input is of no importance therefore for purely static wind design.

The input table defines parameters for **WROU (R9)**, i.e., the **roughness profile of the terrain on the “lee” (luv-side) of the wind-exposed structure** used by SOFiLOAD to compute wind and gust velocity distributions. The profile is represented as a set of up to **9 consecutive sections** extending from the structure outward. Each section has an associated **distance** from the structure and a **roughness value** for that section.

### Table structure (columns)
- **Item**: Parameter name (e.g., `SEA`, `A1`, `R1`, …).
- **Description**: Meaning and modeling intent of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Measurement unit shown in bracket notation.
- **Default**: Default value used if the parameter is not specified.

### Parameters and units
#### SEA (coastal special treatment)
- **Item**: `SEA`
- **Description**: “Distance to the Sea”
- **Unit**: `[km]`
- **Default**: `-200`
- **Meaning**: Controls a special modeling approach for **coastal regions**, intended to prevent wind speed overestimation by representing a **smooth transition between sea and land**. The text indicates SEA creates a steadily increasing roughness profile derived from DWD North Sea measurements, and is intended only for **German North or Baltic Sea / flat-coast** conditions. It should not be used for steep/rocky coasts.

#### Section distances (A1–A9)
For each section *i* (1…9):
- **Item**: `Ai`
- **Description**: “Distance of i-th section to structure”
- **Unit**: `[km]`
- **Default**: `!` for A1 (implying it is required), and `-` for A2–A9 (optional/only used if more sections are defined).
- **Meaning**: Specifies where the section begins relative to the structure. Distances are treated as **(negative) values** in the underlying definition (start distance “to the structure” on the luv side up to 200 km). The model uses these distances to construct the roughness profile with changes occurring over specified ranges.

#### Roughness values (R1–R9)
For each section *i* (1…9):
- **Item**: `Ri`
- **Description**: “Roughness of section”
- **Unit**: `[m]`
- **Default**: `0.05` for `R1` and `0.05` for `R2`–`R8` shown; `R9` is also present in the table snippet with a default of `0.05`.
- **Meaning**: Defines the **roughness measure (z0 in literature)** for the fluid-flow integration constant. The text emphasizes that this value has **no direct physical meaning** despite relating to the commonly cited roughness length *z0*.  
- **Constraints**: Roughness values **> 1.0 m cannot be treated** by SOFiLOAD. If not otherwise provided, the default is **homogeneous roughness** `z0 = 0.050 m`.

### Key modeling implications from the accompanying text
- The roughness profile influences the **wind velocity profile** by creating a **bench (kink/bend)** at certain heights and a **jump in gust velocity profile**, depending on where roughness changes occur in distance from the structure.
- The model limits the profile complexity to **maximum 9 sections** with different roughness.
- An “influence width” with an aperture angle of **60°** is used to compute an effective mean roughness for the wind field.

Overall, this table configures either:
1) a **coastal-specific roughness gradient** via `SEA`, or  
2) a **piecewise-defined roughness profile** using up to nine `(Ai, Ri)` section pairs, defaulting to `Ri = 0.05 m` (homogeneous terrain) unless distances and roughnesses are overridden.

The table defines input parameters for **WTOP topological wind corrections** in a wind-profile generation workflow. It specifies the **type, geometric position, orientation, and dimensions** of a single or limited set of terrain features (e.g., hill, edge, ridge) used to approximate how local topography modifies wind speed distribution, based on wind-tunnel test evaluations (as referenced to Maier‑Erbacher). The elements are characterized in both **global coordinates** and **local directional axes**, and their influence on wind is controlled mainly through **height (H)** and **geometry placement/orientation**.

**Columns**
- **Item**: Parameter name.
- **Description**: Meaning of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Engineering unit used in the model.
- **Default**: Default value used if the parameter is not provided.

**Rows / Parameters**
1. **TYPE (LIT, default “!”)**  
   Selects the topological element type:
   - `HILL` = hill  
   - `EDGE` = edge  
   - `RIDG` = ridge  
   The default is unspecified/flagged (`!`), implying the user must define it.

2. **XM, YM, ZM (m, default 0.0)**  
   Global coordinates of the **epi-centrum** (summit or low point depending on definition).  
   - XM: x-coordinate  
   - YM: y-coordinate  
   - ZM: z-coordinate (elevation reference in global frame)

3. **DX, DY, DZ (unitless direction components, default 0.0)**  
   Defines the **direction/orientation of the main extension** and local axes:
   - **DX**: main extension direction component (with sign important for edges)  
   - **DY**: local x-axis component used to orient the feature’s geometry (hill/edge/ridge)  
   - **DZ**: local x-axis component (3D orientation)  
   Directional sign matters especially for **EDGE**, where the model assumes the **foot line of the elevation lies on the right-hand side of the direction vector**.

4. **H (m, default “!”)**  
   Height of summit above ground at the epi-centrum (relative height). Marked as required (`!`).  
   Interpretation (from accompanying context):  
   - **H > 0** generally **raises wind velocities** and smooths flow in the lower boundary layer, increasing mean velocity while reducing turbulence.  
   - **H < 0** applies opposite influence, but only the “favourable effect” is applied on the save side at **~50%** (as described).

5. **B (m, default 1000)**  
   Width in the **local y-direction** (breadth of the topological feature).

6. **L (m, default “-”)**  
   Length in the **local x-direction** (extent of the feature along the oriented axis).

**Implicit modeling constraints (from context)**
- Topology influence is **nonlinear**; superposition generally is not valid unless plan dimensions differ strongly.
- Standard-code-consistent handling typically allows limited formations; very large-scale elements (e.g., >50–60 km) are already included in atmospheric wind maps, so defining them would effectively **double-count** effects.
- Proper definitions should generally use **no more than two elements**, with one having ~10–30 km extension and the other 1–2 km local scale; invalid configurations trigger error messages.

This table documents the **WSPE** input options used to define the **power spectra of turbulence wind components** and the associated **coherence functions** for a *dynamic wind generation*. It is structured with four columns: **Item** (parameter name), **Description** (meaning/allowed variants), **Unit** (typically “—/LIT”, i.e., no physical unit or a language-defined literal), and **Default** (default value when not explicitly set). Several “see also” references (WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WGEN, WTST) indicate related wind-generation configuration blocks.

## Parameter groups

### 1) `TYPE` — wind spectral model selection (and optional directional spectra)
- **Meaning:** Selects the **general type** of wind spectra used for the turbulence model.
- **Unit:** `LIT` (literal/enumeration style).
- **Default:** `KARM`.
- **Supported values and descriptions:**
  - **KARM** – Karman (1948)
  - **CEN** – Eurocode EN 1991 (2005)
  - **DAVE** – Davenport (1967)
  - **HARR** – Harris (1970)
  - **KAIM** – Kaiman (1970) / Simiu / Scanlan
  - **FMV** – Fichtl/McVenil (neutral)
  - **FMU** – Fichtl/McVenil (unstable)
- **Directional explicit spectra overrides:**
  - **`LON`** – explicit **longitudinal** spectrum
  - **`LAT`** – explicit **lateral** spectrum
  - **`VER`** – explicit **vertical** spectrum  
  Each of these uses default `- / LIT` style entries, indicating that if you provide values here, they override or replace the internally selected spectrum for that direction.

- **`C3D`** – longitudinal factor
  - **Meaning:** A scalar factor controlling the 3D longitudinal contribution/scaling relative to the other directional components.
  - **Unit:** `—`
  - **Default:** `1.0`

### 2) `CTYPE` — coherence function model selection
- **Meaning:** Chooses the **form of the coherence function** used to correlate turbulence between locations/components.
- **Unit:** `LIT`
- **Default:** `ESDU`.
- **Supported values:**
  - **ESDU** – ESDU/Karman
  - **DAV1** – Davenport Wurzel
  - **DAV2** – Davenport Quadrat
  - **KREN** – Krenk

### 3) Coherence model parameters (coefficients / distance factors)
These parameters tune the numerical form of the coherence function for particular `CTYPE` choices. They have **no physical unit** (`—`) and include defaults—most clearly associated with the default `ESDU` coherence setup:

- **`KUU`** – coherency term for **ESDU**
  - **Default:** `0.2206`
- **`KUV`** – coefficients for “half value distance”
  - **Default:** `0.1136`
- **`KUW`** – distance where the coherence value diminishes
  by a factor of 2 (as described)
  - **Default:** `0.1136`
- **`KVU`** – additional coherence coefficient (listed after KUW)
  - **Default:** `0.1103`
- **`KVV`** – coefficient (appears twice in the table due to a duplicated row)
  - **Default:** `0.1672`
- **`KVW`** – duplicated row wording; treated as **same parameter name** in the table
  - **Default:** `0.1672`
- **`KWU`** – coherency for **Davenport/Krenk**
  - **Default:** `0.1103`
- **`KWV`** – coefficient “Cij” in the coherence equation
  - **Default:** `0.1672`
- **`KWW`** – appears as “no defaults so far” in the table
  - **Default:** `0.1672` is shown in the last row area, but the description explicitly indicates no defaults “so far”, suggesting either documentation inconsistency or a placeholder.

Overall, this table provides the **model selection controls (`TYPE`, `CTYPE`)** plus the **key numerical coherence parameters** (`KUU`, `KUV`, `KUW`, etc.), including explicit directional spectrum inputs (`LON`, `LAT`, `VER`) and a scaling factor (`C3D`).

The input table defines a set of **coherence-related parameters** for wind turbulence spectra in different **stability regimes** and for different **turbulence directions/components**. It is organized by row (flow stability and component) and by five columns: **type label**, and four numeric/model columns **C**, **β**, **r**, and **fₘ**.

### Columns
- **(Row label / component type)**:  
  Indicates the atmospheric stability and the turbulence component:
  - **neutral longitudinal**
  - **neutral lateral**
  - **unstable longitudinal**
  - **unstable lateral**

- **C**:  
  A dimensionless coefficient controlling the coherence model amplitude/scale.

- **β**:  
  A stability/height-dependent exponent. In the table it is expressed as a function of the form **(z/18)** with negative powers:
  - neutral longitudinal: **β = (z/18)^(-0.63)**
  - neutral lateral: **β = (z/18)^(-0.35)**
  - unstable longitudinal: **β = (z/18)^(-0.14)**
  - unstable lateral: **β = (z/18)^(-0.04)**
  
  This indicates that β approaches different magnitudes with height z relative to a reference height 18 (units implied by the governing model). More negative exponents (e.g., −0.63) imply stronger height dependence.

- **r**:  
  A second coherence-related shape parameter. It is given with height scaling:
  - neutral longitudinal: **r = 0.845**
  - neutral lateral: **r = 0.781**
  - unstable longitudinal: **r = 1.235**
  - unstable lateral: **r = 1.144**
  
  Larger r values for unstable conditions suggest different coherence decay/shape compared with neutral conditions.

- **fₘ**:  
  A scaling factor expressed as a product of a numerical coefficient and a height-dependent power:
  - neutral longitudinal: **fₘ = 0.03 (z/18)**
  - neutral lateral: **fₘ = 0.1 (z/18)^0.58**
  - unstable longitudinal: **fₘ = 0.04 (z/18)^0.87**
  - unstable lateral: **fₘ = 0.033 (z/18)^0.72**
  
  This encodes how the frequency-related scaling changes with height and differs across stability and component directions.

### Interpretation (high level)
Across all rows, the table provides **parameter sets for coherence/frequency scaling** as functions of **height ratio z/18**, separately for:
- **Longitudinal vs lateral** components (different C, β, r, fₘ values)
- **Neutral vs unstable** atmospheric stability (neutral generally has smaller r than unstable, while the exponents in β and the height scalings in fₘ differ subtly)

These parameters are intended to be used by the coherence/coherence-kernel model (as referenced in the surrounding text about Davenport/ESDU-style coherence handling), ensuring that coherence behavior varies systematically with both **turbulence direction** and **stability**.

The table defines a set of input parameters used to “test” a component (the parameter **TYPE**) by evaluating **coherence** between structural response points in space over frequency. The coherence is computed between a reference point and another point displaced along a specified direction, with optional comparison against the **Krenk/Davenport** coherence formulations.

### Parameter fields and meanings

- **TYPE (LIT, default “!”)**: Selects the component to be tested. The allowed options are grouped by direction:
  - **KUU, KUV, KUW**
  - **KVU, KVV, K VW**
  - **KWU, KWV, KWW**
  These indicate whether the component corresponds to translation/rotation coupling terms (as represented by KU*, KV*, KW* indices).

- **NEIG (–, default 0)**: Number of frequencies used for the computation.

- **LC (–, default 1)**: Load case number associated with the “first eigen value” baseline. This controls which eigen-solution is referenced.

- **XREF, YREF, ZREF ([m]^1001, default 0.0)**: Coordinates of the reference point. These are the starting coordinates for the coherence calculation origin.

- **RX, RY, RZ ([m]^1001, default 0.0)**: Spatial offsets defining the second point and the direction of separation. The comparison point is:
  \[
  (X_{REF}+RX,\; Y_{REF}+RY,\; Z_{REF}+RZ)
  \]
  The displacement vector also defines the coherence “along the direction (RX, RY, RZ).”

- **COMP (LIT, default KREN)**: Selects the comparison curve / reference coherence model:
  - **DAV1** = Davenport, 1977  
  - **DAV2** = Davenport, 1968  
  - **KREN** = Krenk, 1995  
  This governs which analytical formulation is used as the comparison baseline when parameters are provided.

- **CU, CV, CW ([ ], default “-”)**: Coefficients “according Krenk/Davenport.” They are used to compute the Davenport/Krenk comparison curve. If these are specified, the table’s computation includes a Krenk/Davenport-based reference curve.

### Behavioral context (how the parameters affect output)
The coherence calculation has two modes:

1. **If no frequencies are selected (NEIG effectively 0 / no frequency list)**: coherence between the two specific points \((X_{REF},Y_{REF},Z_{REF})\) and \((X_{REF}+RX, Y_{REF}+RY, Z_{REF}+RZ)\) is plotted versus frequency expressed as **\(n \cdot r / U\)**.

2. **If frequencies are selected**: coherence is computed from the reference point **along the specified direction** \((RX, RY, RZ)\) for all selected frequencies, and plotted/presented accordingly.  
Additionally, if **CU–CW** are provided, a **Krenk/Davenport** comparison curve is added. The context notes that Davenport has two common variants: one where the **coherence itself** is targeted, and another where **coefficients for the square root of the coherence** are used.

Overall, the table is essentially a configuration schema for selecting the response component, specifying the spatial points/direction and reference eigen/load context, and optionally providing analytical model coefficients for Krenk/Davenport coherence comparison.

### Table: Wind field / wind load generation parameters (WGEN / WSPE context)

This table specifies the configuration items for generating stochastic wind loads or transient wind fields in the analysis. The overall workflow implied by the table is: choose a **basic wind load case** (identified elsewhere by an LCG such as LC 300), then use **SPECS/SP E C** options to define what kind of wind loading is produced (static mean/gust or turbulent components), optionally control turbulence coherence, and finally define the **time and frequency discretization** needed to generate wind histories. It also includes options for visualization output and database import/export of generated histories.

#### Key columns
- **Item**: Parameter name used in the input.
- **Description**: What the parameter controls.
- **Unit**: Physical unit if applicable.
- **Default**: Default value when the parameter is not explicitly set.

---

### Row-by-row description

1. **LCG (Load case number of basic wind)**
   - Purpose: Selects the *basic wind load case number* that the wind generation refers to. This is the anchor for stochastic generation, where random sequences are tied to a load-case-based initialization in the broader process description.

2. **SPEC (Generate wind load or transient wind fields)**  
   - Purpose: Controls the *type of loading field(s) to generate*. The table documents the allowed keywords and their meaning:
     - **GUST**: Static wind load of peak pressures.
     - **MEAN**: Static wind load of reference mean wind (vb).
     - **TLON**: Longitudinal turbulent unit loading.
     - **TLAT**: Lateral turbulent unit loading.
     - **TVE R**: Vertical turbulent unit loading.
     - **U / V / W**: Generate only longitudinal / lateral / vertical component wind field respectively.
     - **Combinations**: “or combinations U V”, e.g., **UV**, **UW**, **VW**, **UVW** to create multi-component fields simultaneously.
   - Default: **MEAN** (i.e., if unspecified, it generates mean static wind loads).

3. **LCOH (account for local coherency)**
   - Purpose: Enables or disables modeling of **local coherence decay** of turbulence along the beam axis (mentioned in context as decay of coherency to simplify beam loading generation).
   - Options: **ON/OFF**
   - Default: **ON**

4. **T (Total time of wind loading)**
   - Purpose: Duration over which the wind loading history is defined.
   - Unit: seconds
   - Default: **600**

5. **DT (time step of wind loading)**
   - Purpose: Discretization step for the time history (wind evolution).
   - Unit: seconds
   - Default: **0.2**
   - Implication from context: DT must capture important structural response frequencies; for steady wind DT can be set to **0.0**.

6. **FMIN (minimum frequency of spectra)**
   - Purpose: Lower bound of the turbulence spectral content.
   - Unit: Hz
   - Default: **0.0**

7. **FMAX (maximum frequency of spectra)**
   - Purpose: Upper bound of turbulence spectral content; must exceed important structural resonance frequencies to properly excite them.
   - Unit: Hz
   - Default: **1.0** (per table; context notes defaults are oriented to large bridges, may need adjustment for smaller structures).

8. **FDEL (resolution of spectra)**
   - Purpose: Frequency increment used to discretize spectra; must be small enough to avoid non-natural periodicity artifacts in the generated wind.
   - Unit: Hz
   - Default: **0.001**

9. **FLON, FLAT, FVER (explicit time functions for longitudinal/lateral/vertical)**
   - Purpose: Optional explicit time modulation functions. If provided, they define time behavior for the respective turbulence components instead of relying purely on the generated stochastic process.
   - Unit: “–” (no unit indicated)
   - Default: not specified (blank in table)

10. **HTYP (Selection for wind history visualisation)**
   - Purpose: Controls which wind history representation(s) are stored for visualization.
   - Default: none listed

11. **NR0 … NR1 … NR9 (controls what is saved for visualization; up to 10 entries)**
   - Purpose: Defines the selection of elements/types whose wind histories are shown in visualization.
   - Allowed tokens:
     - **BEAM, TRUS, CABL, QUAD, NODE**
   - NR0 is described as the start; NR1–NR9 extend up to 10 selections.
   - Default: none listed

12. **SHOW (Interval to save visualisations)**
   - Purpose: Frequency/stride of saving visualization outputs over time.
   - Default: **10**

13. **FROM (Name of a database with existing history)**
   - Purpose: Import previously generated wind histories from another database (secondary source).
   - Unit: **LIT*** (special literal/type marker)
   - Default: none

14. **TO (Name of a database to receive history)**
   - Purpose: Destination database where generated histories are stored (and possibly later merged).
   - Unit: **LIT***  
   - Default: none

---

### How to interpret the table for RAG usage
This table functions as a schema for wind input generation: it defines **(1) what wind loading to generate (SPEC), (2) whether coherence decay is applied (LCOH), (3) how the wind is discretized in time (T, DT) and frequency (FMIN, FMAX, FDEL), (4) how optional component-specific time functions can override behavior (FLON/FLAT/FVER), and (5) how outputs/inputs are handled through visualization selections (HTYP/NR*/SHOW) and database import/export (FROM/TO).**

 WGEN
 Based on the wind profile and parameters including, turbulence and integral length distribu- tions, defined with the basic load case LFG a transient sequence of loadings will be generated with measured or random wind loading.
 The random properties are assured by the load case number, which is also used as the ini- tialization value for the random sequence. The required number of wind histories has to be derived from the safety concept of the building. For the common design codes and safety factors for wind a number of 11 histories should be adequate in most cases.
 The wind definition thus starts with the basic wind load case, e.g..
 LC 300 W TITL 'Wind basic load case'
 WIND DY 1 XREF 0 0 0 DXR 0.1 1.0 GH 5.0 WROU 0.02 ; WPRO H 100 VBOE 65 ; WTOP ... WSPE EN:DIN
 For a spectral analysis the options TLON, TLAT and TVER create the quasi-static loading based on the turbulence intensity. If the base case has been analyzed, the obtained mean rotations of the sections will be accounted for. The background response may be specified with PSI0 at the load case.
 Selecting components with SPEC, the generation of the individual spectra and wind histories ist triggered. As this is somehow time consuming, it is highly recommended to check first the base load case thoroughly in all details. With the above defined base load case 300 we have:
 LC 301 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 302 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 303 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 ....

content:
LC 301 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 302 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 303 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 .....
 It is possible to change the spectra individually for some histories. In that case WSPE has to be defined with all parameters between the LC and the WGEN definition again. It is also possible to import wind spectra or even complete histories from a secondary data base FROM.
 The generation of the wind history has two steps. The first step (spectra generation) will create form the energy spectra based on the theory given inKovács and Andrä [22] and Kovács [23] an individual Fourier-spectrum for this load case (a discrete Fourier-Integral) for all turbulence components of all nodal points of the structure. The second step (history generation) will then create the discrete wind history via a discrete Fourier-transformation. The spectra generated once may be used for different wind histories: e.g. variant durations of wind, variant time steps or the selection of lower or higher frequencies of turbulence etc..
 The generated windhistories for selected elements may be saved in the database for graphical visualisation with DYNR. The individual components are then available with types V-X, V-Y and V-Z, CFD-Boundary conditions with types U, V and W.
 Some parameters of wind generation (e.g. DT, FMAX, FDEL) may be selected by the user, they have to match however. The frequency step FDEL has to be small enough, otherwise a non natural periodicity of the wind load may be obtained. DT has to be chosen in such a way that all important frequencies of the structure are properly addressed. An optional value of FMAX has then to be larger that those important structural resonance frequencies. For the case of a steady wind it is possible to specify DT 0.0 as special case.
 The wind generation will become very costly on the other side if the parameters are chosen to generous, thus it might be necessary to choose a best compromise. FMAX and FDEL may
 be also changed for tests or prechecks in the evaluation phase of a project to have shorter response times. For the final design however, the parameters should match the statistic nec- essaries. The defaults are selected based on the needs for large bridges. for smaller structures modifications are necessary, e.g. reducing the value of DT, enlarging the value of FMAX.

The defaults are selected based on the needs for large bridges. for smaller structures modifications are necessary, e.g. reducing the value of DT, enlarging the value of FMAX..
 Within the generation of turbulence a decay of turbulence for the end point of an element based on the local decay of coherency along the beam axis is implemented allowing an easier generation of beam loading. For checks of the turbulence it might be requested to switch this option off via the definition of LCOH OFF.
 It is also recommended to start with a primary load case based on the static wind to keep the disturbances of the start up period as low as possible. The best start is to use the same wind field of the mean wind directly as a static load case for this purpose.
 For the static wind generation the wind velocities will be converted to classical loadings, which can be used in other programs as well. If the literal MEAN or GUST has an appendix ":E" the loads will be generated separately, thus the transverse loading is acting with a possible eccentricity in the WPAR referenece point.
 The volume of the data may become rather large, because a nonlinear history will create an own load case for every time step. That is why we recommend to use a separate copy of the database for every history. With the definition of the TO item, a clone of the current database is created containing all necessary data for the wind history analysis. After performing the analysis and all superpositions, the extreme values may be imported into the master via the program DBMERG.

This input table defines the parameters for **WIPT**, i.e., specifying the **coordinates of a wind-tunnel measurement (pressure/force) point** and—optionally—how that point is mapped onto an underlying wind-mesh for subsequent creation of an **influence-function-based areal load pattern**.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter keyword used in the input.
- **Description**: Meaning and purpose of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Expected unit/dimension for numeric entries (where applicable).
- **Default**: Value used if the parameter is omitted.

### Parameters

1. **X, Y, Z (Coordinates)**
   - **Description**: 3D coordinates of the measurement point.
   - **Unit**: `[m]^1001` (model unit scaling implied by `1001`).
   - **Defaults**: all **0.0**.
   - **Role**: These coordinates are essential for locating the measurement point relative to the wind-mesh elements. They are later used by **SOFILOAD** to determine which hull element (triangle/quadrilateral) the measurement point influences.

2. **GRP (Group in wind mesh, optional)**
   - **Description**: Identifies an optional **group** within the wind mesh, constraining where the measurement point is considered.
   - **Unit**: none (`–`).
   - **Default**: `–` (not set).
   - **Role**: Helps resolve ambiguity when multiple meshes/groups exist, ensuring the point is projected/interpreted in the intended region.

3. **TOL (Tolerance in projected direction)**
   - **Description**: Tolerance used in the **projected direction** when searching/matching the measurement point to the mesh.
   - **Unit**: `[m]^1001`.
   - **Default**: **0.01**.
   - **Role**: A numerical tolerance that affects point-to-element detection (e.g., whether the point is considered close enough to be mapped onto a particular element during projection).

4. **ELIM (Limit value for edge point detection)**
   - **Description**: Threshold controlling whether the measurement point is treated as:
     - **centre/inside an element** (0.0) → constant pressure over the element, or
     - **near an edge** (1.0) → bilinear influence shape.
   - **Unit**: none (`–`).
   - **Default**: **0.4**.
   - **Role in context**: Determines whether SOFILOAD uses:
     - a **constant** influence function for the whole element (point inside), or
     - a **bilinear** shape function near edges, with the nearest node potentially receiving a value **> 1.0** due to extrapolation consistent with corner/edge behavior.

5. **MNAM (Name of data base containing wind mesh)**
   - **Description**: References the data base/model containing the **wind mesh** used for mapping.
   - **Unit**: none; shown as `Lit *` (likely a literal/string reference).
   - **Default**: `!` (unspecified/placeholder meaning “required or user-provided”).
   - **Role**: Without MNAM, the program cannot locate the mesh elements onto which the measurement point influence function will be constructed.

### Overall functional meaning
Together, **X/Y/Z + MNAM** identify where each wind-tunnel pressure measurement lies in space and which mesh it should influence. **TOL** and **ELIM** govern geometric matching and whether the mapping behaves like a **uniform element pressure** or a **bilinear edge/corner extrapolated influence**, which is critical for correctly transforming discrete pressure points into equivalent distributed loads.

The image is a small schematic figure illustrating how discrete wind-tunnel measurement points can be converted into an areal pressure distribution via meshing. The overall layout shows two separate perspective panels on a white background, labeled “(a)” and “(b)”, representing two different strategies for placing measurement points relative to a coarse finite element mesh.

**Panel (a)** (left side):
- A rectangular planar surface is drawn in perspective (tilted quadrilateral viewpoint).
- Inside this surface are multiple small **blue circular markers** representing measurement data points distributed across the area.
- A coarse grid is overlaid using **black or dark green dashed lines** that form a rectangular mesh pattern. The dashed lines indicate the boundaries of elements (e.g., triangles/quadrilaterals) used for interpolation.
- The blue markers appear positioned such that each measurement point is **closer to the center** of an element. This is visually emphasized by the fact that markers do not consistently lie on element corners; instead they are distributed within the grid cells.
- Two dashed directions are visible, creating several mesh rows and columns. The markers are placed such that the grid cells each contain one nearby measurement point, matching the description of option (a).

**Panel (b)** (right side):
- Another perspective rectangular surface is shown, but with fewer blue measurement points visible (approximately four).
- The mesh is also represented by **dashed lines**, but the points are arranged differently: several points are nearer to **element corners or along edges** rather than centrally located within a cell.
- One blue marker near the top-left is close to a dashed boundary intersection; another lies near a different corner/edge region. The distribution suggests a “bilinear/corner” influence behavior where interpolation values may extend beyond 1.0 near the closest node, consistent with the described method when a measurement point is near an edge.

**Caption/annotation:**
- Beneath the panels, there is a caption: **“Figure 6.7: Meshing of measurement points”**.
- The labels **(a)** and **(b)** identify the two meshing approaches.

**Relevance to the provided context:**
- The visual distinction directly corresponds to the described two meshing possibilities: (a) data points near the **center** of elements leading to nearly constant pressure per element, versus (b) data points near **corners/edges** leading to **bilinear influence functions** with possible extrapolated values greater than 1.0 at the nearest node.

See also: WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WSPE
 WIPT
 Using a wind tunnel experiment a model of the building is tested yielding integral forces or pressures in discrete points. They vary along time and it is depending on the structure if the loading may be taken as quasi static mean value or if the dynamic effects should be modelled. To convert those pressures to loadings the recommended procedure is as follows:
 • For every measured data item a separate load case is defined.
 • Then a unit pressure of 1.0 is applied in that data point while all other data points have the value of 0.0. This yields a areal distribution of pressure to be taken as influence function of the pressure in that point.
 • Each of this load cases may be taken as static or defined with FUNC as transient. In both cases the applied factors are the real pressures in that data point.
 Assuming that we have an area of the hull of our structure with several measurement data points, we may create a coarse mesh of triangles or quadrilaterals in two ways. We have either the possibility to create this mesh to have each data point near the center of one element (a) or in the corners or near the corners of a bilinear mesh (b):
 Than the coordinates of that selected data point are specified with WIPT. SOFILOAD will create an areal load pattern with the selected shape of the influence function. If the point is inside
 the element a constant pressure for the whole element is created. if the point is near the edge (ELIM) a bilienar shape function is assumed with the value 1.0 in the data point and 0.0 in the distant nodes. Thus the node nearest to the data point will have an extrapolated value > 1.0.
 The influence functions may be then used directly within DYNA or may be converted with STEP to single load cases for ASE.
 Values for ELIM, TOL and MNAM are retained as default for all following definitions.

The image is a technical diagram illustrating **wave loading on an offshore or coastal structure**. The scene is a vertical cross-section of the ocean (blue water domain) with a **cylindrical pile/column** standing on the seabed. The structure is located on the right side of the figure. A **water surface** is shown near the top, with the wave crest region simplified as a curved interface.

Key elements include:

- **Incoming wave propagation:** A **horizontal arrow labeled “c”** at the left indicates the wave travels toward the structure.
- **Coordinate system:** Axes are indicated within the water. A **horizontal arrow “vx”** points to the right, and a **vertical arrow “vy”** points upward, representing the water particle velocity components.
- **Water flow field:** Multiple small arrows appear along the sloping wave-induced flow region, suggesting the **relative water motion due to the wave** as it approaches and passes the structure.
- **Structure geometry:** The pile has a diameter **“D”** shown at the top via a dimension line, indicating the characteristic length for drag/inertia calculations.
- **Force representation:** Two sets of red arrows labeled **“F”** point generally along the direction of interaction with the pile:
  - One set aligns with drag-like effects (depending on the schematic, shown as red arrows on the side facing the flow).
  - Another set corresponds to inertia-related effects. The red arrows are distributed over the height where wave action occurs, implying **wave-induced forces along the structure**.
- **Free surface elevation reference:** A **black dashed horizontal line** marks a reference level in the water (often representing the still-water level or wave elevation reference).
- **Depth/vertical reference:** A “z” label appears near the structure, indicating depth or vertical coordinate relative to the reference level.
- **Mathematical context:** At the bottom, a formula is visible for the combined wave force using a Morison-type expression:
  \[
  F = F_d + F_i = \frac{1}{2}\rho C_d D U^2 + \frac{\pi}{4}\rho C_{hyd} D^2 \frac{\partial U}{\partial t}
  \]
  This indicates **drag (quadratic in velocity)** plus **inertia (proportional to acceleration)**, with parameters for water density \(\rho\), drag coefficient \(C_d\), hydrodynamic/added-mass coefficient \(C_{hyd}\), diameter \(D\), and flow velocity \(U\).
- **Caption/title:** The figure is captioned **“Figure 7.1: Wave Loading.”**

Overall, the diagram conveys that a large-scale, wind-generated stochastic wave field leads to local wave kinematics. When evaluating forces on a submerged cylinder, the formulation separates the wave field from the structure’s presence for kinematics and then accounts for structural motion via **relative velocities and accelerations** in the Morison equation.

Waves on the ocean are primarly created by wind over longer distances. They are an essential loading for embedded structures in the coastal regions or offshore. Wave theories are approximations to reality. When looking at the sea surface, it is typically irregular, three-dimensional and changes in time. The complexity of this time-varying 3 − D surface cannot be adequately described in its whole, and thus simplifying assumptions must be employed in order to arrive at estimates able to represent it.
 The simplest mathematical representation of oceanic waves is provided by the linear wave theory. Linear theory is described by freely propagating, small in amplitude, harmonic waves. The main requirement for the linear theory to apply is that the amplitudes of the waves are small, i.e. small compared with the wave length and small compared to the water depth. This linear theory is also called Airy and can cover many engineering problems with reasonable accuracy.
 When wave heights become larger, the linear theory may not be adequate and finite amplitude wave theories have to be used. These theories are nonlinear and allow formulation of waves that are not purely sinusoidal in shape. For steep waves or waves in shallow water, e.g. waves with flatter troughs and peaked crests, higher order theories will be described such as the Stokes wave theory and the Cnoidal wave theory. Furthermore, the stretching of linear theory is introduced, which compensates for the small amplitude assumption and maps the results into the finite region of their extent.
 Adopting a wave theory, care must be taken to ensure that the wave phenomenon of interest is described reasonably well by the theory, since offshore design depends on the ability to predict sufficiently wave surface profiles and water motion.

**Table 7.2: Stretching Formulas for Horizontal Velocity \(v_x\)**

This table provides explicit expressions for the *horizontal component of particle velocity* \(v_x\) for wave kinematics under a **linear (Airy) wave framework**, modified by a **stretching/compression scheme** to account for waves reaching the actual (possibly finite-amplitude) instantaneous free surface level, rather than using the fixed mean-level reference inherent to linear theory.

The table is organized as a set of alternative formula rows, each corresponding to whether the vertical coordinate \(z\) lies **above or below** the **SWL (Still Water Level)**. It introduces the standard wave parameters used in Airy theory:

- \(\omega\): wave angular frequency  
- \(\alpha\): wave horizontal factor (commonly \(k\), the wavenumber)  
- \(k\): wavenumber  
- \(d\): water depth  
- \(t\): time  
- \(x\): horizontal coordinate  
- \(z\): vertical coordinate measured relative to a datum associated with SWL (as implied by the stretching procedure)

A common phase term appears in all rows:  
\[
\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
indicating a traveling wave in the \(+x\) direction.

### Expressions and how they depend on \(z\)

1. **For a stretched velocity distribution above SWL (\(z+d\) scaling):**  
   \[
   v_x = \omega \alpha \,
   \frac{\cosh\left[kd + z + d\right]}{\sinh(kd)} \,
   \cos(kx-\omega t)
   \]
   (shown in the table as a cosh term with a shifted argument involving \(z+d\)).

2. **For the below-SWL region using the stretched coordinate in the denominator/argument:**  
   \[
   v_x = \omega \alpha \,
   \frac{\cosh\left[k(z+d)\right]}{\sinh\left[k(n+d)\right]} \,
   \cos(kx-\omega t)
   \]
   Here the table introduces another vertical reference \(n\), which is used in the stretching relation (described in the surrounding text) to map linear-theory elevations to the instantaneous surface. Practically, \(n\) functions as a counterpart to the instantaneous displacement used to perform vertical stretching/compression.

3. **Deep-water / Airy-consistent case for \(z>0\) (above a reference elevation):**  
   The table also includes a row for  
   \[
   v_x = \omega \alpha \,
   \frac{\cosh(kd)}{\sinh(kd)}\cos(kx-\omega t)
   \quad \text{for } z>0,\ \text{Airy for } z\le 0
   \]
   indicating that the velocity expression is treated as **constant with height** above the reference level (\(z>0\)), while retaining classical Airy dependence below it.

4. **Piecewise form blending Airy below SWL with linear stretching above it:**  
   A final row presents a piecewise bracketed expression:
   \[
   v_x = \omega \alpha
   \left[
     \frac{\cosh(kd)}{\sinh(kd)} + zk
   \right]
   \cos(kx-\omega t)
   \quad \text{for } z>0,\ \text{Airy for } z\le 0
   \]
   This indicates that above the reference elevation, the velocity is modified to include a term linear in \(z\), effectively representing the stretched velocity gradient.

### Purpose within the methodology

The surrounding text explains that linear-theory particle velocities are **scaled vertically** so that the velocity profile computed in linear theory is “aligned” with the **instantaneous wave surface**. This is described as: the original vertical coordinate \(z\) is replaced by a corrected/stretched coordinate such that \(z\) is adjusted from the mean SWL reference \(d\) and instantaneous surface elevation (related to \(n\)) via a transformation of the form \(d' = \frac{d+n}{d+\eta}\, \cdots\) (the table section refers to the substitution accomplished in Eq. 7.11).

Overall, Table 7.2 is a compact reference for how to compute \(v_x\) in a **linear wave model with nonlinear kinematic effects introduced through vertical stretching/compression**, typically used to better represent near-surface flow kinematics for linear/random waves and to improve design-related load estimates near the free surface.
