**Spectral discretization and seed behavior (from the context):**
- The table ties the irregular wave realization to a **random generator seed equal to the load case number**. This means stochastic wave amplitudes are reproducible per load case.
- It also supports an alternative to default constant frequency spacing: **irrational frequency discretization** can be requested by adding a literal **`:I`** to the spectra type (e.g., **`JONS:I`**), or using a stretching scheme such as **`JONS:IW`**.

**TMA parameterization:**
- For the **TMA spectrum**, the table/narrative states that default parameters **γ** and **α** are taken from **Eq. 7.23 as described by Hughes [40]**. This parameterization allows specification of the equilibrium wind sea spectrum for a given energy level, whereas providing explicit values (e.g., a JONSWAP with γ = 3.3 and α = 0.0081) would effectively transform JONSWAP to a **shallow water spectrum**.

Overall, this input table defines how to model waves either as a **single design wave** or—more commonly for this section—as an **irregular spectrum** characterized by **H (significant height)** and **T (peak period)**, plus spatial placement, water and current properties, and spectral discretization controls (NF, TMIN/TMAX).

 Instead of the single design wave a complete spectra of an irregular wave field may be used. In that case H is the siginficant wave height, while T is the peak period of the spectra. The seed for the random generator is the load case number. Values of NF, TMIN, TMAX etc. are used only for that case.
 Furthermore, the irrational frequency, rather than the default constant frequency interval, can be applied for the calculation of the amplitudes, when using a spectrum. This is done by specifying the literal :I after the input spectra type, e.g. JONS:I or with a stretching scheme JONS:IW.
 For the TMA spectrum, the default values used here for the parameters γ and α are given by Eq. 7.23, as described by Hughes [40]. The main advantage of this parameterization is the ability to specify the equilibrium wind sea spectrum associated with a given energy level. Otherwise a standard input could be given as in JONSWAP spectra, such as for example γ = 3.3 and α = 0.0081, which will just transform the corresponding JONSWAP to a shallow water spectrum.
 The wave kinematics may be enhanced by a constant current. For this an exponential distribu- tion may be specified. For the exponent α a value of 0.17 is found in the literature.

The snow loading in SOFiLOAD is just at the beginning of the total development.
 Wehen defining the design code with NORM it is possible to define the snow zone and the alti- tude about sea level. From those values a basic snow load is derived according the provisions of the design codes.
 • The basic snow load is defined in SOFiLOAD according to EN-1991-1-3 for the climate regions following appendix C according to table C.1 dependant on the country code and the Z-value defined at NORM SNOW (1,2,3,4 or 4.5), and the altitude.
 • For Germany, Austria and Switzerland the national documents have been provided instead: DIN (Zones 1,1a,2,2a and 3), OENORM (2*,2,3,4) and the SIA 261.
 • For Italy the national document DM 2005 with Snow Zones I,II,III according table 3.5 has been implemented.
 Snowloads are available for all free loadings of type LINE and AREA as load type SNOW. The load value then defines the form factor wich is used to be multiplied with the basic snow load on the ground, depending on the inclination of the roof and local aglomerations.
SOFiLOAD enables the transfer of support forces from another database (source) to the cur- rent model (target). This makes it possible, for example, to model the floors of a building independently.

There are essentially two different ways to assign support loads of the source geometry to target geometries: i) manually, by linking the respective involved structural lines (SLN) and structural points (SPT), or ii) (partially) automatically.
 The magnitude and shape of the resulting point and line loads result from the load transfer function and whether the target geometries act independently or as a unit (see modes for target geometries).

1:1 assignment is the simplest (but most elaborate) form of load transfer. Here, support forces of a source geometry are directly assigned to a target geometry, typically source-SLN ↔target- SLN, or source-SPT ↔target-SPT. It is also possible to concentrate support forces of structural lines on a column or to ’smear’ individual support forces on a wall. Whole groups can also be linked together (see Figure 9.1).

content:
Selecting all sources (SRCT ALL) ensures that all loads from the source geometry are cap- tured. With TRGT FALL, all load bearing SLNs and SPTs of the source geometry are duplicated (see Figure 9.3). If the source and target groundplan differ, it is not guaranteed that all loads will be transferred correctly – so loads may fall through openings.
 $ All loads from the source fall down
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT ALL TRGT FALL TYPE MOMT FROM "source.cdb"

The image is a schematic technical diagram (likely from a structural analysis/FEA software manual) showing how automatically assigned loads from a *source line* can be corrected using “OPT IGN” (Ignore) and “OPT MOD” (Modification). Three subfigures labeled **a)**, **b)**, and **c)** depict successive situations.

A horizontal **target structural line** is labeled **103** and is supported by three **structural points** (SPTs) labeled **11**, **12**, and **13** beneath that line. Above, a **source line** is labeled **203**, with multiple small vertical arrow glyphs indicating applied loads distributed along the source. The diagram emphasizes that the automatic targeting can misassign loads: instead of connecting to the intended supporting elements under line 103, the loads may attach to incorrect supports or an unintended line.

- **Subfigure a) (initial situation):** The loads on the source line **203** appear to be distributed automatically to the target system. The text/context indicates that the target line **SLN 103** is mistakenly ignored or misinterpreted, leading to loads not being applied correctly to the intended supports.

- **Subfigure b) (IGN example – ignoring target line):** The **target line 103** is treated as ignored. The load arrows are shown redirected so that the three supports (SPTs **11**, **12**, **13**) closest to the source loads receive them. A central vertical load arrow is drawn down toward **SPT 12**, while additional arrow lines fall toward **SPT 11** and **SPT 13**, indicating the supports are effectively selected “by proximity” rather than by the correct structural line connection.

- **Subfigure c) (IGN example – ignoring source line):** The **source line 203** is ignored. Instead of transferring loads via line-based automatic selection, the loads are applied “manually” to the supports directly. The dashed red line suggests an implied connection/transfer path being bypassed or altered. The load arrows still end up on supports **11**, **12**, and **13**, but now the key point is that the source line is not used for automatic mapping.

Across the top, the image also includes red/green schematic icons and small plus-cross markers indicating node locations or structural points. The surrounding explanatory text (visible below/around the diagrams) describes the software options: **OPT IGN** to ignore either the target line (TRGT) or the source line (SRCT), and **OPT MOD** to correct mis-selections by inserting a **1:1 relationship** between a wrongly chosen target SPT and the intended one (e.g., linking **SPT 21** directly to **SPT 12** in the example).

The image is a textbook-style diagram illustrating how an application assigns loads from “source” geometries to “target” geometries, and how corrective options like **OPT IGN (Ignore)** and **OPT MOD (Modification)** can fix incorrect automatic assignments.

At the top-left, a simplified structural model shows two horizontal members (a top and bottom rectangle) connected by an **inclined diagonal column/bracing**. This represents an inclined column scenario where automatic nearest-neighbor mapping may choose the wrong target point.

The main content is two side-by-side subfigures labeled **(a)** and **(b)**. Each subfigure contains:
- **Green upward arrow** labeled **21** pointing at a small reference point (a structural point, SPT) located above the midline.
- **Black/gray small circular points** labeled **11** and **12** positioned on a horizontal dashed line (representing available target supports/structural points).
- A **red downward arrow** indicating the load direction (typically moment or force) being transferred onto the chosen target location.

### Subfigure (a): Initial incorrect situation
- The **source point SPT 21** (green upward arrow at the top) generates a load.
- That load is **incorrectly assigned to target SPT 11**.
- In (a), the **red downward arrow is positioned above the circular point labeled 11**, indicating the load is acting at SPT 11 rather than the intended support.
- The circular point labeled **12** is present but does not receive the load in this view.

### Subfigure (b): Corrected after applying MOD
- The same **source point 21** is shown again at the top.
- The red downward arrow now aligns with the circular point labeled **12**.
- This indicates that using **MOD** inserts a **1:1 relationship** within the task, directly linking **SPT 21 to SPT 12**, rather than relying on the automatic proximity-based selection that previously chose SPT 11.

At the bottom of the image, accompanying text begins with “**6: Option MOD:** a) Initial situation: load from SPT 21 is incorrectly assigned to the boundary SPT 11 … b) With MOD, the load from SPT 21 is first removed from the selection of sources and then added as a 1:1 assignment.” This text reinforces that the figure demonstrates the workflow for correcting the target mapping for an inclined column using the MOD option.

Overall, the image focuses specifically on the **MOD correction mechanism**, contrasting an incorrect initial target assignment (SPT 11) with the corrected assignment (SPT 12).

For many applications it makes sense to select all loads (SRCT ALL) and then either drop them (TRGT FALL), or automatically assign them to the target geometry (TRGT AUTO). However, as described, in these cases it can happen that the target geometries were selected incorrectly or loads slip through an opening. The OPT MOD (Modification) and OPT IGN (Ignore) options can be used to correct the assignment.
 Example Ignore IGN: In Figure 9.5 a loaded wall ends in three columns. In the target geometry at this point there are three structural points (SPTs 11, 12 and 13) for the columns as well as the structural line SLN 103, which could come from the meshing of the plate, for example. The automatic target selection is not able to detect the supporting columns correctly. Various modifications can be made with IGN to apply the load correctly to the supports.

 b) The target line SLN 103 is ignored. Thus the three supports are closest to the loads from SLN 203 and are loaded accordingly.

 LTD OPT IGN TRGT SLN TRG 103
 c) The source line 203 is ignored and the loads are applied to the supports ’by hand’. Here it is also possible to let the three supports act as one unit (see modes for target geometries) and transfer the moment from the source line SLN 203.
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT ALL TRGT AUTO TYPE MOMT FROM "source.cdb"

The table describes the input schema for the **LTD** command’s record fields, i.e., the parameters that control **transfer of loads from a source database/model to the current target model** as line and point loads. It also specifies the valid **option lists**, the **meaning** of each parameter, the **expected unit/type column placeholder**, and the **default values**.

**Row groups and field meanings**

- **OPT (supplementary option selector)**  
  “A literal from the following list” with enumerated sub-record types:
  - **TASK**: Task record (default indicated as `TASK`).  
  - **SEL**: Supplementary record to further refine the selection.  
  - **IGN**: Supplementary record used to ignore/remove a selection.  
  - **MOD**: Supplementary record for modifying the task.  
  Default for OPT is shown as **TASK**.

- **SRLC (load case id)**  
  Identifies the **load case** (source) whose loads will be transferred.  
  Unit column is blank/“—”, default is marked mandatory with **“!”** (no default).

- **SRCT (source geometry type)**  
  Selects what kind of geometry is used on the source side:
  - **SLN**: structural line  
  - **SPT**: structural point  
  - **GRP**: group  
  - **GUID**: GUID (only for source)  
  - **ALL**: all loads from all SLNs and SPTs  
  Default: **ALL**.  
  The table indicates that when SRCT is SLN/SPT/GRP/GUID, a corresponding **SRC** input is required.

- **SRC (source geometry identifier)**  
  Provides the **ID/GUID** of the source geometry requested by **SRCT**.  
  Default shown as “—” and depends on SRCT selection (mandatory if SRCT ≠ ALL).

- **TRGT (target geometry type)**  
  Selects target side geometry interpretation:
  - **SLN**: structural line  
  - **SPT**: structural point  
  - **GRP**: group  
  - **AUTO**: automatically detect target geometries  
  - **FALL**: “fall-down”; load-bearing source geometries are duplicated  
  Default: **AUTO**.  
  When TRGT is SLN/SPT/GRP, a **TRG** input is expected.

- **TRG (target geometry identifier)**  
  Provides the **ID** of the target geometry requested by **TRGT**.  
  No intrinsic unit; default is “—”.

- **LMAX (subdivision length for target geometries)**  
  “Subdivision length … (deactivated with 0.0)”.  
  Unit: **[m]**, default **0.0**.

- **TRGM (mode for target geometries)**  
  How transferred loads are handled across multiple target elements:
  - **INDI**: individual (each target finds/receives a distribution separately)  
  - **COMB**: combined (targets treated as one unit; total resultant distributed to all)  
  Default: **INDI**.

- **DZ (Z-offset / storey height offset for fall-down)**  
  Used specifically with **TRGT = FALL**.  
  Default **0.0**.

- **TYPE (type of load transmission)**  
  Controls the distribution function from source resultant to target loads:
  - **CONS**: constant line loads; conserves sum of forces  
  - **MOMT**: trapezoidal line loads; conserves sum of forces and moments (with feasibility for moment transfer)  
  - **TRAP**: positive trapezoidal line loads; prevents lifting forces; conserves forces but not necessarily moments  
  Default: **CONS**.

- **FACT (multiplication factor)**  
  “Factor by which all loads are multiplied”.  
  Default **1.0**.

**Overall interpretation**
This table defines how to parameterize LTD load take-down/transfer: select a **source load case** (SRLC), choose what **source geometries** to draw loads from (SRCT/SRC, with ALL as a shortcut), choose how **target geometries** are identified and treated (TRGT/TRG, AUTO vs FALL, and INDI vs COMB), then set the **transfer/distribution mechanics** (TYPE, LMAX, DZ, FACT) and optionally refine the operation using OPT sub-records (TASK/SEL/IGN/MOD).

### Table description: **LTD load take-down / load transfer command (and associated options)**

This table documents the **LTD** record used in a structural analysis workflow to **transfer/assign loads from a source database to the current model**. The command applies loads as **line loads** and **point loads** on the target geometries.

#### 1) Core meaning: **Factor (LTD)**
- **LTD** includes a parameter: **“Factor by which all loads are multiplied”**.
- Default/example value shown: **− 1.0** (no amplification; negative/relative sign is used depending on direction conventions).
- Conceptually, after load transfer, **all transferred loads are scaled** by this factor.

#### 2) Required sequencing with other records
- The table emphasizes that an **LTD record must follow a LC record** (load case creation).
- **LC creates a new load case** in the target database to which the loads are assigned.
- After the mention of **TASK** (load take down definition), **LTD TASK** is used to create a take-down. Then **any number of LTD SEL / LTD MOD / LTD IGN records can follow**.
- For these follow-up records, only **SRCT, SRC, TRGT, TRG** are interpreted; all other settings are inherited from the preceding **TASK** record.

#### 3) Selection mechanism: **OPT with SEL / IGN**
The table explains **LTD OPT**, which modifies geometry selection:
- **SEL**: selects multiple **source and/or target geometries**.
  - Example syntax patterns show selecting multiple source lines: `SRCT SLN` with `SRC 201,202,203`, and multiple targets: `TRGT SLN` with `TRG 101,102,103`.
- **IGN**: removes selected source/target geometries from consideration.
  - Used for “cut-out” corrections after an automatic transfer distribution.

#### 4) Load correction mechanism: **MOD**
- **MOD** enables an **intended 1:1 reassignment** within an LTD TASK.
- Typical use: with `SRCT ALL TRGT AUTO`, loads are automatically distributed, but some loads are misallocated.
- **MOD** is described as shorthand for: **LTD IGN** (remove erroneous source association) followed by a **new LTD TASK** (apply the corrected mapping to a specified target).
- Important note: with **MOD**, only the **source geometry** is removed/ignored; other loads that share the target can remain unchanged.
- Additional constraints: with MOD/IGN, source geometries (and thus associated support loads) are only removed if they are tied to **a single SLN** or if **all corresponding SLNs are removed**.

#### 5) Source/target identification: **SRC/TRG**
The table defines how to specify which structural elements are used:
- **SLN / SPT / GRP**:
  - Source: **SLN/SPT and/or group** and optionally **GUID** (GUID only for source).
  - If SRCT/TRGT requests such item types, the corresponding **input is mandatory**.
- **AUTO**:
  - Attempts automatic matching from all existing **structural lines (SLN)** and **structural points (SPT)** that could represent **walls or columns**.
  - Warns this can produce incorrect associations if source and destination floor plans differ; thus **verification is mandatory**.
- **FALL**:
  - “All load-bearing source geometries are duplicated.”
  - The destination geometry analysis is not performed; this can fail if floor plans contain openings or mismatches.

#### 6) Target geometry modeling mode: **FALL / INDI / COMB**
- The table has two target modeling approaches:
  - **Individual** (**INDI**): each target structure line/point finds nearest source loads and forms a load distribution based on selected transfer type **TYPE**.
  - **Combined** (**COMB**): all target geometries act as one unit; all source loads produce a total resultant that is distributed to all targets based on **TYPE**. Intended for modeling stiff connections (e.g., stiffening building core).

#### 7) Load transfer type: **TYPE = CONS / MOMT / TRAP**
Three distribution types are listed:
- **CONS**: constant line loads; **sum of forces is conserved**. Used for stiff connection behavior.
- **MOMT**: trapezoidal line loads including force and moment representation; **sum of forces and moments conserved** (moments conserved only if targets can take moment).
  - Note: for columns, an equivalent length **0.5 m** is assumed; columns transfer only point forces, so individual column transfer (mentioned via TRGM INDI/COMB) cannot transfer moments.
- **TRAP**: positive trapezoidal line loads; position determined geometrically by resultant location.
  - Prevents lifting forces; however, **sum of forces conserved but moments not conserved**.

#### 8) Direction and moment handling: **DIR and HMOM**
- **DIR** defines the load transfer direction and supports multiple selection:
  - Examples: `DIR XYZ`, `DIR XY` (all horizontal loads).
- **HMOM** de/activates transfer of moments generated from **horizontal forces over storey height**.
  - For moment transfer: horizontal force direction must be enabled (**DIR X/Y/XY**) and **TYPE MOMT** must be selected.
- HMOM supports:
  - Deactivation
  - **AUTO**: height calculated as mean distance between source and target geometry
  - **explicit**: user-specified height (shown as an example value like `5[m]`)

#### 9) Illustrative command examples
The table includes multiple short examples demonstrating:
- Mapping loads from source structural lines to target structural lines using **SRLC**, **SRCT**, **TRGT**, and database source: `FROM "source.cdb"`.
- Using `SRCT ALL TRGT AUTO` for automatic distribution.
- Using `SRCT ALL TRGT FALL` for duplicating load-bearing source geometries without target analysis.
- Modeling stiffening cores with combined targets (`TYPE MOMT`, `TRGM COMB` pattern).
- Transferring horizontal loads and resulting bending moments using `TYPE MOMT DIR XY HMOM ...`.

Overall, the table serves as a specification for configuring **LTD** load take-down: defining **scaling (factor)**, enforcing **record order**, selecting **source/target geometry sets**, enabling **automatic mapping**, and choosing **how loads distribute** spatially and directionally, including moment generation rules.

The input table documents parameters for a **load transfer command (LTD)**, specifically covering **load direction, whether to transfer moments derived from horizontal forces, and the source database specification**. It is structured as columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

### DIR — Load direction
- **Meaning:** Determines the **direction(s)** along which the loads are transferred.
- **Accepted literals:** Multiple selections are possible.
  - **X:** transfers support forces in the global **x-direction**
  - **Y:** transfers support forces in the global **y-direction**
  - **Z:** transfers support forces in the global **z-direction**
- **Unit column:** shows **LIT** (i.e., a literal keyword rather than a physical unit).
- **Default:** **Z**, meaning that by default only z-direction support forces are considered for transfer.
- **Context note:** DIR is referenced in the surrounding documentation as enabling selection like **DIR XYZ** (all loads) or **DIR XY** (all horizontal loads).

### HMOM — Bending moments from horizontal loads
- **Meaning:** Controls whether **bending moments** generated by **horizontal forces over the storey height** are included in the transfer process.
- **Accepted settings:**
  - **OFF:** moment transfer deactivated
  - **AUTO:** automatic height calculation
- **Unit column:** **LIT/−** (literal mode or no physical unit depending on the option)
- **Default:** **OFF** (no transfer of such moments unless explicitly enabled).
- **Important dependency (from context):** For moments to be transferred:
  1. **Horizontal force transmission must be activated** via **DIR X**, **DIR Y**, or **DIR XY**
  2. Transfer function **TYPE MOMT** must be selected

### FROM — Source database
- **Meaning:** Specifies the **name and path** of the **source database** from which the load-bearing geometries/loads are taken.
- **Unit column:** **LIT** (literal string input).
- **Default:** **!** (indicates **mandatory** input; the documentation emphasizes a required value).
- **Role in LTD workflow:** In example command sequences, `FROM "source.cdb"` precedes or accompanies selections of `SRCT`/`TRGT`, indicating the data origin for the transfer.

Overall, this table defines three key inputs controlling **what directional components are transferred (DIR)**, whether **additional bending moments derived from horizontal loading are included (HMOM)**, and where the **source load data is read from (FROM)**.

The table is a parameter reference for specifying geometry input coordinates and related metadata for an **LTDG**-style geometry definition workflow (as suggested by the surrounding context: points, lines, and arcs are created via `LTDG` calls after an `LTD OPT TASK`). It is organized into five columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Each row defines a specific input field and how it should be interpreted when constructing target geometries.

### Coordinate parameters
- **X1, Y1, Z1**: Coordinates of the **start point**.  
  - **Description**: X1 is the X-coordinate of the start point; Y1 is the Y-coordinate of the start point; Z1 is the Z-coordinate of the start point.  
  - **Unit**: `[m]1001` (meters).  
  - **Default**: `!` meaning **required** (no default provided).  
  - **Role in geometry**: For **points**, the instruction indicates only the coordinates for `P1(1, y1, z1)` are given (implying X1, Y1, Z1 are the defined location components depending on how the system maps `P1` fields). For **lines**, `P1` defines the **starting** end of the line segment.

- **X2, Y2, Z2**: Coordinates of a **second point** used to define a line end or an additional arc location.  
  - **Description**: X2/Y2/Z2 are the coordinates of point P2 or another geometry point depending on command context.  
  - **Unit**: `[m]1001`.  
  - **Default**: `*`, meaning **optional/conditional**—present when the selected geometry type needs it (e.g., a line requires both P1 and P2 coordinates).

- **X3, Y3, Z3**: Coordinates of a **circle/arc intermediate point**.  
  - **Description**: X3/Y3/Z3 define the coordinates of a circle point used for arcs.  
  - **Unit**: `[m]1001`.  
  - **Default**: `*`, meaning **optional/conditional**—needed only when defining an **arc**, where a third point lies between start and end on the arc.

### Geometry construction implications (from context)
- For **lines**, the table’s X1/Y1/Z1 plus X2/Y2/Z2 together define the line via start and end points (`P1(1, y1, z1)` and `P2(2, y2, z2)` conceptually matching the described input pattern).  
- For **arcs**, X1/Y1/Z1 (start), X2/Y2/Z2 (end), and X3/Y3/Z3 (intermediate point on the arc) are all required; the system automatically tessellates the arc into line segments, with segment density controllable by a preceding task parameter (e.g., via `LMAX`).

### Metadata fields
- **TITL**: Title / label for the task or dataset.  
  - **Unit**: `-` (none).  
  - **Default**: `LIT12` (a predefined title default).  
  - **Use**: Human-readable identification.

- **GUID**: Globally Unique Identifier.  
  - **Unit**: `-` (none).  
  - **Default**: `LIT36` (a generated or predefined identifier value).  
  - **Use**: Ensures uniqueness for referencing the configuration.

Overall, the table encodes which coordinate sets are mandatory (**X1/Y1/Z1**) versus conditional (**X2/Y2/Z2** and **X3/Y3/Z3**), aligning with the command behavior that `LTDG` can directly create points, lines, and arcs depending on how many point definitions are supplied.

sections: 9.6 LTDG – Load Take Down – Geometry Generation

content:
See also: LTD
 LTDG
 The LTDG command can be used to directly create points, lines and arcs for the target geome- tries. The LTDG command must follow a LTD OPT TASK. LTDG can be called several times and then adds more target geometries to the task (analogous to LTD OPT SEL).
 Note: If a coordinate x, y, z of a point is set, the remaining two must be specified as well.
 For the input of a point, only the coordinates for P1(1,y1,z1) are to be given.
 Lines: To enter a line, enter the coordinates for the starting point P1(1,y1,z1) and the ending point P2(2,y2,z2).
 Arcs: To enter an arc, all points must be specified. Note that the point P3(3,y3,z3) lies between the start and end point on the arc. The arc is automatically divided into line segments. If the subdivision is too coarse, it can be controlled in the preceding TASK with the LMAX command.
 LTD SRLC 1
 FROM "source.cdb"
 SRCT SLN SRC 201 $ Choose source LTDG X1 1 2 3 LTDG X1 0 0 0 x2 10 0 0 $ Choose target-line LTDG X1 0 0 0 x2 10 0 0 x3 5 1 0 $ Choose target-arc
 LTD SRLC 1. FROM "source.cdb”
 $ Choose target-point
